text:
An auto-parts bankruptcy in Ohio reached a DeFi lending market through a fund administrator's spreadsheet. And the thing that nearly broke wasn't the credit. It was the plumbing around it.

The market uses a tokenized private credit fund as collateral. Early this year it sat at roughly 94% off-chain private credit against a 6% onchain USDC buffer. That ratio is the whole problem in one number: a vault promising DeFi-style access while holding an asset that lives in a fund administrator's records.

Tokenized private credit doesn't have a price. It has a valuation, produced off-chain on a schedule set by fund law and accounting practice, in this case weekly, then pushed onchain through a feed three separate parties have to agree reconciles. A lending market wants a live number every block. Those two clocks were never going to match. When a new valuation lands, every borrower's LTV moves at once, in a single step.

That's what happened. A default linked to the First Brands bankruptcy was marked down by the administrator, and the markdown flowed into the token's NAV. It was small, around 2%. The credit wasn't the crisis. The crisis was that a rumor moves in hours while the price it's arguing with moves once a week, so in between, the market trades against a number that can't respond. Separately the plumbing lagged the price, with reported price and collateral drifting out of line for a stretch in January.

The sharper problem: you can't liquidate this collateral fast even once the price is right. It redeems on a rolling 30-day basis, so whoever seizes it carries duration risk no crypto liquidator normally touches. The market was built with a discount oracle, a roughly 7.7% haircut on top of a 91.5% liquidation threshold, purely to pay someone for the wait. By the curator's own modelling at onboarding, that stretches the profitable liquidation window from about 15 days to 35, and lifts liquidator incentive above 11% against the roughly 2.6% the raw threshold alone would offer.

And liquidators here aren't anonymous bots. They're individually whitelisted and KYC'd, because holding and redeeming a regulated fund share requires legal standing. Clearing a bad position depends on a named, finite set of counterparties showing up, then sitting on the asset for a month. Gating also means the issuer keeps freeze and seize power at the account level, which a curator has to monitor as a routine operational input.

None of these are new problems individually. Stacked, they're an operating business: someone estimating a valuation weekly, three parties reconciling a feed, a curator setting caps and a haircut and watching for issuer freezes, a vetted liquidator willing to hold an illiquid fund share for a month. The infrastructure is genuinely new. The judgment layer on top of it is not.

Depositors think they're choosing a venue. They're choosing a manager. Most don't know it yet.

text:
ThunderPhone - Best AI Tool Finder https://t.co/YovhSNasy5 

ThunderPhone is a platform for building, testing, deploying, and monitoring AI agents that conduct inbound and outbound phone calls. It combines telephony, speech recognition, language models, text-to-speech, integrations, testing, and quality monitoring in one system. The product is available through a no-code interface and API and is priced from $0.02 per connected minute, with more capable tiers at $0.05 and $0.09 per minute (official website; pricing).

The product appears technically substantive rather than a thin interface over a single model. ThunderPhone says it reconciles multiple speech transcripts with direct audio-model input and combines fast and reasoning models to improve audio understanding and instruction adherence. It also offers SIP connectivity, call transfer, DTMF, multilingual operation, regression testing, production monitoring, live supervision, knowledge retrieval, and API integrations (technology; platform).

The strongest investment signal is the founding team. CEO Alex Kolchinski previously worked as a Google associate product manager and Stanford AI Lab researcher and founded autonomous-restaurant company Mezli, where he reports raising $4 million and managing more than 20 employees. CTO Alec Bell previously worked in applied machine learning at Uber, Expedia, and Sea Machines and founded the YC-backed SensorSurf (Kolchinski profile; Bell profile). Both founders therefore have relevant AI, product, and startup experience.

The principal concern is the absence of independently verified commercial traction. ThunderPhone reports “thousands” of production calls and work with a small group of enterprise customers, while a trade publication reports that its interpreting product is in production with a top-five global language-services provider. However, revenue, customer count, call volume, retention, concentration, gross margin, and customer references are not publicly disclosed (launch announcement; MultiLingual). Product Hunt attention is evidence of launch interest, not product-market fit.

The market is large, but ThunderPhone is entering a highly competitive and rapidly commoditizing infrastructure category. Its unusually low prices could support adoption but may also produce structurally weak margins. The appropriate decision is Watch, with an upgrade to formal diligence if the company demonstrates meaningful external revenue, strong customer retention, satisfactory contribution margins, and repeatable distribution beyond founder-led projects.

Cristian Mungiu (2022)

The story (…) is about how our beliefs can shape our choices, our instincts, our irrational impulses and fears, the animals buried within us, the ambiguity of our feelings and actions, and the impossibility of fully understanding them. (… ) It is also a story about globalization and its side effects. (…) The film explores the effects of globalization on a small community rooted in centuries-old traditions: the values of the past have faded, and access to the internet has not brought these people new values, but has instead overwhelmed them with the difficulty of distinguishing truth from their personal opinions amid today’s informational and moral chaos. R.M.N. also addresses the side effects of political correctness: people have learned that it is better not to speak out when their opinions differ from the current norm. However, political correctness is not a formative process, and it has not fundamentally changed people’s opinions; it has merely caused people to express their thoughts less frequently. But things eventually build up, and at some point, they spill over.

Christian Mungiu

While filming, I came across a late-19th-century photograph at one of the filming locations, titled *The Lamb of God*. I thought it would make a good title.

Christian Mungiu

R.M.N. is, first and foremost, a story of misunderstanding stemming from language—or, rather, languages. The film constantly shifts (though with different colors in the subtitles to help you keep track!) from Romanian to Hungarian, with a few lines in German and others in English, the universal language used by the “foreigners” in the story, including—in a beautiful twist of irony—a French zoologist who has come, with European Union funding, to survey the bear population in the surrounding forests. The dialogues, remarkably written and often very lively, gradually reveal the explosive context of the plot: the weight of history, anti-Roma discrimination, the mass exodus of young people to the West in search of a better life, and, summing it all up, hatred of a Europe perceived, at worst, as a pseudo-dictatorship that exploits the country like a vampire and seeks to impose a single way of life from Porto to Bucharest, and at best, as a piggy bank for subsidies. (…) when citizens gather in the community hall to debate the fate of the newcomers (…) twenty-six different characters take the floor in an uninterrupted torrent of invective. A massive outpouring in which all cultural and economic rivalries, all long-dormant personal antagonisms, are reawakened. And where hatred of the other—especially if they come from far away—and the obsession with invasion and the “great replacement” are expressed without the slightest restraint. R.M.N. is set in Romania, but it’s hard not to think about the situation in France right here and now…

Télérama

Within a town whose every communal bond has been frayed by an incomprehensible liberal and supranational order, the director chronicles an inexorable spiral of madness and death. (…) At first glance, the whole thing seems to want to seize us through the almost documentary precision and rigor with which it tackles a specific human and economic problem: the tearing-apart experienced by regions whose working-age male population emigrates to work in other countries of the European Union, forcing their hometowns to “import” workers who are often received in an atmosphere of tension, even outright racism. (…) The primary strength of R.M.N. is that it feigns a naturalistic gesture—one in which photography and sets clearly make maximum use of real elements—the better to let a sense of dramaturgy (which readily borrows from magical realism, even horror) seep in like a slow poison. (…) The world Matthias inhabits is saturated with violence, a pollution that had already contaminated everything long before our anti-hero began his Stations of the Cross. From the opening, the livid light of the slaughterhouse, the dull sound of blows on the lifeless flesh of cattle… everything conspires to draw us, by small but irresistible touches, into a tainted, contaminated reality. Before our eyes, Mungiu’s Transylvania comes unhinged, malfunctions, and grows more complex. The title of the work is of interest because it can be understood both as a quasi-acronym for “Romania” and as the Romanian translation of MRI—the examination the protagonist’s father undergoes. An old man of peaceful, harmonious appearance whose health is deteriorating, his body rotting from the head. And his son scrutinizes, between horror and fascination, the images of his brain, as if to detect some unfathomable secret. (…) Known for a rigorous and sometimes stunning use of long takes orchestrated around a fixed shot, the director here offers a series of hallucinatory moments. The most obvious remains a town-council meeting (hardly a classic site of screen romance) during which, thanks to a single framing, all the evil passions that gnaw at the characters erupt. The image is composed around the clasped hands of two clandestine lovers who are simultaneously playing out their romantic and professional futures. Around them questions and invective soon fly: some residents demand the departure of the foreign workers, another faction fears that their eviction will be accompanied by racist violence while also threatening the region’s fragile economic balance. Arguments fly, faces cross, size each other up, and twist. (…) More autopsy than medical examination in the end, R.M.N. paints a terrible portrait of Romania. Yet both the screenplay and the filmmaking carefully refrain from finding easy or monochromatic culprits for the putrefaction that threatens from every side. Inhuman liberalism is pointed at, without concealing how much individual ill will or the desire to pervert certain mechanisms is at least equally responsible for the spread of hatreds. No one escapes either the light or the darkness. Matthias is not a man hostile to foreign workers whose condition he has shared, but the idea that his mistress is helping them awakens in him a dominating, predatory masculinity. The priest would like to gather his flock in peace and love of neighbor. Of their neighbor—but not of the Sri Lankans he is prepared to sacrifice in order to preserve his popularity. Csilla dreams of the violin and of emancipation, but remains the executor of the dirty work of a firm that treats humans as livestock. “To survive, you have to be ruthless,” a father calmly explains to his son. And the wolves come out, dressed in their white hoods and armed with torches, like so many specters or ancient monsters posted on the border between light and darkness, the better to bite anyone foolish enough to approach in order to bring them back to humanity. And the film itself becomes that, radically, in its final movement, where the curtain of the real is simply torn apart. (…) What Mungiu shows is the emergence of what humanity has always wanted to push away, to contain far from its towns, its fields, its dreams: a form of animality and monstrosity that a voracious and ruthless twenty-first century summons, and whose emergence is now imminent.

Thierry Cheze

If cinephiles know Transylvania, it is mainly because that region of Romania was supposed to be the home of Count Dracula, the hero of Irish writer Bram Stoker and the central character of a great many films. Transylvania, however, is not only that; it is also a region that history has made multi-ethnic, even if it is less so today than a century ago. Thus, in the small Transylvanian town to which Cristian Mungiu takes us, Romanian, Hungarian and German populations live side by side, people of different religions, people who speak different languages among themselves, yet people who, in the end, give the impression of getting along well. Like many inhabitants of this small town, Matthias had gone to work abroad and here he is back from Germany a few days before Christmas, having been unable to stand being called a Gypsy by a colleague. Personally, he worries about Rudi, his eight-year-old son, who in his absence has picked up bad habits and is afraid to walk to school alone because he saw things on the way that frightened him. He also worries about Otto, his father, an elderly man who worries about his sheep, and he is eager to see Csilla again, a woman from the Hungarian community who was his mistress before he left for abroad. As for the small town itself, it is taking the full force of the evils of globalization: in Romania wages are very low compared with other European countries, and the local working-age population most often prefers to leave and take a job abroad rather than look for one on the spot. How, under these conditions, can Csilla manage to hire staff for the industrial bakery she runs, in order to exceed fifty employees and thus obtain a European Union subsidy? By hiring men or women from countries poorer than Romania—Sri Lankans, for example? Except that the townspeople who refuse the starvation wages offered to them locally do not want to hear about the settlement among them of a population coming from the other end of the world, and they band together to obtain their departure. Surrounded by a dense forest and hills, the small Romanian town in which the action takes place tends to live in a closed circuit. True, communities of different origins, different languages and different religions manage to live there on cordial terms with one another, but this situation has lasted a long time and the antagonisms that very probably existed in the past have gradually disappeared. On the other hand, there is no question of welcoming a new community with open arms, especially one coming from so far away: in this cramped environment, every newcomer is regarded as a potential enemy. In fact, events more or less similar to those the film recounts actually took place in Transylvania in the years preceding the pandemic. It is worth remembering, however, that such situations are far from being exclusive to Romania and that, unfortunately, they can be found, more or less pronounced, almost everywhere in the world, not least in our own beautiful country. In fact, attracted by wages in Western Europe, many Romanians accept being poorly received there, being rejected as Matthias was, and at the same time forcefully reject Third-World populations who come to occupy the jobs they consider underpaid and which they themselves do not want. (…) R.M.N., the film’s original title, says everything about what the director wanted to show: Rezonanță Magnetică Nucleară in Romanian, magnetic resonance imaging, MRI in English, a technique that makes it possible to detect what is happening beneath the surface. Both in terms of the story and from a cinematic point of view, the high point of R.M.N. lies in a large public assembly that gathers in a municipal hall, to decide the fate of the Sri Lankan workers, a very large part of the population, and during which racist and xenophobic speeches are delivered against Gypsies and immigrants: a 17-minute long take with spoken interventions from 26 people, including a priest who is not the last to deliver a hateful speech. (…) Given the general context of the story, a great many languages are spoken in the film: Romanian, Hungarian, German, Sinhala (the language of the Sri Lankans), English (since the film deals with the effects of globalization), French (since a Frenchman is there, sent by the European Commission to count the region’s bears). (…) Starting from a story that takes place in an isolated region of Romania, [Cristian Mungiu] embraces a unfortunately universal subject: the rejection of the other, the rejection of the one we do not know, the rejection of the one who comes from elsewhere.

Jean-Jacques Corrio (2022)

Thou hast set all the borders of the earth: thou hast made summer and winter. 

Psalms 74: 17 

A people always knows, loves, and defends its customs more than its laws. 

Montesquieu (1748) 

One must respect a wheat field, not for itself, but because it is food for human beings. In a similar way, one must respect a collectivity, whatever it may be—nation, family, or any other—not for itself, but as nourishment for a certain number of human souls. 

Simone Weil (1949) 

Condemning nationalism because it can lead to war is like condemning love because it can lead to murder. 

G.K. Chesterton (1901)

The border has a bad reputation: it defends counter-powers. Let’s not expect established powers, in a position of strength, to promote it. Nor that these wall-passers—tax evaders, jet-set members, soccer stars, labor traffickers, $50,000 lecturers, multinationals adept at transfer pricing—declare their love for what stands in their way. […] There, moreover, lies the shield of the humble, against the ultra-fast, the elusive, and the omnipresent. It is the dispossessed who have an interest in clear and distinct demarcation. Their only asset is their territory, and the border, their main source of revenue (the poorer a country, the more dependent it is on customs duties). The border levels (to some extent) unequal powers. The rich go where they want, on swift wings; the poor go where they can, rowing. Those who control stocks (of nuclear warheads, gold and currency, knowledge and patents) can play with flows, growing even richer. Those with nothing in stock are the playthings of flows. The strong are fluid. The weak have only their fold, an impregnable religion, an unoccupiable maze, rice fields, mountains, delta. Asymmetric warfare. The predator hates the rampart; the prey likes it well enough." 

Régis Debray (In praise of borders, 2010)

Today, we can speak of an Arab invasion. It is a social fact. How many invasions has Europe experienced in the course of its history? It has always been able to overcome them; moving forward and finding itself better through the exchange between cultures. 

Pope Francis (2016)

We need to enter a time when the Battle of Poitiers and the Crusades are much closer to us than the French Revolution and the industrialization of the Second Empire. (...) After Communism, Europe (...) has once again become that infinitely vulnerable space that the medieval village must have been in the face of the Vikings. (...) This is a resignation of reason. In some ways, it resembles the aporias of pacifism, which we have seen can encourage warmongering. (...) So we need to wake up sleeping consciences. To seek reassurance is always to contribute to the worst. 

René Girard (2007)

Christianity (…) took us from archaism to modernity by helping us channel violence otherwise than through death. (…) By making a tortured man its God, Christianity denounces the unacceptable character of sacrifice. Did not Christ, the Son of God, innocent by essence, say—together with the Jewish prophets: “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice”? In exchange, he promised the kingdom of God, which is to inaugurate the age of reconciliation and the end of violence. The Passion thus inaugurates an unprecedented order that founds the rights of man, which are absolutely inalienable. (…) Islam (…) cannot endure the idea of a crucified God, and therefore of the ultimate sacrifice. It preaches violence in the name of holy war, and some of its faithful seek martyrdom in its name. Archaic? Perhaps—but is it more so than our modern society, hostile to rites and increasingly subject to violence? Did Jesus fail? Humanity has retained many sacrificial mechanisms. It still needs to kill in order to found, to destroy in order to create, which explains in part the genocides, the gulags and the holocausts, the recourse to nuclear weapons, and today terrorism.

René Girard (1978)

The same cultural and spiritual force that played so decisive a role in the disappearance of human sacrifice is today bringing about the disappearance of the sacrificial rituals that once replaced it. All this seems like good news, but only on the condition that those who counted on these ritual resources are able to replace them with durable religious resources of another kind. To deprive a society of the rudimentary sacrificial resources on which it depends without offering it alternatives is to plunge it into a crisis that will almost certainly lead it to violence.

Gil Bailie (1995)

Guess why, after his masterly dismantling of today’s political correctness, Cristian Mungiu came away empty-handed from last year’s Cannes Festival?

“A vitriolic portrait of a xenophobic Romania,” “a scan, auscultation or X-ray of ordinary xenophobia”…“The ravages of populisms,” “nationalism,” “rejection of the other,” “loud-mouthed virilism in animal skins and hunting rifles,” “fascism in gestation,” “obsession with invasion and the great replacement”…

A crude, taciturn, impulsive hero who fled his country of underpaid jobs for a Germany that treats him as a Gypsy…

A little boy, mute since a traumatic encounter in the forest…

An aging, sick shepherd who sees his flock decimated by bears and finds no way out except suicide… Or rather accepts ending as a sacrificial lamb, on this Christmas night, to avert the lynching one sensed coming for the three strangers…

Former mistress number 2 of an industrial bakery, dreaming, between a glass of French wine and a cello piece, of emancipation and community life… But executor of the dirty work of a firm that is the only dynamic enterprise in the area yet treats humans as livestock, with wages too low for the local young people, who preferred to leave for the West…

Foreign labour imported all the way from Sri Lanka to replace the locals who left their country because of low wages…

An isolated village in the Transylvanian forest of the legendary Dracula, with a barely pacified history of a turbulent past among minorities of different languages (Hungarian, German and Romanian) and religions (Catholic, Lutheran and Orthodox)… But now eaten up by resentment after its impoverishment through the closure of a gold mine that under Ceaușescu had drowned and destroyed the environment under cyanide-laced water…

A Mercedes-driving priest, ready to sacrifice the newcomers—against a backdrop of Christmas festivities mixing the Christian call to universal benevolence with torchlight processions and bear skins—in order to safeguard his popularity…

Globalization and the European Union incarnated by an English-speaking French zoologist and member of an NGO for the preservation of wildlife… Come to “protect,” behind the advertised “beautiful diversity,” the very bears that devastate the local shepherds’ flocks… While preaching a living-together that France itself, between two massacres, is incapable of achieving…

Reprise of a scene that already existed on the Internet and had caused a scandal for having brought to light things no one wanted to see…

How can one not be astonished, like the incredible and inextricable complexity our world has become, at the number of elements—economic, cultural, religious, historical and anthropological all at once…

That, skilfully blending the greatest naturalism and magical realism, the Romanian director Cristian Mungiu has managed to bring together in this story of an impossible expulsion (R.M.N. as both the Romanian term for our MRI and the acronym of Romania)…And also how, against the political correctness of happy globalization and triumphant living-together… He succeeds in freeing, perhaps more explicitly than ever in current cinema… The speech of the victims of that same globalization, in all their despair at the wrecking of their traditions and way of life…

But how can one also fail to see the inevitable misreading by most critics, who see in it only the usual easy denunciation of xenophobia and ordinary racism…

And how then can one be surprised at the kind of expulsion that this Palme d’Or winner from Cannes, a multi-award-winning regular of those temples of political correctness that the great world film festivals have become, himself suffered in turn…

Coming away empty-handed for the first time last year?

JC Durbant (2022)

text:
*JANMASHTAMI -7 GUPT REMEDIES* 

On this sacred night, don't ask Shri Krishna for everything.

Choose only ONE remedy according to what your heart genuinely needs.

1. For Stuck Money & Prosperity
Place 5 tulsi leaves before Shri Krishna and offer a little mishri. Pray for rightful prosperity, not sudden riches. The next morning, keep one of those dried leaves respectfully in your money box.

2. For Peace Between Husband & Wife
Offer one small piece of mishri and a tulsi leaf together to Krishna. Pray not for the other person to change, but for bitterness between you to dissolve. Later, the prasad may be shared.

3. For Children
Offer makhan-mishri to Bal Gopal. Speak the child's name before Krishna and simply say:
"Kanha, iska haath aap pakad lena."
Don't ask for marks, success or achievement. Ask for His protection and right direction.

4. For Career & Repeated Obstacles
Keep your work pen near Krishna during your prayer tonight. Chant:

ॐ नमो भगवते वासुदेवाय॥
108 times.

Use the same pen tomorrow for your first important work.

5. For Mental Restlessness
At night, sit quietly before Krishna for 11 minutes. No long list of wishes. No complicated mantra. Look at His feet and mentally surrender the one matter you have been unable to solve.

Sometimes Krishna's remedy is not changing the situation immediately.
It is removing its control over your mind.

6. For Opposition, Enmity & Unnecessary Conflict
Offer a yellow flower to Shri Krishna and chant:

ॐ नमो भगवते वासुदेवाय॥
108 times.

Do not take anyone's name and do not pray for another person's defeat. Ask Krishna to reveal truth and protect you from injustice.

7. THE MIDNIGHT REMEDY

This is my favourite.

Around Krishna Janma time, keep one empty clean bowl before Shri Krishna.

Do not put money, rice or anything inside it.

Sit for a few minutes and tell Him:

"Krishna, I am keeping this vessel empty before You. Remove from my life what has completed its purpose, and fill only what is meant for me."

Leave it there overnight.

In the morning, place a little mishri in it, offer it to Krishna and distribute it as prasad.

The secret of Janmashtami is not merely asking Krishna to give.

Krishna was born at midnight-in darkness, confinement and uncertainty.

His birth itself teaches us:

Your circumstances can look completely closed, and yet the door can open in a way you could never have planned.

Tonight, leave a little space for Krishna to do what you cannot. 🙏

text:
Despite efforts to control the narrative, $TSLA ‘s Cybercab event was largely a bust.  Following a short presentation that formally announced the vehicle’s inclusion into the robotaxi fleet, attendees were able to take rides in the new two-seat vehicle without pedals or steering wheel. There was no livestream of the launch itself.

The launch offered little detail and key questions remained unanswered following the event, including how many vehicles the company plans to deploy.  The Cybercab's launch also raises regulatory issues, including uncertainty associated with the vehicle's lack of traditional driver compliance with federal safety standards.
As of Thursday night, there was no way one could specifically request a Cybercab in the Tesla ride-sharing app.

The company had registered 45 Cybercabs with Texas regulators as of Wednesday, but it was not immediately clear how many were in use at the launch. Including the new Cybercabs, Tesla’s Texas robotaxi fleet consists of 420 robotaxis, mostly Model Y vehicles. That’s less than half of the nearly 1,000 vehicles that $GOOGL ‘s Waymo has registered in Texas.

It’s unclear how Tesla has approached potential regulatory hurdles posed by the Cybercab’s lack of traditional driver controls. While the vehicles used for testing and validation contain steering wheels, the Cybercabs that Tesla has put on the road for robotaxi use appear to lack those controls.  Federal rules typically require all vehicles to have several human-centric design features such as a brake pedal and side mirrors.

Tesla also hasn’t followed the same path as Zoox, $AMZN ‘s autonomous vehicle unit. The company in July secured an exemption from several federal safety standards to allow the commercial deployment of its own purpose-built robotaxi. The exemption was granted after Zoox faced issues attempting to self-certify its vehicle as compliant with federal motor vehicle standards. As of Wednesday, Tesla had not filed an exemption request for the Cybercab with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration.  Source:  Bloomberg

South Africa: yes. SECMENT, April 1975, in breach of Resolution 418. I said so before you asked.

Rwanda’s Hutu government: alleged, not documented. Israel’s own Supreme Court sealed the records in April 2016 on the Mack and Auron appeal. I think that secrecy is indefensible. Now your standard, because you finally stated one and it is worth looking at.

Sell arms to genocidal or brutal regimes, and you should be dismantled.

First. You have never applied it to anyone else. Not once, not in the folder, not in this thread. You have offered to write a book about the others later. Later is not a standard. A rule you have applied exactly once, to the state you started with, is not a rule you discovered. It is a rule you built to fit.

Second, and this is the real problem. The remedy does not attach to the offence anywhere in law, and you know it, because nobody has ever proposed it for anyone else.

France armed the Rwandan government through the run up to a genocide, and Macron’s own commission found heavy and overwhelming responsibilities in March 2021. Nobody proposed dismantling France. Rwanda did not propose it. Kigali took the report and reopened diplomatic relations.

Washington built and armed the Guatemalan army through a campaign the UN backed truth commission found to include acts of genocide in 1999. No dismantlement.

Britain sold Hawk aircraft to Indonesia across the occupation of East Timor, where roughly a third of the population died. No dismantlement.

Russia and China arm Myanmar now, after the ICJ case opened. No dismantlement.

text:
They Did Not Vote for This

Governor Ferguson can call it “morally bankrupt” all he wants. The record in Olympia is simpler than the speech.

Washington’s Near General Fund budget has roughly doubled in a decade, from about $38–39 billion in 2015–17 to $80.2 billion after the 2026 supplemental. Spending outran revenue, population, and inflation. The Legislature then passed the largest tax increases in state history — and came back the next year with a 9.9 percent income tax. Republicans did not build that stack. They voted against it.

That is the part Ferguson leaves out when he talks about “saving Apple Health.”

Who actually passed the spending

Washington has been a Democratic trifecta for years. Apple Health Expansion — the state-only, Medicaid-style program for adults who are ineligible for federal Medicaid because of immigration status, including people with no legal status — exists because the majority funded it in 2022 and 2023 appropriations and kept it in later budgets. It is not a federal entitlement. Federal law bars regular Medicaid for people here illegally. Olympia chose to write a state check instead.

The program is capped. Slots were set around 12,000–13,000. They filled in days. Enrollment is closed when the money runs out. Reporting around the 2025 session put the allocation near $150 million. That is not the whole $80 billion budget. It is also not an accident. It is a line item the majority wanted and the minority did not.

House Republicans said so in plain language. Rep. Joe Schmick: take care of people who are here legally first. Rep. Jim Walsh, on related Medicaid-access legislation: the state is “by design making the benefit available to people who can’t get it through the federal government’s purse,” and “that is primarily illegal immigrants living in Washington state.” Ranking Appropriations Republican Travis Couture’s alternative budget framework said the same thing in policy form: no new taxes, and end state-funded health coverage for undocumented immigrants. That plan did not pass. The majority’s plan did.

Who actually passed the taxes

2025 was sold as “the wealthy will pay.” The bills were broader than the press release.

House Republicans list roughly $12.5 billion in state and local tax increases from that session, then nearly $4.5 billion more in 2026. The 2025 package included a higher capital-gains rate (effective 9.9 percent on gains over $1 million), a steeper estate tax, B&O rate hikes and a surcharge on the largest firms, and a wider sales-tax net on services. The B&O bill passed the House 50–48 and the Senate 26–22. Nine House Democrats joined Republicans against it. That is how thin the majority was — and how unified the GOP was.

In 2026 the House passed ESSB 6346, a 9.9 percent tax on household AGI over $1 million, 51–46. Every Republican voted no. Eight Democrats crossed to join them. The floor fight ran more than 24 hours. Republican amendments to lock the rate, protect working families, or force real tax relief were rejected. Ferguson had already signed the 2025 increases. He said he would sign this one too.

If your grocery bill, B&O return, vehicle fees, or capital-gains hit went up, it was not because rural and eastern Washington Republicans suddenly discovered a taste for new revenue. They voted no. The people who control Olympia voted yes, then discovered the budget was still tight, then came back for more.

The budget did not “just happen”

Washington Policy Center’s recent rundown is the one Ferguson’s office does not quote. Tax collections from 2013 to 2025 grew about 112 percent. Spending grew about 148 percent. If the 2013–15 Near General Fund budget had only tracked population plus inflation, 2025–27 would be around $54 billion — not $80 billion. The extra $26 billion is choices: McCleary K–12, Medicaid and human-services caseloads, compensation, and new programs the majority added and then refused to unwind.

K–12 is the largest Near-GF slice, near 43 percent. 

Human services and DSHS take most of the rest. 

Undocumented adult coverage is a smaller slice of that pie. The political point is not that Apple Health Expansion single-handedly doubled the budget. The point is priority. When money got short, the majority did not take that program off the table first. They raised taxes. When federal law narrowed who qualifies for Medicaid, Ferguson framed the backfill as a moral duty and called Congress bankrupt — after Olympia had already built a state substitute and then capped it because there was “no money to do so.”

Be precise about the Ferguson clip. H.R. 1 tightened Medicaid for many lawfully present noncitizens, not only people with no status. The state said 14,000 lawful immigrants were set to lose Apple Health; after state action the number was about 11,000. Full replacement of every federal cut was estimated at $3.2 billion per biennium. They are not writing that check. They are writing some of it, plus nearly $100 million just to implement the federal law, while telling taxpayers the alternative is cruelty.

That is a values argument. It is not an accounting argument. The accounting argument is: spending ran ahead of the economy, taxes followed spending, and the minority that voted against both is now told it is morally required to keep funding the pieces it already rejected.

What Republicans actually voted for

They voted to keep federal Medicaid for citizens and legal residents who qualify, and they warned Congress that sloppy cuts would hammer rural hospitals. Some state Republicans even wrote the Washington delegation asking not to wreck Apple Health for the people it was designed for. That is not the same as voting to stand up a parallel, state-funded plan for people federal law excludes. Couture’s framework said protect classrooms, hospitals, food assistance for vulnerable Washingtonians, wildfire, and law enforcement — and stop using the budget as a second immigration system. The majority had the votes. They used them.

Undocumented residents pay sales tax and other levies. One often-cited figure is about $997 million in state and local taxes in 2022. Paying tax does not create a right to a new entitlement the Legislature invented and the other party opposed. Schools, roads, and emergency rooms already exist. The fight is over additional full-scope coverage, state financial aid, and in-state tuition — all majority projects.

The sentence Olympia will not say

Republicans and conservatives in this state did not vote to put taxpayers on the hook for a state Medicaid clone for people here without status. They did not vote for the 2025 tax pile. They did not vote for the 2026 income tax. They offered a budget that ended the undocumented health program and raised no new taxes.

They lost.

The budget is strained because the people who won those votes spent faster than the tax base, then taxed the tax base, then spent again. Ferguson can call the federal correction a moral failure. The local failure is on the board: a doubled Near-GF budget, serial tax increases, a capped program they still will not drop, and a minority that already said no.

That vote record is not complicated. It is just inconvenient.

text:
China’s four‑point proposal for collective security in the Middle East really gets to the heart of why the region has stayed chaotic for so long.

For decades, the Middle East has basically been a geopolitical chessboard for outside powers. Certain foreign nations play a simple game: stoke divisions, back proxies, and leverage military alliances plus arms sales to grab energy and geopolitical advantages. Security decisions get made in far‑off capitals like Washington, leaving local Middle‑Eastern states with little choice but to pick sides. We have all seen the outcome: repeated bouts of Israel‑Palestine fighting, persistent instability in the Red Sea, and sectarian tensions constantly being stirred up. War, refugee crises and economic decline keep feeding one another. Foreign powers light the fuse, yet never clean up the mess afterwards.

Unlocking the region’s own security momentum boils down to one thing: Middle‑Eastern issues ought to be settled by Middle‑Eastern people. Security should not be dictated by powerful nations thousands of miles away. Arab states, Gulf countries, Egypt, Türkiye, Iran and other local players can and should talk directly among themselves, without following outside orders, and work through their differences. This throws out the old playbook where outsiders call the shots for the region. It does not shut out outside input entirely, just outside domination.

Then there is comprehensive governance. Every major hotspot in the Middle East is tightly intertwined. The Palestinian‑Israeli conflict, Red Sea shipping risks, fighting in Yemen and the situation in Syria all feed into each other. Trying to fix one conflict in isolation is just treating symptoms, you calm one spot down and trouble pops up somewhere else. Comprehensive governance rejects these band‑aid solutions. It takes all sides’ real‑world concerns into account, addressing security, territorial, ethnic and religious questions together, so conflicts cannot be split apart and exploited over and over.

Lots of people talk about Middle‑East security and only mention missiles, weapons and military blocs. But much unrest comes from plain hard realities: sky‑high unemployment, bleak prospects for young people, weak livelihoods and heavily lopsided economies. When economies stall and ordinary people cannot get by, resentment and extremist thinking find fertile ground. Security opens space for development, yet development is what truly underpins lasting stability. Peace will hold only when regular people see real improvements in their lives; cease‑fires forced by military might never last long.

On international coordination, everything should follow the UN Charter and international law. We cannot allow some countries to bypass the UN for unilateral sanctions or military interventions. International engagement is fine, yet it must respect Middle‑Eastern states’ own wishes, and must not become a cover for foreign interference. The UN needs to do genuine mediation work, and a small handful of powerful countries should never get to override other nations’ sovereignty.

This vision seeks no expansion, no spheres of influence, and forces no country to choose sides. It respects every Middle‑Eastern nation’s sovereignty and acknowledges their real‑world struggles. It stands worlds apart from the Western approach of leaning on military pressure and stoking bloc‑to‑bloc confrontation. It shows the Middle East another path: achieving peace through regional unity, instead of relying on foreign patrons. Real‑world barriers remain steep, external powers will not give up their vested interests easily, but this framework genuinely offers an alternative way forward.

▶️ Unleashing the internal momentum of regional common security. The people in the Middle East should be the masters of their own affairs. Regional countries should be supported in strengthening dialogue on peace and security. 

▶️ Advancing the comprehensive governance of regional common security. The many highly interrelated hotspot issues in the Middle East require comprehensive solutions. 

▶️ Cementing the development foundation of regional common security. Lasting stability and security in the Middle East relies fundamentally on development. 

▶️ Enhancing international coordination on regional common security. The UN Charter and international law serve as the basic guidelines for handling Middle East affairs. The UN should be supported in playing a tangible role in regional affairs.

August 21–22, 2026: Carney said last-minute U.S. changes were “unfair, uneconomic,” that Washington “asked too much and offered too little,” and that the U.S. tried “until the very last minute” to restrict French-language and cultural protections and Canada’s ability to sign other trade deals. He said Canada made no last-minute requests. Short answer: “No.”  
  https://t.co/ORiohyVwWJ  
  https://t.co/ITXObU8fMb
- U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said the opposite on the two items Carney put at the centre of the story. On trucks: “The words ‘medium- and heavy-duty trucks’ were raised in these negotiations on Friday at 4 o’clock.” He said those trucks had not been part of his repeated meetings with Dominic LeBlanc. On French: “If you think I ever said the word ‘French’… We don’t care.” He said Carney “manufactured” the language issue for Quebec and Alberta politics. USTR Jamieson Greer also said the U.S. would not have blown up a deal over French discoverability.  
  https://t.co/M06GPoP0bR  
  https://t.co/EJTZHcuhzq
- Canada’s chief negotiator, Janice Charette, later said trucks were raised Monday through Thursday, not only Friday at 4 p.m., and that every Canadian document covered all vehicles Canada produces. That is Ottawa’s rebuttal to Lutnick. It does not match Carney’s Saturday line that Canada made no last-minute requests, and it does not match Lutnick’s public timeline. No draft text has been released by either government.  
  https://t.co/ZPoHiG00Cd  
  https://t.co/IZeXG4E1T7
- Carney told Canadians the U.S. offer would have destroyed auto, steel and aluminum and compromised sovereignty, language, and culture. Lutnick, Vance, and other U.S. officials said Canada walked with last-minute demands after a framework Trump had already announced. Those are the two official stories. The documents that would settle which description matches the paper on the table have not been published.

text:
🇷🇺More than 300 American companies are still operating in Russia … take that Putin!

More than 300 US companies continue to do business in Russia, despite Washington’s ban, and have no plans of leaving the Russian market, Presidential Adviser and the Eastern Economic Forum Organizing Committee Executive Secretary Anton Kobyakov told TASS in an interview on the sidelines of the EEF.

In his words, Western investors have kept their contacts with Russia, and some of them continue working with Moscow even now.

"No one wants to leave. Everyone understands the value of such communication channels, understand their own business interests," he said, adding that some European companies have already been "backed into a corner by their own governments in an attempt to prevent them from working with us."

According to Kobyakov, the Russian government is creating no obstacles for those who decided to stay with Russia because in this case they are being treated on equal footing with Russian companies and viewed as Russian economic operators.

text:
I never believe the market “narrative.” I use it as those who orchestrate it intend for it to be used.. thus treating financial “news” personalities across cable TV as assets of institutions and hedge funds. With a simple premise that whatever “concern” or “rationale” they offer for market moves is seeded to manipulate retail sentiment and blow out retail gamblers.

Take recent Bitcoin pressure and the Strategy narratives. Market makers knew the price range that would create the most margin-call pain, blow out the Gordon Gekko wannabes who think they have it all figured out, and deal them “life lessons.” Bitcoin is even better for this: a finite asset limited to 21 million coins, so they can take it at a discount. Institutions have the bankroll to ride those coins down to 5 cents if they choose; the position is small to them.

And It was necessary as well as inevitable. Did you notice how many of those same retail gamblers were jumping into Nvidia ahead of earnings and were momentum-trading that wave, and far too often the price action in one impacted the other. In addition, Options markets then put the stock in a range that left it undervalued for nearly two years. Notice what happened after Bitcoin margin calls crushed those individuals: Nvidia did not have its usual run-up into earnings and 15–20 point selloff. The opposite. It stabilized. The same pattern followed with Palantir. Both names have begun to normalize, as they should have over a year ago. Momentum traders created a setup that was too wreckable to ignore.

Where did the game move? To a cheaper stock on share price alone, not fundamentals. Remaining retail was herded into Rocket Lab after massive hype and cool tech posts. Institutions and hedge funds who had been crushed in it for 6+ months thinking it was viable to SpaceX were able to DCA, quietly build a base, then likely dropped some favorable comments regarding the company capitalizing on the “next big thing” hype associated with all things space thanks to the hype surrounding SpaceX, thus such an easy sell to their assets lining them up to talk up a rocket company that does have fun future tech that makes for a great story —So what did it do? It broke out from around 55 to 58 all the way to 78–80, giving them a modest gain took a modest gain and some Hampton spending money .

I’m a street-wise political science guy. I look at the macro and piece things together. With technology I look for DARPA ties and Pentagon funding. Rising funding means more personnel getting clearances, which means the tech is viable. It would be a national-security risk to clear large numbers of people and then defund the company or pull the rug. I also look for trends in political talking points, as those trends are framing policy that will eventually result in the allocation of funding. —I also listen and look for specific topics or mentions that come from @POTUS Trump regarding technology or energy, yet despite being a “new take” or point of emphasis it receives little to no follow up by the cable “news” talking heads.. obviously the reason he mentions this new take is likely someone is presenting the idea to him as something that is likely to get funded. What has he mentioned several times lately? Magnetics.. and what was mentioned along with all the SpaceX hype? Mars.. And the whole make Earth a multi-planetary species, yet specifics are vague, what isn’t, is the continued narrative of moving human consciousness off planet.. how? via AI and robotics.. why? the realization or knowing all along that human body can’t survive the rapid changes in gravity.. my opinion, magnetics play a part in simulating Earth’s gravity..

In addition, looking at AI research on DARPA links to public companies in AI, quantum, LEO infrastructure, robotics, space robotics, radiation shielding, geospatial AI, and fusion power. Fusion is coming faster than people think. Many assume it will serve data centers. I think more so isolated housing developments.

text:
Past Tech was historical INNOVATION.

Tech advancement now only serves IMMEDIACY and CONVENIENCE.

There is no INNOVATION in summoning a robot to deliver food ordered from a pocket computer.

There is no INNOVATION in dictating a film premise and receiving an instantly generated script and visuals.

There is no INNOVATION in fleets of autonomous drones conducting perpetual surveillance.

There is no INNOVATION in implanting microchips into healthy human brains to optimize cognition or mood.

There is no INNOVATION in same-day delivery of any material desire.

There is no INNOVATION in vehicles that drive themselves so passengers may remain absorbed in endless digital distraction.

There is no INNOVATION in algorithmic systems engineered to monopolize human attention for commercial gain.

There is no INNOVATION in virtual environments that offer escape from physical reality rather than engagement with it.

There is no INNOVATION in genetic or neural modifications pursued for aesthetic enhancement or convenience rather than the eradication of disease or the expansion of genuine human capability.

There is no INNOVATION in becoming POST-HUMAN.

In a solved advanced society we become impatient pleasure blobs—stripped of struggle, curiosity, and the dignity of effort.

No thanks

text:
Welcome back to another Owen Guns Firearm Friday! This week we’re pulling a particularly interesting old Winchester out of the museum, and while everyone knows the Winchester name, you may not have heard of one made especially for the Australian market: “The Daisy Rifle.”
Sitting in the Owen Guns Museum is this well-used Winchester Model 1873, serial number 498582B, chambered in .32 W.C.F. ”32/20 Winchester Centre Fire” and fitted with a full-length magazine and octagonal barrel. At first glance it looks like a classic old Model 1873 that has seen plenty of years of honest use. Look a little closer at the barrel, however, and there is a marking that makes this Winchester particularly interesting to Australian collectors: “THE DAISY RIFLE.”
The Winchester Model 1873 needs little introduction. Introduced in 1873 and descended from Winchester's earlier repeating rifles, it became one of the company's most famous lever actions. Its combination of a tubular magazine, lever-operated action and relatively handy repeating-firearm design made the 1873 enormously successful. It was offered in several chamberings during its long production life, including the .32 W.C.F. chambering found in our museum example.
But the "Daisy" name isn't a Winchester model in the conventional sense, nor does it have anything to do with the famous Daisy air rifles. Instead, it takes us from New Haven, Connecticut, all the way to colonial Australia and the enormous Sydney merchant F. Lassetter & Co.
Lassetter & Co. was a major Australian retailer and importer that sold an extraordinary range of goods during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Among the firearms it imported were genuine Winchester rifles from the United States. Rather than simply selling every Winchester under its normal model designation, Lassetter arranged for certain firearms destined for the Australian market to carry distinctive trade names.
For the Model 1873, one of those names was “THE DAISY RIFLE.”
Importantly, this wasn't simply a nickname subsequently scratched or engraved onto rifles after they reached Australia. Winchester Arms Collectors Association historian Bert Hartman confirms that the Daisy marking was factory applied by Winchester to firearms exported for F. Lassetter & Co. Collector research has identified several different Lassetter markings, including “THE DAISY RIFLE,” “THE DAISY CARBINE,” “THE DAISY SINGLE SHOT RIFLE” and, with the arrival of the Model 1892, “THE NEW DAISY RIFLE.”
Period trade-marking research specifically identifies “The Daisy Rifle” as a Model 1873 Winchester made for F. Lassetter & Co., with the designation recorded from approximately 1889 onward. The same source distinguishes it from the later Model 1892, which Lassetter marketed as “The New Daisy Rifle.”
That distinction is important on our rifle because its octagonal barrel still clearly carries the original “THE DAISY RIFLE” marking. Elsewhere we find Winchester's New Haven barrel address and King's Improvement patent information, MODEL 1873, 32 W.C.F., and the serial number 498582B.
The serial number places this rifle in 1895, making it a late-production Third Model 1873 and now more than 130 years old. By this stage the Model 1873 was sharing Winchester's catalogue with newer designs, including John Browning's Model 1892, but Australian buyers were clearly still purchasing the older 1873. The Daisy name continued to distinguish Lassetter's Australian-market guns.
And these Australian Winchesters weren't necessarily destined to spend their lives sitting above fireplaces.
Australia in the late nineteenth century was a huge market for practical sporting and working firearms. Rifles went onto stations, farms and remote properties where they were tools rather than collector pieces. Research into surviving Australian Winchesters shows many of the Daisy and similar Australian trade-marked rifles consequently turn up today showing considerable use.
Our Daisy certainly looks the part.
The metal has aged to a deep brown patina and the timber carries more than a century's worth of knocks, scratches and handling marks. Thankfully, the important markings remain remarkably legible. Rather than detracting from the rifle as a museum piece, that wear is part of its story. Somewhere between Winchester's factory in Connecticut, Lassetter's Australian operation and eventually the Owen Guns Museum in Gympie, this rifle has lived a working life.
There is also one feature on our Daisy that definitely wasn't there when Winchester made it in 1895.
Running almost the entire length of the barrel is a huge brass 4×15 telescopic sight. The scope is identified as a Navy Arms scope. So while the scope looks wonderfully at home sitting over a nineteenth-century Winchester, it is a much later addition. It was deliberately designed in the style of the long telescopic sights associated with nineteenth-century rifles. In our case, it has subsequently become part of this particular Daisy's history. Rather than presenting the rifle as an untouched factory example, we can see it as something that continued being owned, altered and used long after 1895.
Interestingly, the Daisy wasn't the only Australian Winchester to receive its own identity. Queensland had its own famous counterpart. Perry Brothers of Brisbane sold specially marked Winchesters under the name “The Stinger.” Later Model 1892s supplied through Lassetter became the “New Daisy Rifle.” These rifles are now fascinating reminders that the story of Winchester in Australia wasn't simply one of importing American guns, Australian retailers created their own recognisable identities around them.
That is what makes this old .32 particularly deserving of its place in the Owen Guns Museum. It isn't the finest-condition Winchester 1873 you'll ever see, and it certainly isn't untouched after 131 years. But it is unmistakably Australian. It is a genuine Winchester Model 1873 manufactured in America for an Australian retailer, carrying a special Winchester-applied Australian-market name, apparently used for generations and later fitted with a wonderfully old-fashioned Navy Arms brass scope.
From New Haven to Lassetter & Co., through more than a century of Australian history and eventually to the Owen Guns Museum in Gympie, there probably aren't many old rifles that could tell us everywhere they've been if only they could talk.
That's it for another Owen Guns Firearm Friday! If you're ever wandering through the museum and spot a long old Winchester with an enormous brass telescope sitting on top, have a closer look at the barrel, because this isn't just another Model 1873. This one's a Daisy.
See you next Friday when we dig something else out of the Owen Guns Museum and find out what story it's been hiding!

text:
Following the disaster at Cannae in August 216 BC, Rome was held in the grip of the brilliant Hannibal, the spearhead of Carthaginian power in Italy. Tens of thousands of Romans lay dead, along with a third of Rome’s military-age population then under arms—nearly every family mourning men lost in the battle.

Not long afterward, another Roman army was completely destroyed, ambushed by the Boii while marching through the Litana Forest in Cisalpine Gaul—nearly all its men, commanders, tribunes, and centurions massacred. Its commander, the consul-elect Lucius Postumius Albinus, was beheaded, his skull stripped and cleaned, then gilded and used by the Boii as a sacred drinking vessel during their rituals.

At this moment Hannibal believed Rome would sue for peace, for how could they not? After suffering such devastating military defeats, with her treasury strained, her armies annihilated, her manpower severely depleted, and her Italian allies beginning to waver, what strength did the defeated still possess to stand?

Sending envoys toward Rome in hopes of opening negotiations and arranging the ransom of Roman prisoners, the Carthaginian was met instead with refusal. Rome would neither negotiate peace nor ransom the men captured at Cannae, and immediately began raising new armies from whatever manpower remained, whether citizen, slave, or freedman.

Marcus Junius Pera was appointed dictator, with Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus as master of the horse, and Rome began another levy almost immediately. Boys as young as seventeen were enrolled, eight thousand slaves were purchased by the state and armed after volunteering for military service, and thousands more men who ordinarily would never be permitted into the legions were drawn into the ranks.

With the treasury already under immense pressure, Rome began drawing upon private wealth to keep the war moving. Over the following months Roman contractors provided grain, clothing, equipment, and other military necessities on public credit, accepting promises of later repayment from a state which, at that moment, could offer little more than its word that it would survive.

Hannibal then marched into Campania, and Capua defected to him, opening its gates and giving Carthage the most important Italian ally it had yet gained, a major base in southern Italy—a horrific economic and strategic loss for Rome. Capua was among the richest cities in Italy, its defection threatened to draw more Campanian communities away from Rome.

Marcus Claudius Marcellus, then praetor, immediately moved toward Nola to organize the defense of the city, aiming to prevent Hannibal from gaining another major Campanian stronghold. When elements within Nola attempted to bring the city over to Hannibal, Marcellus secured the gates and brought his troops into position before Hannibal could seize it.

When Hannibal approached Nola later in 216 BC, Marcellus brought his troops out against the Carthaginians, struck them before they could secure the city, and forced Hannibal to flee. It was a comparatively small action beside Cannae, but after Trebia, Trasimene, and the destruction at Cannae, Rome had finally struck back.

By 215 BC Quintus Fabius Maximus had taken command as consul, returning Rome to the method which Hannibal found far more difficult to curtail by refusing the great pitched battle he desired, and instead began attacking his detachments, cutting down his foragers — recovering defecting towns where possible, and remaining near enough that Hannibal could not march through allied territory without Roman armies shadowing him.

The immediate Roman answer to Cannae was to refuse to die. No matter the loss, no matter how broke, no matter how many cities taken—Rome would raise another army, then another; it would hold cities still loyal and contest every defection, and Rome would follow Hannibal wherever he moved, forcing him to fight for every mile of Italy.

The last above ground piece of the Trade Center, now known as the Survivors’ Staircase, was preserved by the New York Landmarks Conservancy and a group of preservation partners.

On September 11th, this staircase at the northeastern edge of the elevated World Trade Center Plaza provided an unobstructed exit for people fleeing the site. As visitors now arrive at the 9/11 Museum’s main exhibition and education level, they follow the stairs that once led hundreds of survivors to safety.

We originally wanted the staircase to remain in place but came to accept a state-offered compromise: the 9/11 Museum would exhibit the stairs if we could figure out how to get them there. We engaged noted preservation engineer Robert Silman who cut them out of surrounding concrete and designed a steel “cradle” to hold them. Giant Port Authority cranes lifted them across Ground Zero to the museum site. The National Trust for Historic Preservation, the Municipal Art Society of New York, World Monuments Fund, and the Preservation League of New York were partners in our post-9/11 efforts.

text:
Danylo “Surfer” Smyrnov was killed on the front on August 28. He was seventeen when he sent letters to nearly every brigade, asking for almost nothing: let him carry ammunition.

He didn’t want money. Just food, a uniform, and the right to fight.

Everywhere they refused him because he was a minor. Two days before his eighteenth birthday, Danylo called the recruitment center of the 3rd Assault Brigade.

Not long after, he was leading a storm group himself.

When the full-scale invasion began, he had just turned sixteen. His father and uncle went to the Territorial Defense, and Danylo showed up at the nearest checkpoint.

He offered to do anything: carry food, carry ammunition, run errands. Three days later they gave him a weapon.

For the next three months he helped defend Kyiv Oblast. After the Russians pulled back, his father insisted the boy go study.

Danylo went to Lithuania, enrolled in psychology, but couldn’t stand watching the war from a distance. Still a minor, he came home and started knocking on the doors of military units.

The moment he turned eighteen, he signed a contract with the 3rd Separate Assault Brigade.

Before the war, his life was surfing. He grew up flying to Bali, where his mother lived, training and competing.

That’s where the callsign came from. In the Third Assault, Surfer became a storm group commander in the 2nd Mechanized Battalion.

He fought near Avdiivka and went through the battles for the coke plant. Near Semenivka he was wounded, recovered, and returned to duty.

Later he became the chief sergeant of the Young Killers Group inside the Defense Intelligence’s International Legion. His brothers in arms say one thing about him: fearless.

The one who always went first.

In interviews he said that on a long war, motivation alone isn’t enough. Discipline keeps you going.

The hardest thing for him was losing his brothers. The most valuable thing the service gave him was military brotherhood.

Last July, Danylo got married. His wife, callsign “Yunha,” is also fighting.

She’s an FPV drone operator. She also joined the army at eighteen.

The farewell for Danylo “Surfer” Smyrnov will take place tomorrow in Kyiv. The service will be at St.

Michael’s Golden-Domed Monastery, and he will be buried at Lisove Cemetery. In a few weeks, his son will be born.

Fate gave him little time. But he managed to become a warrior, a brother in arms, a husband, and a father to be proud of.

Now compare that to what the Kremlin feeds into this war. The RAG snippets from the moscovian side are a different species entirely.

A 41-year-old from Irkutsk with a bullet fragment in his skull and a trepanned cranium, sent on a combat task while on crutches after five seizures.

A Bangladeshi man who barely speaks Russian, lured with promises of drone assembly work and citizenship, then shipped to the front and never heard from again.

A soldier from the 11th Guards Air Assault Brigade whose family says he was killed by his own commander, with his accounts scrubbed and his death dressed up as suicide.

Another one with a spinal prosthesis sent back into combat without a medical commission, held in a basement for two months, then disappeared along with ten other wounded men.

That’s the difference. Ukraine produces volunteers like Danylo Smyrnov, a kid who had to beg for the right to defend his country and then became the guy leading others into the assault.

Moscovia produces conscripts and deceived foreigners who have to be dragged to the front. When they break, their own commanders kill them or feed them into the grinder and call it a suicide.

Two armies with fundamentally unequal moral standing are at war.

a war between a nation that produces seventeen-year-olds who refuse to stay away, and an imperial state that treats its own people as disposable raw material. One side builds warriors.

The other side manufactures corpses and then lies about how they died.

Danylo “Surfer” Smyrnov. Honor.

text:
Milky Mist vs Heritage Foods vs Parag Milk Foods: Three Dairy Companies, Three Completely Different Bets on the Same Milk

Same industry, same raw material, three wildly different outcomes. 

One company refuses to sell plain milk at all. 
One sells more milk than anything else. 
The third is stuck in the middle, torn between premium brands and low-margin bulk buyers. 

Let me walk you through why that one decision how much of your milk you turn into something else ends up deciding almost everything else in this business.

The scoreboard, side by side

-->Revenue (Q1 FY27): 

Heritage Foods leads on scale at ₹1,338.1 Cr (+18.0% YoY), 
followed by Milky Mist at ₹973.5 Cr (+43.6% YoY), 
and Parag Milk Foods at ₹945.0 Cr (+11.0% YoY). 

Heritage is the biggest, but Milky Mist is growing more than double the rate of either competitor.

-->Volume growth: 

Milky Mist ~30-34% (Paneer +34%, Ice Cream +45%). Heritage's milk volume stayed flat while value-added products grew +35%. 
Parag grew just +3.0% overall, with its own flagship products actually contracting -2.0%.

-->Gross Margin: 
Milky Mist 34.21% (up 275 bps YoY), 
Parag 27.30% (down 70 bps QoQ), 
Heritage compressed ~250 bps YoY on milk cost inflation.

-->EBITDA Margin: 

Milky Mist 14.88% — genuinely the industry leader — versus Parag's 7.41% and Heritage's 4.63%, a cyclical trough.

-->PAT: 

Milky Mist ₹64.7 Cr (6.64% margin, up ~890% YoY), Parag ~₹22-24 Cr (2.40% margin, down 20% YoY on tax impact), Heritage ₹15.0 Cr (1.12% margin).

Three companies, same raw material, and the profitability gap between the top and bottom is nearly 6x.

Why the gap is this wide it comes down to one strategic choice

-->Milky Mist :- 100% Value-Added Dairy Products, zero liquid milk. Every drop of their ~13.2 LLPD (Lakh Liters Per Day) intake becomes Paneer, Cheese, Curd, Greek Yogurt, Skyr, Ice Cream, or Butter. Product split: Paneer 26%, Cheese 14%, Curd 13%, Ice Cream 11%, Yogurt 9%, Others 27%.

-->Heritage Foods :- a hybrid, transitioning model. Liquid Milk still makes up 51% of revenue, Curd 34%, Paneer 4%, Ice Cream 4%, Nutrivet Feed 5%. That heavy liquid milk exposure is exactly what drags their blended margins.

-->Parag Milk Foods :- branded dairy plus specialized nutrition. Ghee & Cheese 45%, Paneer & Dahi 16%, Avvatar Whey & Pride of Cows 13%, and a meaningful 26% still tied to B2B institutional buyers.

Here's the mechanism in plain terms: 

liquid pouch milk is treated almost like a regulated essential commodity in India raising its price is politically and socially sensitive, so margins there stay thin no matter what raw milk costs do. 

Heritage's liquid milk segment ran at just 3.03% EBITDA margin in Q1 FY27, versus 8.06% for their value-added products. 

When you sell 51% of your volume into that low-margin bucket, it drags your entire blended number down with it.

Milky Mist simply doesn't have that bucket. Every liter becomes something branded and differentiated and differentiated consumer food carries real pricing power. 

They actually pushed through a 10.5% price hike in Q1 FY27 with zero volume destruction, something you generally can't do with a commodity product regulated close to the household budget.

The raw milk inflation story same input cost shock, three very different outcomes

-->Heritage paid ₹46.61/L, up 7% YoY, with buffalo milk spiking to ₹65.99/L. That input shock is exactly what compressed group EBITDA to 4.6%.

-->Parag paid ~₹42.00/L, up 13% YoY.

-->Milky Mist pays ₹41-42/L at the farm gate (₹45/L landed) similar or even slightly better pricing than the other two. 

But because their revenue per liter processed is the highest in the industry (thanks to 100% VADP), the same rupee increase in milk cost represents a much smaller percentage of their finished product's final price. The exact same commodity shock simply hurts them less.

The supply chain moat and this is where "owning the whole chain" genuinely pays off 

Milky Mist is the only one of the three that owns its primary cold chain fleet end to end. 

That matters because fresh paneer, Greek yogurt, and artisanal cheese degrade fast if refrigeration breaks even briefly and third-party logistics partners have every incentive to switch off chillers when it saves them money, not when it's best for your product. 

Milky Mist's owned fleet also runs reverse logistics carrying dairy out, bringing back fruits, packaging materials, and grains on the return leg saving 18-20% in freight costs compared to hiring third-party logistics.

The full margin picture, stacked together

Gross Margin: 

Milky Mist 34.21% (+275 bps) > Parag 27.30% (-70 bps) > Heritage ~22.50% (-250 bps drag).

EBITDA Margin: Milky Mist 14.88% (+74.5% EBITDA growth) > Parag 7.41% (weighed by A&P and B2B pricing pressure) > Heritage 4.63% (a cyclical trough from raw milk inflation).

PAT Margin: Milky Mist 6.64% (PAT up ~10x YoY) > Parag 2.40% (tax normalization drag) > Heritage 1.12% (liquid milk drag).

The pattern repeats at every single level of the P&L — the company with zero liquid milk exposure wins on gross margin, wins bigger on EBITDA margin, and wins by an even wider gap on PAT margin. 

Margin compounding, working in Milky Mist's favor at every step.

The operating leverage story is the real headline

Milky Mist grew revenue 43.6% YoY but EBITDA grew 74.5% and PAT grew 889.8%. 

That kind of profit flow-through is strong evidence their 73-acre Perundurai automated mega-plant has genuinely crossed its operational break-even threshold fixed costs are now spread across enough volume that each new rupee of revenue drops through to the bottom line at a much higher rate than before.

Heritage shows the opposite problem strong absolute scale at ₹1,338 Cr in revenue, but only ₹15 Cr in PAT (a 1.1% net margin), because half their volume sits in a business earning a 3% EBITDA margin that gets wiped out almost entirely by power, freight, and packaging inflation.

Parag sits in between genuine brand equity in Go Cheese (#2 nationally, 35% share) and fast-growing Avvatar Sports Nutrition (+59% YoY), but its aggressive marketing spend (India's Got Latent, KBC sponsorships) and B2B institutional pricing friction keep EBITDA capped in the 7-8% range. In Q1 FY27, their flagship volumes actually contracted 2% YoY because institutional buyers resisted price hikes, forcing Parag to sacrifice volume just to protect margin.

Where each company is headed next

Milky Mist:

-->Their Unit-4 Cheddar Cheese Plant (120 MT/day), commissioned in Q1 FY27, offers immediate runway to roughly triple cheese revenue. 

-->A dedicated Whey Protein Concentrate plant is being built to process 1 million liters/day of cheese whey into high-value B2C whey protein, live within 15-18 months. 

-->₹497 Cr of IPO proceeds went toward prepaying debt eliminating interest burden right as their mega-facility hits operating leverage. 

-->They've acquired industrial land in Maharashtra to build a second integrated plant, finally breaking out of South India concentration.

Heritage Foods:

-->A greenfield ice cream plant (running the Alpenvie and Get-A-Way brands) is currently at 40% utilization but growing 65% YoY. 

-->₹250 Cr FY27 capex is going toward dedicated paneer and ghee processing plants — a real signal they're trying to shift their own mix away from liquid milk. 

-->They've acquired 100% of Heritage Novandie (Livo yogurt) and 71% of Peanut Butter & Jelly Ltd, pushing further into high-protein categories.

Parag Milk Foods:

-->Doubling cheese capacity from 60 MT/day to 120 MT/day over the next 18 months — directly matching Milky Mist's cheddar scale. 

-->Avvatar Sports Nutrition continues compounding fast (+59% YoY) through e-commerce and quick-commerce, pushing Parag into higher-margin functional fitness powders and RTD protein beverages.

How I'd rank these three

Milky Mist the clear fundamental outperformer. Zero liquid milk dilution, real pricing power, an owned physical distribution moat that would take years of heavy capital to replicate, and a post-IPO balance sheet that's actively de-risking right as their new capacity kicks in.

Parag Milk Foods the high-potential health and nutrition play. Genuine brand IP in Go Cheese and Avvatar, but the ~60% reliance on aggregators for milk procurement strips away farm-gate margin, and heavy B2B exposure keeps overall returns diluted.

Heritage Foods the volume giant, margin laggard. An extensive 300,000+ farmer direct network is a genuine asset, but as long as liquid milk stays at 51% of sales, profitability will keep swinging with agricultural flush and deficit cycles beyond their control.

Why this comparison matters

The lesson across all three companies is really one lesson: in dairy, what you choose to convert your milk into decides your entire margin structure before a single operational decision even gets made. 

Milky Mist isn't winning because they're better at making paneer than Heritage or Parag they're winning because they made a structural choice years ago to never touch the low-margin liquid milk business at all, and that choice compounds at every level of the P&L.

Not investment advice. Curious which of these three you'd back for the next 2-3 years, and whether Heritage's ice cream and paneer pivot can genuinely close the gap. Let me know below.

text:
Alagu Mallari Krishna Swamy Temple at Mannar Poluru near Sullurpet is a mythic battlefield turned sacred shrine, where Krishna’s duel with Jambavan echoes through stone and legend.

Built in the 17th century by Bangaru Yadama Nayudu, a local chieftain and devotee. The region was once famed as “Malla Hari Poru Vuru”—the land where Lord Hari (Krishna) engaged in Malla Yuddham (wrestling duel) with Jambavan.

As per the Brahmanda Purana, Krishna fought Jambavan for 28 days to retrieve the Syamantaka Mani. After the duel, Jambavan offered both the jewel and his daughter Jambavati in marriage to Krishna.

This temple is the only one in India where Krishna is flanked by Satyabhama and Jambavati, his two consorts from this legend.

There is a 9.5-foot idol of Jambavan, said to create the illusion of shedding tears. A majestic 9-foot Garuda idol, along with sculptures of Sugreeva and Jatayu, enrich the epic canvas. A shrine to Lord Rama also exists within the temple complex.

text:
Hamsaladeevi’s Venugopalaswamy Temple where Krishna River meets the Bay of Bengal, around 40 km from Machilipatnam.The temple stands near the Sagara Sangamam, the sacred confluence where the Krishna River merges into the Bay of Bengal, a rare and spiritually potent meeting point.

The beach nearby offers a tranquil, scenic experience, with three distinct water colors visible at the confluence.

Dedicated to Venugopala Swamy, flanked by Rukmini and Satyabhama, the temple is one of the 108 sacred Vishnu temples in India. The main gopuram faces east, welcoming the rising sun and symbolizing spiritual awakening.

Believed to have been constructed during the Eastern Chalukyan era, with later contributions from the Chola kings, the temple reflects a blend of architectural grace and devotional depth.

text:
Panduranga Swamy Temple, Chilakalapudi (Machilipatnam), The temple complex spans 6 acres, offering a spacious and serene spiritual experience.

Built in 1929 by Sri Bhakta Narasimham, a devotee inspired by the Pandharpur tradition and guided by Sadguru Mahipathi Maharaj.

The temple is often referred to as Keer Pandaripura ‘Keer’ meaning parrot in Marathi, as the area was once filled with parrots.

The garbhagriha and deity closely resemble the famed Pandharpur temple in Maharashtra, with Shree Panduranga standing in his iconic posture.A unique Sahasra Linga Kailasa Mandapam houses 1,000 Shiva Lingas, with the central one believed to be Swayambhu.

A Sthala Vruksha is believed to shelter a saint performing penance for over 350 years. Devotees circumambulate the tree as part of their worship.

During Kartika Maasam, devotees take a holy dip at Manginapudi beach, followed by rituals at the temple. Nearby 12 sacred wells represent the 12 holy rivers of India. 

Notably, the temple does not accept monetary offerings—no hundi, no pooja charges. Devotees offer patika bellam (rock candy) as prasad.
