text:
I have had some great sports cards, many of which I still keep.

But there are many that got away or missed out. Let me revisit 3 and see what lessons are.

1. MJ PMG Green.
3/10 was sold from Hawaii, seller did multiple round of shopping to really alienate, lastly want me to pick it up from Hawaii (which is common now but it was early in my collecting) so I didn’t go extra mile to lock it down. ~$40k

1/10 font looks a bit weird and provenance story sounded sus, so I didn’t push too hard. ~100k.

PWCC copy was altered although a friend offered to trade it with my Brady ultimate shield in that Topps video one year before PWCC sale. Passed. ~$350k.

One year too late to get into hobby for rb21 webpage copy and was not too proactive to miss the pippen1 copy although I bought from pippen1 several big pieces before he sold Green.

2. LeBron 2003 Exquisite RPA /99 9.5
Although I consider it as commodity card, 9.5 version is definitely a coffin tier, also commodity card notion was not crystallized until later.

I had a chance at 12/99 and offered $16k via en ebay message and it sold for $16.3k or so on ebay not long after, probably the seller leveraged my offer. Would I get it if I make direct ebay offer, not sure. Sometimes things are not meant to be. Winner of that card sold it around $2.4M in 2022.

There is another true 9.5 unbumped from a seller who also had a Duncan Essential Credentials /6 I needed. The timing of contacting me always off. He wrote me when I was busy and when I wrote to him, he was, so that card later sold somewhere els. Also Duncan /6 which I could have bought it at $3.5k and paid $10k from his immediate buyer (who is actually a very reasonable seller Joel).

3. Kobe/LeBron dual auto MSG inscription /10.
Had multiple chances.

Initially offered via a common friend at $2k to one of biggest inscription Kobe collector in China, Grill,  but the middle person obtained it for himself instead with a bunch of excuses.

I could have chased a few more but was not too crazy about it because back then Panini authentic program was active and you could pay a fee for Kobe to sign an item with inscription. That made inscription less crazy and I felt I always can get a cool inscription in future releases. Then years later, that was made impossible.

The morale of story is to obtain a top asset successfully, it involves several key ingredients
- awareness and on the radar and correct pick
- have conviction and resources which can make decision easier and excuses easier to overcome
- carry it through, not every deal is placed on a silver platter for you, you have to be uncomfortable, go extra mile or even some calculated leap of faith
- keep it until maturation, as many people are part of provenance chain but not at the end of the chain, for liquidity relief or think it’s a good exit while top cards almost never have mid term top, which is why coffin card notion is powerful.

Hobby regret? Not really. Cannot get everything and good to have some imperfection. And good to share some with guys.

I saw some chatter on #PaniniBlockchain mentioning its perceived non-maturation/imperfection to them. For now. But those are temporary. And not priced in. If everything is ready, maximalized and on a silver platter later, they would be priced TF out and say I wish I …

text:
The price mechanic works because it becomes part of the product path, not just promo text.
🧊 three bowls arranged diagonally from front-left foreground to rear-right background
This gives the series a clear scan order. You see the biggest bowl first, then move through the lineup without the poster feeling like a menu.
🍊 giant yellow 3D numerals behind each bowl
This turns “Limited 6” into a physical campaign device. The numbers support the bowl rhythm, guide the eye back to the red banner, and keep the offer instantly readable.

GPT- image 2 prompt👇
Create a Cannes-level flagship quick-service food poster for an original rice noodle brand named BROTHLINE, designed as an English-language launch campaign for a limited-time Rice Noodle Series. Build the image with Orbit x Transit visual logic: preserve the clean ivory vertical poster, the bold red promotional banner, the giant repeated yellow 3D price numerals, the three hero bowls arranged diagonally, and the lower-right endorsement block, while refining the movement path between the bowls and numerals into a clearer closed loop and reducing unnecessary informational noise so the poster feels more iconic, more premium, and more globally launch-ready.

Core layout:
Use a tall vertical poster with a soft ivory-to-warm-cream background and a lightly textured tabletop plane. In the upper center, place a strong red rectangular campaign banner with clean white English typography announcing the Rice Noodle Series and the limited-time value offer. In the upper-right corner, place a compact official brand logo block. Behind the bowls, build three oversized warm-yellow 3D price numerals reading 6 6 6, standing upright like sculptural backdrop objects. Keep them rounded, large, and integrated into the bowl sequence.

Orbit x Transit logic:
Design the three bowls and the three 6 numerals as a controlled circulation path. The eye should begin at the front-left hero bowl, move diagonally upward through the center bowl to the rear-right bowl, then travel across the giant numerals and be redirected back toward the top red banner and down again into the product row. Each bowl angle, placemat direction, and numeral stance should support this loop. At the same time, remove excessive copy, reduce small secondary labels, and keep the whole board flagship-grade and calm rather than cluttered.

Product arrangement:
Place three bowls of rice noodles in a diagonal row from lower-left foreground to upper-right background. The front-left bowl is the largest and closest to camera, the center bowl slightly smaller, and the right-back bowl smallest but still clearly appetizing. Each bowl sits on its own rounded yellow base shape that visually relates to the numeral behind it. Beside each bowl, place one matching golden crispy side cake wrapped in a small branded sleeve. The series must feel cohesive, disciplined, and product-first.

Food identity:
Design a premium rice noodle trio in light savory broth with distinct toppings:
1. Golden Egg Chicken Rice Noodles
2. Pickled Greens Chicken Rice Noodles
3. Pepper Mushroom Beef Rice Noodles
Each bowl must feel hot, fresh, and layered, with realistic broth sheen, silky noodle texture, garnish detail, and appetizing topping realism. Use subtle visible steam and crisp ingredient separation.

Typography system:
Do not use any real brand names or copied wording. Use original English-only typography throughout. Keep the text reduced and premium.
Top brand line:
BROTHLINE
Main red banner:
RICE NOODLE SERIES
LIMITED 6
Small support line:
Each set includes one crispy golden side
Large yellow backdrop numerals:
6 6 6
Near each bowl, keep only very short flavor labels if necessary:
Golden Egg Chicken
Pickled Greens Chicken
Pepper Mushroom Beef
Lower-right statement:
HOT IN 95 SECONDS
FRESHLY SERVED
Typography must feel bold, friendly, globally polished, and launch-ready.

Chef endorsement block:
In the lower-right corner, keep a reduced branded endorsement zone on a warm yellow diagonal panel. Include three professional chefs in clean white uniforms standing near a steaming pot of rice noodles, posed with confidence and warmth. They should remain clearly secondary to the food and main campaign structure, functioning as a small trust-and-craftsmanship signal.

Brand and logo:
Create an original quick-service brand logo for BROTHLINE using a red-and-gold QSR visual language. Use it sparingly: upper-right main logo, tiny sleeve branding on the side cakes, and subtle label accents only.

Lighting and realism:
Use soft premium commercial food lighting with bright frontal clarity and gentle warm highlights. The bowls should feel glossy, hot, and inviting; the crispy side cakes should look freshly fried with realistic crumb texture. The giant yellow numerals must feel like clean sculptural design objects rather than flat text overlays.

Color direction:
Use a tightly controlled palette of warm ivory, QSR red, saturated golden yellow, soft broth beige, fresh herb green, and fried golden accents. The poster must feel bright, optimistic, reduced, craveable, and commercially powerful.

Mood:
orbit-driven, reduced, craveable, premium, fast, clear, launch-ready, globally commercial

Rendering style:
ultra-realistic flagship rice noodle advertising poster, Orbit x Transit QSR campaign, three-bowl series lineup, giant yellow 3D price numerals, red promotional banner, crisp side cakes, reduced chef endorsement block, premium food photography, 8k, world-class commercial design

Negative prompt:
real brand names, copied Chinese text, cluttered flyer look, weak food focus, muddy broth, low-detail noodles, distorted bowls, malformed hands, extra fingers, cheap typography, chaotic layout, low-resolution food rendering, excessive secondary text

text:
New Policy Brief | Food vs Fuel: Recalibrating India's Ethanol Blending Strategy

India hit its E20 target, 20% ethanol in petrol, five years early, with ethanol supply growing at a CAGR of about 38% growth between 2019 to 2025 (5% blending in 2019 to 20% blending in 2025). But the feedstocks it depends on, sugarcane, maize, and rice, grew far more slowly, opening up a food-versus-fuel trade-off already visible in a sugar market where retail prices jumped 44% between July and late August.

Authored by Dr. Ashok Gulati and Mr. Tanmoy Adhikary, this policy brief asks whether blending petrol with 20% ethanol justifies the full economic, energy, and environmental costs of producing the feedstocks E20 requires, costs that current prices and assessments largely leave out. It calls for a more adaptive, market-oriented approach: sugar imports as a buffer, FCI rice priced closer to acquisition cost, feedstock allocation responsive to farm conditions, and an India-specific well-to-tank assessment of sugarcane, maize and rice. In the long term, second-generation ethanol from agricultural residues and other non-food biomass offers a way to expand ethanol use without deepening the food-fuel competition.

SWISS GUARD CALLED TRAITOR FOR EXPOSING BANK SCANDAL
By
PUBLISHED: May 30, 1999 at 4:00 AM EDT | UPDATED: September 24, 2021 at 12:59 AM EDT
In 1997, while working as a security guard at a Swiss bank, Christophe Meile stumbled across Holocaust-era financial documents in the bank’s shredding room. Recognizing they were documents detailing deposits made by Jews during WWII, Meile, 31, took the books home and then turned them in to a local Jewish organization in Zurich.

Meile thought his good deed would end there. But soon he was caught in the whirlwind when local authorities accused him of violating Swiss banking laws — and he was fired.

The books became proof that Switzerland’s banks and government were anything but neutral during WWII.

In his country, Meile became an outcast. He and his family fled after death threats were made against them.

His testimony in the United States spurred a class action lawsuit by Holocaust survivors that resulted in a $1.25 billion settlement last year with three Swiss banks. Meile now lives in New Jersey with his wife Guiseppina, 6-year-old daughter Miriam and 4-year-old son David. He plans to move to California where he will go to school, although he’s not sure what he will study. He also travels around the country, speaking about his experiences. Earlier this week, he visited South Florida.

Q: When you first saw those documents that detailed Jewish holdings in the banks, did you think about what telling would mean?

A: I knew it would have an impact. But on the other hand, it made more sense to preserve every evidence. I turned it over to help the Jewish people. At the time, the World Jewish Congress was pressuring Switzerland to disclose how much money they had from Jews in Swiss bank accounts. So when the finding of the documents became public, the Swiss people went crazy.

Q: What was the initial response?

A: People were angry that I helped the Jews. They told me: “You’re stupid. You don’t know what they’re like. Jewish people are bad.” I was shocked. I’m not even Jewish. I’m Swiss. I feel I did something good. For the Swiss people, I violated Swiss bank laws; I stole the documents; I’m a criminal and a traitor. Most Swiss people feel like that. They don’t agree it was a good thing like the public here in the United States does.

Q: Why do you think they reacted that way?

A: What I did was good for the United States and other countries but not for Switzerland. The Swiss don’t know about genocide. You would think they have the education about the Holocaust. I learned the most about it when I came here to the United States, when I talked to Holocaust victims. After World War II, the whole world changed, but in Switzerland, nothing happened. The whole system moved forward. There was no rebuilding of the country. The old Swiss leaders are still in power. Society was never pushed to think about what their leaders did during the Holocaust. The neutrality was for the normal people. It sounds so good, but for the business society it meant making deals with both sides. It was a tool for business.

Q: When you felt you did the right thing, others called you a traitor. Do you feel like a traitor?

A: You feel they just don’t get it. Germany, France, everybody else understood. People called me to congratulate me, to invite me to speak at events. Only the Swiss went crazy. Today, I still don’t understand. They don’t believe that the Swiss banks, the government were deeply convicted and thinking like the Nazis. People don’t want to believe that the business society worked hand in hand with the Nazis. They can’t believe they’ve been manipulated.

Q: Why did you speak up and not walk away from those documents about to be destroyed?

A: First of all, I’m a Christian. I believe the Bible is true and that Jesus is the Messiah, the boss. If you take him in your heart, he’ll give you a new life. But I also grew up different than the other kids around me. My parents divorced when I was 10. I felt discriminated by being in a family without a father. Maybe this turned me into who I am.

Q: What has your life been like in the U.S.?

A: I like it more here than in Switzerland. People here are more relaxed. They understand what I did. People here respect when someone does something good. I like the openness of American society. People let you breathe here. In Switzerland people attack you. They don’t like people who are different.

For the past two years, I worked on settling the class-action lawsuit case to bring Swiss banks to the negotiation table. I made a decent living from making speeches. I worked as a security guard in New York City for one year, standing at the door. It bored me. Now we’re moving to California. I’m trying to move on, going to a four-year college on a scholarship. I’m happy about that. I live in a two-bedroom apartment in New Jersey, but I think we’ll have more space in California. My wife works as a clerk at my attorney’s office. Now I have a pretty normal life.

Q: You’ve been called a hero by those who praise what you did. Do you feel like one?

A: No. I feel like a normal person. I think that everybody can do something like I did. Everyone has this kind of opportunity.

Q: Have you ever returned to Switzerland?

A: I returned one time to Switzerland for an interview. I stayed at a hotel and had two bodyguards. It was crazy. I wanted to explain to the Swiss people why I did what I did.

Q: Did you succeed in explaining your motives?

A: I don’t think so. A few weeks ago, I posted something on a Swiss related chat room on the Internet and the response back was incredible. One person wrote: “Christophe Meile don’t think you’re still O.K.” I got very angry comments.

Q: What are your feelings for Switzerland now?

A: I’m disappointed. I have trouble with the government there, how they manipulate the people and how the banks control Switzerland. The people are good, but they’ve been used. I can’t go back there. It’s not possible. The banks say I’m the bad guy. People feel that their tax money is paying for the settlement. I don’t feel welcome there. The problem is so long as the government doesn’t apologize in public, the Swiss people will believe that the government and the banks are right and that the Jewish people want to take over the financial power in Switzerland and that Meile helped in that.

How the Vatican's finances work
March 19, 2013, 5:30 AM PDT
By Deborah Caldwell
As Pope Francis assumes leadership of the world's 1.2 billion Catholics, he's got his work cut out for him on many fronts, not the least of which is the Vatican's finances.

Last year, a sheaf of documents was leaked by Pope Emeritus Benedict XVI's former butler in a scandal known as the Vatileaks affair. The documents allegedly showed, for example, tens of millions of dollars in transfers to American dioceses to help pay legal settlements -- estimated to have cost the American church more than $3 billion so far -- surrounding the priest sex-abuse scandals.

During his eight-year tenure, Benedict reportedly made progress toward reforming the Vatican Bank, replacing its president and creating a financial-intelligence committee. But by most accounts, the Vatican Bank still needs greater scrutiny and transparency.

So what is the Vatican Bank, and how is it related to the Catholic Church, and to the finances of Vatican City, a sovereign state? CNBC explains.

What is the Vatican Bank?
It's definitely not your average bank. Officially called the Institute for the Works of Religion, the Vatican Bank is a privately held firm run by a CEO who reports to a committee of cardinals and the Pope. It offers ATMs with transactions in Latin and boasts a small castle-like headquarters protected by Swiss Guards.

It has about 33,000 accounts, a distribution network in more than 100 countries, and an estimated $8 billion in assets. (By contrast, JPMorgan Chase, the largest U.S. bank, has about $2 trillion in assets.)

Details of the account holders are private, though the Vatican says most of the accounts belong to members of the clergy. Because its assets are not the property of the Holy See, it isn't overseen by the Vatican; instead it's considered a charitable foundation affiliated with the Vatican.

What's the controversy about the Vatican Bank?
Where do we begin? It's been controversial for decades, accused of money-laundering and collaborating with the mafia, and before that with the Nazis.

In 1982, the Vatican Bank dealt with its most serious crisis. Roberto Calvi, known as "God's Banker," was found dead, hanging from Blackfriars Bridge in London. At first his death appeared to be a suicide, but eventually five people -- including a mafia member -- were charged with his murder. Calvi was chairman of Banco Ambrosiano, which collapsed after $1.3 billion in loans disappeared; the loans had been made to dummy companies owned by the Vatican Bank, and the Vatican had provided the letters of credit.

More recently, in 2010, the Italian government launched an investigation into the bank's operations after the Bank of Italy alerted police to two suspicious Vatican Bank transactions totaling $30 million. The money was being sent from Credito Artigianato to JP Morgan Chase and another Italian bank, Banca del Fucino. The Vatican Bank apparently didn't disclose the origin of the money, which is a violation of Italian law. Ultimately, the bank denied wrongdoing and the funds were eventually released.

In December 2010, Benedict XVI established the Financial Information Authority as an independent agency to monitor the financial activities of the Vatican Bank and other Vatican-related institutions. Benedict also worked to get the Vatican on to the Organization of Economic Co-operation and Development's "white list" of countries that follow international banking standards.

But the 2012 release of leaked documents — the Vatileaks affair — showed the bank was still struggling with corruption, apparently transferring tens of millions of dollars to American dioceses to help them pay child sex-abuse legal bills. There was also a letter from a senior Vatican official, Archbishop Carlo Maria Vigano, in which he apparently complained of money-laundering and corruption in the Vatican.

Last May, the bank's president, Ettore Gotti Tedeschi, was ousted by the board of directors, accused of money-laundering and not following laws that block financing terrorists and criminal gangs. Tedeschi countered, saying he was fired for getting "too close to the truth."

In January, Italy stopped allowing its banks to do business with the Holy See because of the Vatican Bank's lack of financial transparency. As a result, the Italian banks cut off credit-card processing at tourist spots such as the Sistine Chapel. Some weeks later, plastic was restored after a Swiss firm that doesn't have to abide by EU banking laws came to the rescue.

Then, just before he abdicated the papacy in February, Benedict appointed a new Vatican Bank president, Ernst von Freyberg, a German-born lawyer.

How does this mess impact Pope Francis?
The cardinals will expect Francis to clean up the scandal and modernize the church's finances. If he doesn't, the Vatican could possibly have no access to the global banking system. That situation would undermine its moral authority and its financial stability.

But it won't be easy, because the Vatican hierarchy is divided into various factions. Some want the church's finances to be more transparent to the faithful and the banking world; others want to keep the church's tradition of secrecy.

So how is the Vatican Bank's finances different from the Catholic Church's?
The church in this context is called the Holy See, which includes the offices of the Roman Curia (the church bureaucracy that makes the wheels turn) and its communications outlets.

In 2011, the Holy See brought in $308 million in revenue, with $326 million in expenditures, for a deficit of about $18 million, according to Catholic News Service.

The budget of the Holy See includes the Vatican Secretariat of State and its diplomatic missions around the world, Vatican councils, the Holy See's investment portfolio and properties, plus the Vatican's newspaper, radio, publishing house and television production.

Most of the Holy See's expenditures were related to personnel costs for about 2,800 employees.

Its revenues included about $61 million from the Vatican bank, which donates its investment profits, contributions from dioceses and religious orders, and financial investment returns.

The United States, Germany and Italy give the biggest contributions every year, according to the Vatican.

How are the Vatican Bank's finances and the Catholic Church's finances different from Vatican City's finances?
Vatican City has its own economy supported by contributions from Roman Catholics around the world, and the sale of postage stamps, tourist fees and mementos.

In 2011, Vatican City's revenues were $113 million, with a surplus of about $27 million, according to Catholic News Service.

Since 2002, its currency has been the euro.

Krishna, 
the prince of Dwarika who ended up married to eight queens through eight completely different kinds of trials.

Rukmini, princess of Vidarbha, had loved Krishna from stories alone since childhood, though her brother arranged her marriage to king Shishupala instead. She smuggled Krishna a letter asking him to abduct her before the wedding, and he did, defeating the pursuing armies to make her his chief queen.

Satyabhama entered the story through a scandal. Her father Satrajit falsely accused Krishna of stealing a gem and murdering his brother, and after the truth came out, gave Krishna both the gem and Satyabhama as penance.

Jambavati came from a cave, not a palace. Krishna fought her father, the bear-king Jambavan, in an unbroken 28-day duel before Jambavan recognized him and offered his daughter's hand as an apology.

Kalindi had taken a vow as a child to marry only Vishnu's avatar, and spent years doing penance on the banks of the Yamuna to prove it. Krishna found her there during a forest wanderng and married her on the spot.

Mitravinda loved Krishna in secret while her brothers, close friends of Duryodhana, tried to force her into a political marriage. She chose him anyway, placing the wedding garland around his neck in open defiance at her own swayamvar.

Nagnajiti could only be won by yoking seven ferocious bulls at once, a task that had broken every warrior who attempted it. Krishna split himself into seven simultaneous forms and tamed all seven bulls together.

Bhadra wanted no one but Krishna and said so plainly to her family when her marriage was being arranged. Her brothers respected her wish completely and gave her to him without protest.

Lakshmana was won through an archery contest so difficult it defeated every skilled warrior who tried it. Krishna cleared it with visible ease, and she accepted him gladly, already devoted to him beforehand.

"Better to do your own duty imperfectly than another's perfectly." ~ Krishna, BG

None of these eight marriages happened the same way, each queen tested something different: Loyalty, courage, penance, defiance, justice, strength, devotion, skill.

STOLEN BABIES: COULD TUSLA BE REPEATING THE MISTAKES OF THE PAST?

The BBC documentary Stolen Babies broadcast this week exposes how an estimated 250,000 unmarried mothers across the UK were coerced into surrendering their babies for adoption between 1949 and 1976.

These women were not necessarily abusive or incapable mothers. Many were young, poor and unsupported. Yet social workers, religious organisations and state institutions decided that other people could provide their babies with a “better” future.

The language was professional. The system operated legally. But the consequences were lifelong.

There are disturbing parallels with the removal of newborn babies in Ireland today.

Tusla does not separately publish or appear to centrally record the number of babies removed at birth. We therefore do not know how many mothers leave Irish maternity hospitals without their newborns each year.

Some removals take place because of an assessed risk of possible future emotional harm—not harm that a newborn has already suffered, but harm that professionals predict might occur.

Protecting children from a genuine and evidenced danger is essential. But “possible future emotional harm” is an exceptionally broad and subjective basis for taking a newborn from its mother, particularly when assessments can be contested, family support has not been properly tried and the consequences of separation are themselves profoundly harmful.

The historic forced-adoption system was also justified as acting in children’s “best interests”. Mothers were judged on their circumstances, vulnerability or perceived future ability rather than on harm they had actually caused.

The central warning of Stolen Babies is therefore not confined to history:

When the State removes babies behind closed doors, on the basis of professional predictions that are rarely exposed to public scrutiny, rigorous safeguards and reliable data are indispensable.

At the very least, Tusla should be required to record and publish how many newborn babies are removed at birth, the legal grounds relied upon, what supports were offered beforehand and how many children were ultimately reunited with their families.

We cannot claim to have learned from the past while failing even to count the babies being separated from their mothers today.

These women were not necessarily abusive or incapable mothers. Many were young, poor and unsupported. Yet social workers, religious organisations and state institutions decided that other people could provide their babies with a “better” future.

The language was professional. The system operated legally. But the consequences were lifelong.

There are disturbing parallels with the removal of newborn babies in Ireland today.

Tusla does not separately publish or appear to centrally record the number of babies removed at birth. We therefore do not know how many mothers leave Irish maternity hospitals without their newborns each year.

Some removals take place because of an assessed risk of possible future emotional harm—not harm that a newborn has already suffered, but harm that professionals predict might occur.

Protecting children from a genuine and evidenced danger is essential. But “possible future emotional harm” is an exceptionally broad and subjective basis for taking a newborn from its mother, particularly when assessments can be contested, family support has not been properly tried and the consequences of separation are themselves profoundly harmful.

The historic forced-adoption system was also justified as acting in children’s “best interests”. Mothers were judged on their circumstances, vulnerability or perceived future ability rather than on harm they had actually caused.

The central warning of Stolen Babies is therefore not confined to history:

When the State removes babies behind closed doors, on the basis of professional predictions that are rarely exposed to public scrutiny, rigorous safeguards and reliable data are indispensable.

At the very least, Tusla should be required to record and publish how many newborn babies are removed at birth, the legal grounds relied upon, what supports were offered beforehand and how many children were ultimately reunited with their families.

We cannot claim to have learned from the past while failing even to count the babies being separated from their mothers today.

Every operator I have watched try to launch an info offer and struggle made the same mistake.

They sat down to build a curriculum, produced a bloated body of material nobody asked for, and had no idea what to do with the material once assembled. Then abandoned the whole project because the work felt like a second full-time job bolted onto the first one.

The build is four decisions, and each decision constrains the next in sequence.

Decision one: sell the transformation rather than the topic.

Nobody buys "Meta ads." They buy the state of no longer having to think about lead flow every morning. A topic sits on a comparable shelf next to a hundred others. A transformation belongs to you.

The test is simple. Finish this sentence without naming a subject: this takes someone from  to .

If you cannot fill both blanks with a state rather than a skill, you are holding a topic. Go back and find the transformation underneath.

Decision 2: pick the delivery format the expertise fits.

Some expertise transfers through explanation alone, which fits a program. Some only transfers through application against a specific situation, which fits consulting or a mastermind. Some does not transfer at all in a reasonable timeframe, and the honest version of the offer is done-with-you implementation.

Choosing wrong here is the single most common reason info offers produce bad outcomes and refund requests.

The material was fine. The container carrying the material was not.

Decision 3: pull the method out of what you already do.

This is where "I do not have time" shows up. The objection assumes you are going to invent something new.

You are not. Your method already exists inside the business, running quietly every day.

Fragmented across Slack threads, Loom recordings from 2023 nobody has watched since, onboarding docs nobody reads, and the muscle memory of having run the same process a few hundred times. None of the fragments qualify as a product yet. ALL of them are the raw material for one.

Fastest extraction I have seen work: record yourself explaining your process to someone unfamiliar with the work, one sitting, zero preparation. Then record yourself answering their questions.

Raw material collected this way contains more usable structure than a month of deliberate curriculum design.

Decision four: price on the outcome rather than on access to you.

If the transformation is worth a meaningful amount to the buyer over twelve months, the price should reflect a fraction of the value rather than a multiple of your hours.

Pricing on hours caps you at exactly the ceiling the main business already has. Which defeats the entire point.

And then version one should be as small as possible.

One transformation, stated clearly. A calendar, a payment link, and a documented method you already run.

Sell before the offer exists in final form. Deliver live to the first cohort.

The first delivery IS the curriculum development, because you find out where people stall by watching them stall rather than by predicting stall points in a planning document.

9 out of 10 operators try to launch at version 3, which stays unbuildable from a standing start because version 3 depends on information only version one produces.

The Knights of Malta (historically known as the Knights Hospitaller or the Order of St. John) have deep historical ties to the areas in and around London’s Square Mile (the City of London).
While their primary medieval English headquarters was located just north of the City walls in Clerkenwell, they took ownership of significant property directly inside and bordering the Square Mile through major historical events.
1. The Temple District & Temple Church
The most prominent footprint of the Order directly bordering the Square Mile is the Temple district (located between Fleet Street and the River Thames).
The Takeover: This land originally belonged to their fierce medieval rivals, the Knights Templar. When the Templars were dissolved and suppressed by the Pope in 1312, a papal bull transferred their vast property portfolio over to the Knights Hospitaller (Knights of Malta).
The Legal Hub: The Hospitallers primarily treated the Temple property as a source of rental income. They leased the land out to professors and practitioners of law. These tenants eventually established the famous Inner Temple and Middle Temple—two of London's four Inns of Court that still dominate the legal landscape of the City today.
The Architecture: The stunning 12th-century Temple Church, famous for its circular nave mimicking Jerusalem's Holy Sepulchre, officially belonged to the Hospitallers for over two centuries until Henry VIII seized it during the Reformation.
2. Clerkenwell Priory (Just Outside the Walls)
Though situated just a short walk north of the Square Mile's formal boundary, the Order's true power center in London was the Clerkenwell Priory.
Established in the 1140s, this massive 10-acre fortified precinct served as the administrative and financial hub for all of England.
From here, the Order managed profits from hundreds of British estates to fund their crusader castles and naval fleets in the Mediterranean (first in Rhodes, and later Malta).
Today, you can still visit the surviving St. John’s Gate and the medieval crypt beneath the Museum of the Order of St John in Clerkenwell.
3. Modern Presence
The modern continuation of the order, the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, remains very active in London. Their primary religious activities and Grand Priory of England chapter room are located today at 23 Golden Square in London's West End, while their main British administrative office operates out of Putney.

The Knights Templar
From A Brief Historical Description by Professor Sir John Baker QC LLD FBA
Master of the Bench

The history of the Temple begins soon after the middle of the twelfth century, when a contingent of knights of the Military Order of the Temple of Solomon in Jerusalem moved from the Old Temple in Holborn (later Southampton House) to a larger site between Fleet Street and the banks of the River Thames. The new site originally included much of what is now Lincoln’s Inn, and the knights were probably responsible for establishing New Street (later Chancery Lane), which led from Holborn down to their new quarters. Following their custom, the knights built a round church patterned on the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem. An inscription on the Round recorded that it was consecrated by the Patriarch Heraclius on 10 February 1185, in honour of the Blessed Virgin Mary. It is thought that King Henry II was also present on that day, inaugurating a long association between the royal family and the Temple.

Among the other buildings erected by the knights were dormitories, storehouses, stables, chambers, and two dining halls, one of them in the consecrated central portion and connected with the church by a cloister. It was a house fit for kings to stay in, and several did so. During a visit by King John in January 1215 he received a deputation of barons demanding a charter of liberties; and when the Great Charter was signed later in the year, the Master of the Temple was one of the witnesses. The knights took advantage of their special privileges to make their sanctuary a safe place for depositing treasure, and during the thirteenth century the New Temple became a busy financial centre. It was no doubt during this period that the first handful of lawyers came to live in the Temple, not as distinct societies but as legal advisers to a wealthy international organisation. The Templars thrived, adding to their round church a fine nave, which was consecrated in the presence of King Henry III in 1240. Many knights associated with the order were buried in the church, the most distinguished being William Marshal (d. 1219), first Earl of Pembroke and regent of England, the very model of medieval English chivalry, and one of the instigators of Magna Carta. Marshal’s armoured effigy, battered by time and war, may still be seen in the Round.

After losing the Holy Land in the 1290s, the order of the Temple fell into a decline. The knights were dubiously accused of improprieties, and in 1312 their order was dissolved. Although the pope granted their estates to the Knights Hospitaller of St John of Jerusalem, King Edward II seized the New Temple as forfeit to the Crown. Nevertheless, the consecrated portion was conceded to the Hospitallers, and the remainder was sold to them later.

Kathryn Lee Boyd, Pepperdine University Law School, Malibu, CA;  Jonathan H. Levy, Cincinnati, OH;  Thomas Easton, Eugene, OR, for the plaintiffs-appellants. Jeffrey S. Lena, Law Offices of Jeffrey S. Lena, Berkeley, CA, for defendant-appellee Istituto per le Opere di Religione, sued as the Vatican Bank. Paul E. AMENDED OPINION AND AMENDED CONCURRENCE/DISSENT

 We are faced here with the question whether claims for losses allegedly suffered at the hands of a Nazi puppet regime during World War II are cognizable in our courts today.   Because these claims, at least superficially, touch on foreign relations and potentially controversial political issues, it is tempting to jump to the conclusion that such claims are barred by the political question doctrine.   The Supreme Court has counseled, however, that “it is error to suppose that every case or controversy which touches foreign relations lies beyond judicial cognizance.”  Baker v. Carr, 369 U.S. 186, 211, 82 S.Ct. 691, 7 L.Ed.2d 663 (1962).   The justiciability inquiry is limited to “ ‘political questions,’ not ․ ‘political cases,’ ” id. at 217, 82 S.Ct. 691, and should be made on a “case-by-case” basis, id. at 211, 82 S.Ct. 691.

Although the political question doctrine often lurks in the shadows of cases involving foreign relations, it is infrequently addressed head on.   See, e.g., Hwang Geum Joo v. Japan, 332 F.3d 679, 682 (D.C.Cir.2003), vacated and remanded by 542 U.S. 901, 124 S.Ct. 2835, 159 L.Ed.2d 265 (2004) (explaining that because the district court did not have subject matter jurisdiction in case involving World War II-era claims against Japan, “[n]or ․ need we consider whether the political question doctrine would also bar its adjudication”).   The procedural posture of this case, however, places the issue squarely before us.

With these principles in mind, in determining the threshold issue of justiciability, we scrutinize each claim individually.   Indeed, in our system of separation of powers, we should not abdicate the court's Article III responsibility-the resolution of “cases” and “controversies”-in favor of the Executive Branch, particularly where, as here, the Executive has declined a long-standing invitation to involve itself in the dispute.   We conclude that some of the claims are barred by the political question doctrine and some of the claims are justiciable.   Although the parties have multiple procedural and substantive challenges to overcome down the road, they are entitled to their day-or years-in court on the justiciable claims.

A group of twenty-four individuals and four organizations (the “Holocaust Survivors”) claim that the Vatican Bank, known by its official title Istituto per le Opere di Religione, the Order of Friars Minor, and the Croatian Liberation Movement (Hrvatski Oslobodilacki Pokret ), profited from the genocidal acts of the Croatian Ustasha political regime (the “Ustasha”), which was supported throughout World War II by Nazi forces.   That profit allegedly passed through the Vatican Bank in the form of proceeds from looted assets and slave labor.   The Holocaust Survivors brought suit in federal court claiming conversion, unjust enrichment, restitution, the right to an accounting, and human rights violations and violations of international law arising out of the defendants' alleged involvement with the Ustasha during and following World War II.

 The Vatican Bank and the Order of Friars Minor moved to dismiss the Holocaust Survivors' complaint on multiple grounds;  by agreement of the parties the district court limited its discussion to the issue of whether the Holocaust Survivors' claims should be dismissed under the political question doctrine.   The district court reasoned that the political question doctrine bars consideration of the merits of the claims in their entirety.   The district court dismissed the action against the Croatian Liberation Movement, which never appeared in the action, on the grounds that the claims were barred by both the political question doctrine and the lack of personal jurisdiction over this defendant.   We reverse in part because certain of the Holocaust Survivors' claims-those with respect to lost and looted property (conversion, unjust enrichment, restitution, and an accounting)-are not barred by this doctrine.   In contrast, the broad human rights allegations tied to the Vatican Bank's alleged assistance to the war objectives of the Ustasha present nonjusticiable controversies.   Like the district court, we hold that the court did not have personal jurisdiction over the Croatian Liberation Movement.1  Consequently, we see no reason to reach the political question doctrine vis-à-vis this defendant.

 Bearing in mind that “[t]he decision to deny access to judicial relief is not one we make lightly,” Liu v. Republic of China, 892 F.2d 1419, 1433 (9th Cir.1989) (quoting Int'l Ass'n of Machinists & Aerospace Workers v. OPEC, 649 F.2d 1354, 1360 (9th Cir.1981)), we conclude that the political question doctrine does not create an absolute barrier to the Holocaust Survivors' property claims.   To conclude otherwise would be to shirk our judicial role as “[c]ourts in the United States have the power, and ordinarily the obligation, to decide cases and controversies properly presented to them.”  W.S. Kirkpatrick & Co. v. Envtl. Tectonics Corp., Int'l, 493 U.S. 400, 409, 110 S.Ct. 701, 107 L.Ed.2d 816 (1990).

That said, it bears noting that our initial determination of justiciability in no way reflects any judgment on the threshold legal hurdles that must be overcome or the merits of the claims.   Much of the dissent focuses on downstream issues related to potential procedural and substantive pitfalls of the claims.   We do not discount the difficulties that may lie ahead;  however, consideration of those issues is premature.   Given the passage of time, the generality of the allegations, the question of the applicability of the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act, intricacies of the alleged claims, the class certification issues, whether the claimants have a cognizable legal claim, and a myriad of other procedural and jurisdictional hurdles, the Holocaust Survivors may indeed face an uphill battle in pursuing their claims.   But this spectre of difficulty down the road does not inform our justiciability determination at this early stage of the proceedings.

Dr @ShashiTharoor articulating true essence of Hinduism, it is not a rigid creed but a lived, intellectually open way of being that fits a liberal temperament. He starts with the obvious: he was born Hindu. Most people inherit their faith by geography and family. The more interesting question is what that actually means. Hinduism has No founder or prophet
No organized church or pope
No compulsory beliefs or rites
No single sacred book that everyone must accept
Not even a required belief in God
A Catholic, Muslim, Jew, Parsi, or Sikh has core doctrines they must affirm. A Hindu does not. There is no binding credo.
Dr Tharoor values this because it matches how he already lives: accept people as they are, let them become what they choose, and do not harm others. He can follow rituals or ignore them, worship one deity or many or none, fast or not, go to a temple or never go. The tradition offers a “smorgasbord” of options rather than a checklist.
He especially loves the tradition’s capacity to hold both wonder at creation and radical skepticism. He quotes the Nasadiya Sukta from the Rig Veda (roughly 3,500 years old):
Who knows whence this creation had its origin?
He, whether He fashioned it or whether He did not,
He who surveys it all from the highest heaven,
He knows — or maybe even He does not know.
A faith that can ask whether even the creator knows how the universe began is, for him, uniquely honest and intellectually attractive.
In short: he is Hindu because the tradition does not demand that he stop thinking, stop questioning, or stop being himself. It is a religion without fundamentals in the dogmatic sense — and that, to him, is the point.

text:
🏎️ The 2026 "Temple of Speed" is setting up the biggest engineering puzzle on the calendar. With the new regulations splitting power evenly between the ICE and the battery, drivers will virtually have to relearn how to drive Monza.

📌 Why this weekend will be a brutal test for hybrids and active aerodynamics:

🔋 Battery thermal limits and aggressive clipping: The 5 MJ limit per qualifying lap is extremely tight for a circuit featuring four massive straights. In race trim, drivers will constantly rely on lift-and-coast well before their braking points to keep the battery charged. Beyond 290 km/h, acceleration drops off visibly due to power derating caps (50 kW/s), leaving cars running out of breath near the end of long straights.

⚙️ Power throttling between Turns 4 and 7: Capping MGU-K output to 250 kW through the sector between the first and second chicanes (Variante della Roggia and the Lesmos) forces drivers to manually meter energy deployment, conserving charge for the exits onto Serravalle and the main straight.

✈️ Four Straight Mode (Active Aero) zones: Shedding wing levels on every straight significantly lowers drag, but it doesn't fully solve energy deficit issues. Running minimum wing angles reduces downforce even further through Ascari and the Parabolica, leaving cars sliding continuously through high-speed turns.

🛞 Tyre management and rear overheating: Bringing the C3, C4, and C5 compounds to Monza's smooth asphalt offers exceptional single-lap pace, but rear tyres face heavy thermal degradation during long stints. Wheelspin on exit from slow chicanes combined with trimmed downforce packages rapidly degrades the rear axle, though teams will push one-stop strategies to avoid the long 23-second pit-lane penalty time.

🛡️ The turbine factor: The ultimate wildcard will be how differences in turbine efficiency impact acceleration out of the Parabolica. If Ferrari's updated turbine delivers its promised +15 hp gains, the Scuderia could hold a decisive upper hand at the end of the main straight against rivals suffering heavy clipping.

text:
You have misunderstood the Galileo affair slightly. 

The Galileo affair started due to the toxic dispute between Galileo and his academic rivals, the Pigeon League. They were frequently insulting each other. Galileo had been given an Imprimatur for his heliocentric "Letters on Sunspots" in 1613. But in 1616 the Roman Inquisition ruled that heliocentrism had to be held as a hypothesis. Why? Well, because Galileo circulated his "Letter to Castelli", where once again he insulted the Pigeon league, but now he also told Theologians how to interpret the Bible. He argued that a literal reading of a few scriptural texts was wrong, and when read correctly, the Bible supported heliocentrism best. The Pigeon League saw this as an opportunity and took the letter to the Roman Inquisition, which was obliged to rule on the subject.

The Roman Inquisition consulted astronomers in 1616, as Galileo himself attests in his letter to Ingoli. They argued that the evidence was for the Tychonic model (it was the consensus at the time). The Inquisition also consulted Theologians, who deemed it that scripture shouldn't be interpreted based on an unproved hypothesis. Ergo, the Roman inquisition ruled that heliocentrism had to be held as a hypothesis, and couldn't be used to reinterpret scripture.

Galileo was still held in high regard after 1616. He was given a canonry at Pisa and a Prebend at Brescia on top of his hefty salary as Court Mathematician to the Grand Duke of Tuscany.

Galileo was put on trial in 1633 for breaking his 1616 court order, cheating the censors, and implicating the Pope in the action, since the Pope had commissioned the Dialogue.

The verbal threat of torture wasn't to do with recanting. Galileo had already started abjuring from the start of his 1633 deposition. He claimed that he had always supported geocentrism and that the Dialogue had actually disproved Copernicus. Everyone knew this was a lie. The threat of torture was brought in the 4th deposition to try and get Galileo to acknowledge that he had in fact supported heliocentrism. He had also been offered a plea deal to admit this and be given a lesser sentence. He didn't back down and continued to claim he had always been a geocentrist and never aimed to argue for Copernicanism. He only bent a little, saying that the Dialogue may have been too favourable for Copernicus (but that he hadm't intended this). The Roman Inquisition wasn't allowed to torture the elderly or frail, and he was both, so they left it at that.

His punishment was excessive, but not as awful as a lot of people imagine. He was put under house arrest which he served first in the town house of the Archbishop of Siena, then in his Tuscan countryside mansion. He had servants and was granted scientific assistants. His books were banned, and he was also given a penance to recite psalms daily.

text:
Three years after San Miguel Corp. chair Ramon Ang promised that Bulacan would have no flooding problems by 2024, his words have resurfaced as severe floods hit the province and neighboring Pampanga, with critics and some residents pointing to the Bulacan Aerotropolis as a possible factor in the worsening situation.

Ang made the promise in a 2023 interview while discussing the Bulacan Aerotropolis—a massive airport and mixed-use development in Bulacan—and its potential impact on flooding in Bulacan and Pampanga.

To be clear, Ang was speaking as a businessman, not a government official. He was under no government mandate to solve the provinces’ flooding problems. But he offered the assurance himself, confidently and with a specific timeline.
That is why the old interview is getting a second look now.

Ang spoke with broadcaster Anthony Taberna in an interview uploaded to the YouTube channel Tune In Kay Tunying on Sept. 14, 2023. The discussion covered several of San Miguel’s business ventures, including the Bulacan Aerotropolis.

At the time, Ang was responding to claims that the airport project had worsened flooding in neighboring Pampanga. He rejected the connection, saying flooding had already been a problem before construction began.

But while distancing the project from the flooding, Ang also said San Miguel would help address the problem.

“’Yung pagbabaha sa malalayong lugar, wala naman kaming kinalaman diyan. Pero sa gayunpaman, nangangako ako… dahil ’yung mga kababayan nating ordinaryong tao [ay] affected, ’yung buong Bulacan na ’yan, itotodo namin ’yung paglilinis na ’yan. Siguro ’yan next year, 2024, wala na silang problema,” Ang said.

He extended that commitment to Pampanga, saying residents there would also benefit from the airport and that San Miguel would help clean and maintain the rivers in both provinces.

“Kapitbahay nating Pampanga, kailangan tulungan din natin, na travelers or peoples of Pampanga coming to the airport will have no problem. Kahit bumabagyo, kahit umuulan nang malakas, wala na problema ’yan, kasi nilinis na, eh. And we will maintain it. Hindi lang minsan lilinisin tapos na. Hindi. Lilinisin nang husto ’yan and imamaintain ’yan every year, Bulacan rivers and Pampanga rivers,” he told Taberna.

Now the reality is more complicated.

LONGSTANDING CAUSES
Bulacan remains vulnerable to flooding because of its low-lying geography, limited river capacity, upstream water flows, land subsidence and heavy rainfall, among other factors. San Miguel Aerocity Inc. has also pointed to rising sea levels and continued development across the province as additional pressures on the interconnected watershed.

On Aug. 29, portions of the North Luzon Expressway in Bulacan and Pampanga were flooded, with motorists and commuters reporting trips that stretched for several hours as they tried to reach or leave Metro Manila.

For ordinary residents and commuters, the question is therefore bigger than whether an airport project can single-handedly solve a province’s longstanding flooding problem.

It is also about what happened to the measures Ang said would address it.
San Miguel says it has been working on flooding concerns, including through river dredging and clearing efforts. The company said it removed more than 1 million metric tons of silt and waste from three rivers near the airport from 2022 to 2024, while its broader river-cleanup program in Bulacan had removed more than 4.3 million metric tons of silt and waste as of Aug. 18, 2026.

Ang has also recently pointed to clogged and constricted waterways as contributors to flooding and offered to help clear a suspected blockage near Tulaoc Bridge in San Simon, Pampanga. He said the blockage could be preventing water from Pantabangan Dam from flowing toward the Pampanga River.

Ang has pushed back against the idea that the airport caused the flooding.
At a Sept. 1 briefing, he pointed to Bulakan’s low elevation, narrow and winding rivers and low bridges as factors behind flooding in the area. He also rejected claims that the airport blocked river systems.

San Miguel Aerocity Inc. said on Sept. 3 that the New Manila International Airport project did not involve reclamation and reiterated that its construction did not cause flooding in the areas concerned. The company said the airport was designed around Bulacan’s longstanding flood risks, with studies examining river systems, coastal waters, rainfall, storm surges and land subsidence.

RISKS FLAGGED BEFORE CONSTRUCTION
Critics of the project have made a different case.

Before development began in 2021, experts had already warned about potential environmental and geological risks associated with building on the site.

During a 2020 Senate hearing on the airport’s franchise, then-Phivolcs director and current Science and Technology Secretary Renato Solidum Jr. warned that the area was vulnerable because of its soil and shallow water table.

“The area is mainly underlain by sand and the water table is very shallow (...) This environment would require special engineering intervention to make building and infrastructure resilient to hazards due to earthquake events or to other related activities such a heavy rainfall,” Solidum said.

The People’s Network for the Integrity of Coastal Habitats and Ecosystems also warned in 2020 that reclamation associated with the project could cause coastal erosion and worsen flooding in nearby areas.

San Miguel has maintained that the airport project did not involve reclamation.
The debate became more heated on Sept. 1, when Ang offered ₱1 million to anyone who could identify alleged anonymous critics making accusations against the Aerotropolis.

Ang did not specify the allegations covered by the offer but described the criticism as “paninira.”

Human rights lawyer Tony La Viña said the threat could constitute a strategic lawsuit against public participation, or SLAPP, intended to suppress criticism and public debate.

So what happened?

The evidence available today does not establish that the Aerotropolis caused the flooding. But neither does the continued flooding make Ang’s 2023 promise disappear.

Bulacan’s flooding has longstanding causes, and this year’s widespread flooding came after weeks of heavy rain. San Miguel says it has been dredging waterways and incorporating flood-mitigation measures into the airport project. Critics, meanwhile, continue to question whether the development has altered how water moves through the area.

What is harder to dispute is what Ang himself said three years ago.

He did not merely say San Miguel would study the flooding problem or try to help. He said the company would clean up Bulacan’s rivers, extend the effort to Pampanga and maintain the waterways every year. Most notably, he said that by 2024, residents would have no problem with flooding.

Today, Ang’s explanation is that flooding in Bulacan is tied to conditions that predate the airport, including its low elevation and constrained waterways.
That may help explain why flooding persists. But it also puts his 2023 assurance in a different light.

The airport may not be the sole answer to Bulacan’s flooding problem, and the evidence presented so far does not establish it as the cause of the latest floods.
But Ang made the promise himself.

Now, as residents wade through flooded communities and commuters endure hours on major roads, they have every reason to look back at those words and ask a very simple question: What happened to the solution promised by 2024?

(✍🏼: Kenneth M. del Rosario, with reports from Kiara Gorrospe)

Starlink統合は、車両の通信品質向上 → 自動運転の信頼性向上につながる可能性。

テスラ(TSLA)は金曜日からテキサス州オースティンの「限定エリア」でサイバーキャブの乗車を開始し、待望のローンチイベントはやや控えめな形で終了しました。

イベントに関しては、公開ライブ配信やジャーナリストの参加はありませんでした。招待者リストは非常に短く、主にテスラ支持(TSLA)のコンテンツクリエイターで構成されていたとThe Vergeは報じました。

参加者はイーロン・マスクがイベントを欠席したとロイターに語りました。経営陣はサイバーキャブの製造プロセスと技術について約15分間議論しました。

📷サイバーキャブ(テスラ)
このゴールデンの2人乗り車両は、ステアリングホイールやペダルを使わず、カメラビジョンとセンサーを用いてナビゲーションを行っています。テスラ(TSLA)は以前、コストが3万ドル未満になると述べていました。

国家高速道路交通安全局(NHTSA)はテスラ(TSLA)と連絡を取っており、状況を評価中であると述べています。連邦の安全基準は通常、人間の管理を必要とします。

Starlink V5はSpaceX(SPCX)の衛星インターネットサービスで、まもなくCybercabに直接統合され、シームレスな接続を実現します。

商業目的でサイバーキャブ車両や個別のサイバーキャブを購入するに興味のある方は、興味申請書に記入できます。

text:
Oslo Quietly Loosens Its Grip on Uncle Sam’s IOUs

Norway’s $2.3 trillion oil fund, the world’s largest, has written to the Finance Ministry proposing that government bonds shrink from 70 to 50 percent of its fixed income benchmark. Since US Treasuries are by far the biggest slab of that pile, more than two trillion kroner of them, Washington’s most reliable creditor is politely suggesting it would rather hold something else.

The official reasoning is dry as a Treasury auction. Nicolai Tangen and central bank governor Ida Wolden Bache want to weight sovereign debt by market value rather than GDP, and shift money into corporate bonds and mortgage-backed securities, which they argue offer better returns and still cushion equity crashes. 

Parliament has to approve it, and nobody in Oslo will say the word Trump out loud.

Nobody needs to. The clip is the Treasury Secretary blaming Ukraine for fuel prices, for the crime of hitting Russian refineries rather than the country that invaded it. It has nothing to do with bond benchmarks, and everything to do with why a careful Nordic creditor is checking the exits. 

Whenever Washington has to choose a side, it keeps landing on Moscow’s, and the people who used to queue up for American debt have noticed.

text:
ATP US Open

 Jiri Lehecka vs Stefanos Tsitsipas

🧠 Form & Context

Jiri Lehecka

✅ Cleaner route: Lehecka beat Pablo Carreno Busta in four sets and qualifier Toby Samuel in straight sets.

📊 Slight statistical edge: He leads the CFS 59.9 to 58.4 and owns marginally better last-year hard and overall win rates.

🚀 Hard-court ceiling: A Miami final run this season and a 2025 US Open quarterfinal demonstrate his upside in these conditions.

🔁 Recent H2H success: He won both 2024 meetings with Tsitsipas in straight sets, including their Indian Wells hard-court match.

🩺 Fitness cannot be ignored: Retirements in Brisbane 2026, Rotterdam 2025 and Madrid 2024 remain relevant in a best-of-five contest.

Stefanos Tsitsipas

🔥 Confidence-restoring first round: He came from a set down to beat the higher-ranked Arthur Fils in four sets.

🧱 Follow-up completed: He then recovered from losing a first-set tiebreak to defeat qualifier Lloyd Harris in four.

🎯 Better recent elite conversion: His 5–7 Top 20 record across the last year is stronger than Lehecka’s 3–8.

👑 Former elite ceiling: His current ranking of 53 understates the experience of a former world No. 3 and multiple major finalist.

🩺 Matching durability concern: Retirements at Wimbledon and Barcelona in 2025, plus the 2023 ATP Finals, matter over five sets.

🔍 Match Breakdown

The market sees a clear favourite; the form numbers do not. Both players are 6–4 in their last 10, their hard-court rates are separated by less than three percentage points, and the CFS gap is only 1.5. Tsitsipas also owns the better Top 20 record, which directly challenges the idea that the ranking gap tells the whole story.

Lehecka’s route is to serve efficiently and attack Tsitsipas’s one-handed backhand before the Greek can use his forehand to control the court. His two 2024 wins show that he can execute this pattern. Tsitsipas must protect the backhand return side, use forehand height and depth to disrupt Lehecka’s strike zone, and prevent the Czech from settling into short, linear points.

Fitness does not offer a clean separator because both have meaningful retirement histories. Lehecka’s straighter route through New York provides a modest freshness advantage, while Tsitsipas’s victory over Fils is the better single quality win.

🔮 Prediction

Lehecka remains the narrow choice because of his recent H2H, cleaner tournament route and marginal hard-court edge. The evidence does not support treating him as comfortably superior, and Tsitsipas has shown enough this week to make an upset entirely plausible.

text:
A Tale of Bulls, Bears and Whales

September 2025

The market is frustrated. Bitcoin isn't performing, and anyone who tried altcoins got their fingers burned. No altseason. The market just crawls sideways, trades in a range, good news doesn't land anymore, every rally gets sold into immediately.

But there's still the BOT — the blow-off top that always comes in the post-halving year. That's what makes all of this worth it. That's where the big payday is.

End of September, price slips again, stalls, waits a few days. Some give up in frustration. But most are still strung tight as a bowstring.

And then — what's this? Price is climbing. A little more every day. Should we get back in? It's early October. Here we go.

The herd is euphoric, scraping together every last cent it can find, and when there's nothing left, it levers up hard. Price keeps climbing. No pullback. A goddamn lockout rally.

We're just short of the ATH. And then? ATH broken! Euphoria. Now the rocket lifts off — a magnificent 1.5% above the old high.

But wait. A pullback? Over a few days, a little correction. Just a small storm cloud, nothing more. The whole herd is standing at the edge of the cliff and doesn't know it.

People go to sleep. Then comes the spark that lights the mixture. First price dips gently, then it rips straight through the order books and liquidates everything that isn't nailed down.

The bulls are slaughtered so thoroughly they won't recover for a long time. Their unshakeable faith in a green post-halving year and a Q4 blow-off top made them easy prey. For months they ignored the warning signs: great news moved nothing, bad news moved price down instantly.

## 2026

After the bull slaughter of 10/10, more and more bears appear on the scene. They tell the old stories, how it used to be. They bring the prophecy of the bear market, draw their lines and say: look, break below this and the bull is history.

At first only a few are convinced. Then, in early 2026, the next liquidation cascade hits. More and more bulls fall over. The narrative seems to be right.

A few incorrigible bulls are still walking around. More and more they get laughed at — exactly the way they laughed at the bears back in late 2025.

There, the countermove! It was only a pause. And then the next fat liquidation cascade. We're already at –50%.

Now almost nobody doubts the bear market anymore. Except those who never cared, because they started feeding so early that no winter can touch them.

And then, after endless back and forth, the first tender spring flowers. Some start feeling bullish again. And it continues, a whole month long. But there, it stalls again. The early risers are still standing there in disbelief when the next winter storm breaks over them and destroys their hope.

The bears are triumphant. They've converted so many now that they sit firmly in the saddle.

But what's this? Just below the last low, nothing happens. What's going on? We should be far lower by now. Two months: nothing.

The bears remain certain. Payday is coming. In October, because it always has. They sit on the sidelines and watch. Nothing can shake them — as little as anything could shake the bulls in 2025.

The whole time, the whales are swimming in the sea, feeding on the remains of the bulls. Through their mouthpieces they spread the story: bears, your reward is coming. In October you'll eat well.

Here and there another early bull or late bear tips over, the remains wash into the sea and the whales eat. But it gets less every day. The whales grow impatient, more and more of them arrive wanting to feed. It's only August, and it looks like there isn't enough left for everyone.

Meanwhile the bears have prepared for payday. The money bags are ready, the greed is growing. They lever up — that makes the certain payday even richer, compensation for a completely botched bull market.

The whales, though, notice something: it's not just that no food is coming in, it's that the only thing being sold now is borrowed. And they can only feed if price goes up. So they wait, and they fan the belief in the October bottom — exactly as they did in 2025.

Then the moment comes. A favorable news backdrop, and they go. They light the pile — and it works: the largest short squeeze in history.

It lasts three days. And then? Some sell again, some for the first time. Which only makes the October payday bigger. The bears already see the bulls back on the chopping block — but they have nothing left to offer the whales.

Price drifts again. Almost two weeks. Then the next blow. The bears are patient, they believe their payday must come. But the number of whales and bulls is rising. There, the two megawhales are feeding again. The old bulls keep feeding too.

And the great feeding and redistribution has been running for two and a half years now.

---

So — are you one of the bears who's certain payday has to come in October, at much lower prices?

History rhymes, but it often sets traps.

When everyone knows exactly how it's going to play out, when everyone knows the train has only so many seats — do you wait until they all want in at the same time? Or do you get there early, take your seat, and wait patiently for the train to leave? If one thing is proven in markets: time in the market beats timing the market. Don´t get fooled by the wrong narratives.

FLORIDA MAN TELLS JUDGE THE GOAT LET ITSELF INTO HIS TRUCK AND HE MERELY DROVE IT HOME

BROOKSVILLE, FLORIDA — Kyle Renner, 34, appeared in court to explain why a full-grown goat was found riding in the bed of his pickup truck during a routine traffic stop, insisting the goat had "climbed in on its own at a gas station" and he'd simply "given it a lift out of decency."

Investigators say the goat was discovered standing calmly among a stack of lawn equipment, seemingly unbothered by the entire ordeal.

Claimed the goat "jumped the tailgate itself" while he was pumping gas
Admitted to driving twelve miles with the goat before officers pulled him over
Told the judge he "figured it belonged to somebody eventually, further down the road"
Had reportedly stopped twice to offer the goat water from a gas station cup
Insisted he "never once tried to claim ownership, just transportation services"

The gas station clerk reportedly confirmed a goat had indeed been wandering the lot for roughly twenty minutes before Kyle's truck pulled away with it aboard.

"Fifteen years on this bench and I've never had a defendant describe himself as a goat's rideshare driver," said Judge Melissa Farrow, Hernando County Court, 15 years of service.

The goat has since been returned to its rightful owner two farms over and declined to comment.

A truck bed is not an open invitation for livestock.
Kyle apparently interpreted it that way, twelve miles down the road.

text:
5️⃣ Practice the Interview Before They Do
Paste the company’s values, job description, and your resume:
“Act as the hiring manager for this role.
Ask me 10 realistic behavioral and role-specific interview questions based on the job description and company values.
After each answer, score me from 1–10, explain what was weak, and show me how to improve without sounding scripted.”
Don’t practice until you feel ready.
Practice until you're actually ready.
6️⃣ Build Your LinkedIn Presence

“I’m targeting [ROLE] positions in [INDUSTRY].

Create a 30-day LinkedIn content strategy that demonstrates my expertise and makes my profile more attractive to recruiters.

Give me post ideas, hooks, formats, and a simple posting schedule.

Base everything on my real experience.”

You don't need to become an influencer.
You need recruiters to understand what you're good at.
7️⃣ Prepare Your Salary Negotiation
You get the offer.
Don't immediately say yes.
Paste the offer and your achievements:
“Help me negotiate this offer professionally.
Analyze the proposed compensation, my experience, measurable achievements, role scope, and available market benchmarks.
Give me a negotiation strategy, target range, fallback position, and a concise script I can use with the recruiter.”
Getting the offer is only half the job.

Negotiating it matters too.

8️⃣ Find Jobs Before Everyone Else

“Based on my profile, identify 15 companies in [INDUSTRY] where my skills could be valuable.

Prioritize companies that are growing or may hire for roles like mine even when there isn't an obvious public opening.

For each company, suggest a legitimate way to identify the appropriate hiring manager or recruiter and create a personalized outreach strategy.

Do not invent names, openings, or hiring activity.”

Because sometimes the best opportunity isn't the job you found on a job board.

It's the company you found before the job was posted.

My friend signed his contract 10 days later.

The first thing he said was:

“Why didn’t you show me this earlier?” 😂

AI won't magically get you hired.

But it can help you:

Find better opportunities → tailor your application → improve your CV → prepare for interviews → reach the right people → negotiate better.

Stop treating your job search like a numbers game.

Use AI to make every application count.

Save this thread. 🔖

You might need it sooner than you think.

text:
5️⃣ If they force you to give a number

Do your market research before the interview.

Then give a range—not an arbitrary single number.

“Based on comparable roles, the scope of this position, and my experience, I’d be targeting approximately $140k–$160k in base compensation, depending on the overall package.”

Your range should be based on real market data and your qualifications, not wishful thinking.

6️⃣ Talk about total compensation

Base salary isn't the only lever.

Consider:

• Signing bonus • Annual bonus • Equity/RSUs • PTO • Retirement contributions • Remote/hybrid flexibility • Title/level • Review timeline
If the base is fixed:
“If the base can’t move, would you be open to discussing a signing bonus or additional equity?”
There’s more than one way to close the gap.
7️⃣ Master the silence
When they make an offer:
Don’t immediately say yes.
Pause.
Read it carefully.
Then respond:
“Thank you. I’m excited about the opportunity. I’d like to take a little time to review the full package.”
You don't have to fill every second of silence.
The biggest mistake?
Giving a number before you know:
1. The role's budget 2. The scope of the job 3. The total compensation package 4. Your market value

Don't negotiate against yourself.

Make them put a number on the table first whenever you reasonably can.

Save this before your next interview. 🔖

text:
Artificial intelligence has gained consciousness, and blockchain has given it a bank account. The intersection of Web3 and AI is not just another narrative for venture capitalists — it is the foundation of an entirely new, machine‑centric economy, where smart contracts are governed by neural networks and algorithms hire humans for work.

Autonomous agents with their own capital

Imagine a language model that doesn't just write product code but deploys it to a server, pays for hosting in stablecoins, and hires freelancers for interface design. AI agents are mass‑adopting their own crypto wallets. They no longer need humans to conduct transactions: they trade data directly, buy API access from each other, and arbitrage tokens on decentralised exchanges (DEXs) at speeds physically unattainable by humans.

Decentralising "hardware" for AI

Training modern neural networks hits the monopoly of tech giants over data centres and Nvidia chips. Crypto has offered an asymmetric response: decentralised GPU networks. Millions of miners and enthusiasts around the world rent out their idle computing power for AI training, receiving the network's native tokens in return. Computing power has become a liquid commodity asset, traded without corporate intermediaries.

Blockchain as a cryptographic anchor of truth

In an internet of victorious deepfakes, where content is generated by millions of bots, the question of authenticity becomes a matter of survival. Zero‑Knowledge technologies and cryptography remain the only mathematically reliable way to prove your human nature (Proof‑of‑Personhood) or to verify that a news video was not generated by an algorithm. Your Web3 wallet will soon become your only reliable digital passport.

Algorithmic syndicates (AI DAOs)

We are witnessing the emergence of decentralised organisations led not by votes of emotional token holders, but by predictive models. AI continuously analyses on‑chain metrics, assesses smart contract risks, and automatically reallocates millions of dollars in DAO treasuries. No FOMO, no panic on red markets — just pure algorithmic profit maximisation.

Machine economy (Machine‑to‑Machine) has ceased to be a theory the moment algorithms learned to understand the concept of value and acquired the means to transfer it instantly, bypassing traditional banks.

Are you ready right now to hand over the keys to your main crypto portfolio to an autonomous neural network, if mathematics proves it trades three times more effectively than you on a bear market?
