text:
The Navy Is Turning Electricity Into Ammunition

Directed energy is giving America’s warships a bottomless defensive magazine — replacing multimillion-dollar missiles with a few dollars of electricity, and making the fleet harder to kill than ever.

On Wednesday, Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle publicly described one of the most important changes in naval history, one I’ve been telling you about for some time now: “a ship’s electrical power will increasingly become a measure of its combat power.”

Sounds like science fiction, doesn’t it? Combat power is measured in guns, torpedoes, aircraft, missiles, VLS cells, right? Every shot consumes something physical. Every magazine runs dry.

But that world is ending. Fast.

High-energy lasers and high-power microwave weapons are beginning to turn a warship’s electrical generation into defensive firepower. Instead of answering every incoming drone, rocket, or missile with another, more expensive, physical projectile, the Navy is increasingly taking a page out of Israel’s Iron Beam playbook — using electrons and photons to fire again and again as long as the ship can generate the power and dump the heat.

That’s not just some marginal improvement. Indeed, it’s straight out of Star Trek. It’s the beginning of an entirely new kind of magazine, and thereby a new era.

Cheap drones helped force the issue. Shooting down a $30,000 drone with a multimillion-dollar missile is a terrible nightmare for the defender, even when the interceptor works flawlessly. The attacker is highly incentivized to throw whole drone swarms at the target, and at some point, the defense can’t help but be overwhelmed, not by better tech but by simple economics.

Insoluble, right? It’s one of the reasons certain commentators keep telling us the age of the aircraft carrier is over, that the greatest warships of our time are vastly expensive sitting ducks. But that prognosis has consistently ignored the characteristically American innovation that always solves such problems. Why accept the enemy’s cost curve when you can change it?

A single SM-6 interceptor costs about $6 million; the SM-3 anywhere from $11-$35 million. But Israel’s newly operational Iron Beam laser, jointly developed with the United States, costs just $2 per shot. 

Epirus’s Leonidas can kill entire drone swarms with high-power microwaves. Lockheed Martin CEO Jim Taiclet says his company is already using a 300-kilowatt laser in live-fire testing against drones and actual cruise missiles, and moving toward 500 kilowatts. The Navy has already put lasers to sea.

Under President Trump, this is moving fast into deployment, production, and a broad-based defense architecture — alongside expanded missile production, AI-enabled battle management, and a national nuclear-power renaissance. Golden Dome and the Golden Fleet are already being designed around directed energy systems, making the fleet — and ultimately the American people — increasingly invulnerable to attack from above.

The drone age was supposed to make the surface fleet obsolete. Instead, it provoked a revolution.

Reports of the Carriers’ Death Were Greatly Exaggerated

No platform benefits more from this revolution than the one the “experts” have been burying for most of the last century: the aircraft carrier.

The technology changes; the obituary stays the same. First carriers were supposedly too vulnerable to submarines. Then Soviet bombers and long-range cruise missiles. Then satellites and precision-guided weapons. China developed the DF-21D and DF-26 “carrier killer” ballistic missiles. Hypersonics were going to finish the job. Now it’s drone swarms.

Yet somehow the carrier keeps getting harder to kill. There’s a reason.

The entire “carriers are obsolete” argument makes the same dumb mistake over and over again: it extrapolates the attacker’s technology while freezing the defender’s technology in place.

That is not how anything works. Ever.

China did not spend decades developing anti-carrier missiles because carriers don’t matter. It built them because carriers matter enormously. A carrier isn’t just a runway. It’s sovereign American territory that moves: a floating airbase, command node, intelligence center, and overwhelming concentration of air power that requires no foreign government’s permission to appear off an enemy coast.

Moreover, an aircraft carrier doesn’t sail around by itself, just waiting for somebody to shoot it. It‘s the center of an enormous moving defensive system extending hundreds of miles beyond the hull. A carrier strike group can detect threats, confuse them, destroy the incoming weapon — or send an air wing more powerful than most countries’ entire air forces to destroy the launch sites before a shot can be fired.

All of that costs a lot. The world’s dominant economy can afford it. But what if it didn’t have to?

Last October, AeroVironment demonstrated its LOCUST laser aboard the USS George H.W. Bush, CVN-77. It effortlessly destroyed its targets, with a kill rate of 100 percent. But even more impressive was how easily the capability was added. LOCUST was not designed into the carrier during construction, or installed during a years-long overhaul.

No. The palletized LOCUST system was forklifted onto Bush’s flight deck, plugged into the ship’s nuclear-generated power, and put straight to work. Navy Decoded reports that Bush subsequently carried LOCUST into combat operations against Iran.

Iran thought it could blow up a carrier. It couldn’t lay a glove on it.

Carriers possess an abundance of everything directed-energy weapons need: tremendous electrical generation, enormous physical volume, sophisticated sensors, powerful cooling systems, advanced command-and-control, and a crew capable of maintaining complex machinery at sea for months at a time.

And suddenly, their nuclear reactors matter in an entirely new way.

For seventy years, the great operational advantage of nuclear propulsion was endurance: a carrier did not need to stop every few days for fuel. In the laser age, the reactors increasingly become part of the weapons system. They don’t just push the ship through the water. They generate the ammunition on demand and at the speed of light.

The Ford class already produces vastly greater electrical power than the Nimitz class specifically to support electromagnetic catapults, advanced sensors, and assorted “future systems.” The ships that follow can be designed with even more. 

The new nuclear-powered Trump class battleships can take the idea further still, with the electrical and thermal margins needed for larger lasers, railguns, ever more powerful sensors, and weapons we have not yet invented.

Those BBGNs can make a carrier strike group nearly invulnerable from above. They can also be nearly invulnerable by themselves.

Clearly, non-nuclear surface combatants — which make up most of today’s Navy — will have less power to spare. This just makes the carriers even more essential to fleet air defense until the Trump class comes online. And if the carriers are bristling with high-powered lasers, they’re even less vulnerable still.

Indeed, all of this turns the standard argument on its head. The bigger the ship, the more room it has for power generation, cooling, sensors, redundant systems, weapons, and defensive layers. The enormous nuclear-powered warship that looked like an inviting target in an age of finite missile magazines may become the ideal host for the weapons that make saturation attacks futile.

The carrier isn’t dying. It’s becoming a fortress.

The Revolution Doesn’t Have to Wait

Nor is there any need to wait for newly designed ships to deploy this technology.

Caudle is explicitly calling for modular, containerized laser systems like the one tested on the Bush that can be put quickly aboard ships already in service. It’s the right call: the Navy mustn’t let the perfect become the enemy of the good. Field the system, iterate it, scale it: a process of continuous improvement. 

It’s this exact philosophy that allowed a startup, SpaceX, to eclipse every long-established launch provider. It’s a lesson Caudle wants the Navy to learn.

And the revolution is already bigger than lasers.

Epirus’s Leonidas system has demonstrated something no missile battery can imitate: one electromagnetic pulse defeating a 49-drone swarm (and that number will grow). Lockheed’s MORFIUS takes high-power microwave energy airborne, flying into a swarm, frying electronics, and returning to recharge. 

Lasers offer precision; microwaves offer mass effects. Both draw from the same underlying advantage: the ship can keep generating power indefinitely, long after any number of missiles are gone.

That’s where AI-enabled battle management matters too. These systems don’t fight separately. Just as they share the same reactor, they increasingly share the same picture of the battle, allowing the ship to decide in milliseconds which weapon should kill which target.

The beam alone is not the weapon. The integrated kill chain is the weapon.

And because that kill chain is modular, the Navy can keep making it better without waiting years or even decades for new ships. Every improvement can be folded into the fleet already at sea.

Better still, every defensive job electricity takes over frees up something far scarcer: the missiles.

Defend With Lasers, Attack With Missiles

That may be the biggest payoff of all.

Former Pacific Fleet intelligence chief Jim Fanell points to a change that began after the Cold War. Under Reagan, the Maritime Strategy had a brutally straightforward purpose: if war came, take the fight to the Soviet Navy and destroy it.

But as the Soviet threat disappeared, the Navy’s finite missile magazine was increasingly devoted to other missions — first striking targets ashore, then increasingly defending the fleet itself. Ballistic missile defense accelerated the trend. The drone revolution threatened to take it to an absurd extreme, with some of the most sophisticated weapons ever built consumed merely keeping cheap flying bombs from exhausting the fleet.

Directed energy reverses that trend.

Every defensive engagement transferred from a missile to electricity leaves another missile in its cell. That is more than a savings. It restores offensive power. The physical magazine can increasingly return to what it ought to be: the arsenal with which the Navy destroys the enemy.

In a period in which far more VLS cells are being retired than can be replaced, this matters a lot. Every remaining cell needs to be on mission: killing enemy bases and ships, not messing around with incoming drones.

A Navy does not exist merely to survive the enemy’s attack. It exists to take command of the sea. So defend with electricity. Save the missiles for the attack.

And if Beijing starts the war, use those missiles to sink its fleet.

It turns out Star Trek gets a little more real every day.

(If you like these posts but would enjoy better formatting, more pictures, and proper supporting links, you can read them on my website. Link in bio.)

What makes Klamath Blue-Green Algae so interesting?
Klamath Blue-Green Algae (AFA) is a naturally nutrient-rich freshwater algae traditionally harvested from Upper Klamath Lake in Oregon.
Its complex nutritional profile includes chlorophyll, carotenoids, amino acids and naturally occurring pigments and phytonutrients.
One particularly interesting component is PEA (phenylethylamine), a naturally occurring trace amine also produced by the human body. PEA is involved in signalling within the nervous system and has attracted scientific interest in areas including mood, attention and neurological function.
Klamath algae is also valued for its naturally occurring pigments, including phycocyanins, which continue to be studied for their antioxidant and other biological properties.
Rather than providing one isolated nutrient, Klamath Blue-Green Algae offers a naturally complex whole-food nutritional profile.

text:
1. 🇨🇦🇺🇸 September 11, 2001: When U.S. airspace was shut down, Canada accepted 224 diverted flights carrying more than 33,000 passengers. Small Canadian communities fed, housed and cared for thousands of stranded Americans and travellers.

Neighbours show up.

2. 🇨🇦🇺🇸 After 9/11, Canada didn't just send thoughts and prayers.

More than 40,000 Canadian Armed Forces members served in Afghanistan.

158 Canadian soldiers died. More than 2,000 were wounded.

Canada answered when its ally was attacked.

3. 🇨🇦🇺🇸 Hurricane Katrina, 2005: About 1,000 Canadian Forces personnel took part in Canada's relief mission to the United States.

Canadian warships, aircraft, medical personnel, Coast Guard crews and supplies headed south.

That's what allies do.

4. 🇨🇦🇺🇸 Here's one Katrina story Americans rarely hear:

A Canadian search-and-rescue team from Vancouver went into devastated St. Bernard Parish, Louisiana and rescued 119 stranded people.

Canada was there.

5. 🇨🇦🇺🇸 After Hurricane Katrina, Canada sent three Royal Canadian Navy ships and a Canadian Coast Guard vessel loaded with humanitarian supplies to the U.S. Gulf Coast.

Canadian sailors helped clear waterways, inspect infrastructure and restore navigation.

6. 🇨🇦🇺🇸 Katrina overwhelmed U.S. Coast Guard resources so badly that the U.S. asked Canada for help.

Canada deployed two military search-and-rescue helicopters to Cape Cod, freeing American resources to respond in the disaster zone.

That's an ally.

7. 🇨🇦🇺🇸 Superstorm Sandy, 2012: After restoring power at home, roughly 400 utility workers from 25 Ontario utilities headed into the United States to help turn American lights back on.

Bucket trucks crossed the border by the convoy.

8. 🇨🇦🇺🇸 Hurricane Harvey, 2017: Canada loaded an RCAF Hercules with emergency supplies and flew them directly to Texas after FEMA accepted Canada's offer of assistance.

Canada also supplied formula, cribs, linens, hygiene supplies and other necessities.

9. 🇨🇦🇺🇸 Canadians donated more than $1.9 million through the Canadian Red Cross toward Hurricane Harvey relief in Texas and Louisiana.

Not because Americans owed us anything.

Because that's what neighbours do.

10. 🇨🇦🇺🇸 Iran, 1979–80: Six American diplomats escaped capture when the U.S. Embassy in Tehran was seized.

Canadian diplomats hid them in their homes for nearly three months, at enormous personal risk, and Canada provided passports that helped get them safely out of Iran.

The "Canadian Caper" was real.

11. 🇨🇦🇺🇸 Korean War: More than 26,000 Canadians served alongside U.S. and other UN forces.

516 Canadians died.

At Kapyong, a Canadian battalion's performance was so extraordinary it received the U.S. Presidential Unit Citation.

12. 🇨🇦🇺🇸 Pearl Harbor was attacked on December 7, 1941.

Canada declared war on Japan that same day and fought alongside its allies through the Pacific War.

Canada didn't need to be convinced that an attack on its neighbour mattered.

13. 🇨🇦🇺🇸 Canada helps defend the United States every single day.

NORAD isn't an American organization that Canada happens to participate in. It's a binational Canadian-American command jointly defending North American airspace.

Our defence has been integrated for generations.

14. 🇨🇦🇺🇸 California wildfires, 2025: Canadian help went south again.

Québec water bombers fought the fires. Alberta sent elite wildfire crews. British Columbia sent specialized personnel and firefighters.

When Americans needed help, Canadians showed up.

15. 🇨🇦🇺🇸 Canadian firefighters helping Americans isn't some one-time gesture.

Canada and the U.S. routinely send firefighters, aircraft and emergency resources across the border when the other country is overwhelmed.

16. 🇨🇦🇺🇸 You don't have to like Canada's government.
    You don't have to like our policies.
    You don't even have to like Canadians.

But saying Canada hasn't been there for the United States is simply historically false.

text:
What federal law can do:

The Protection of Pupil Rights Amendment (PPRA) already covers surveys and screenings that ask about a student’s mental or psychological problems. In late August 2026 the U.S. Department of Education told districts that these kinds of mental-health screenings generally require parental notice and written consent, and that calling them “optional” does not automatically get a district out of that duty.

Parents can file a PPRA complaint with the U.S. Department of Education if a school administers a covered screening without following those consent rules.

Congress can pass a stricter nationwide opt-in law. Rep. Mary Miller already introduced a bill to require written parental consent before this kind of screening. That bill is not law yet.

Lawsuits can still be filed arguing the Illinois opt-out system conflicts with PPRA or parental-rights precedents. A legal group has already asked the federal government to look at the Illinois law on that basis.

What federal law cannot do by itself:

Education is mostly a state function. Illinois can require its public schools to offer a screening. Washington cannot simply cancel that state law with a press release.

PPRA is an enforcement and funding-conditions statute. It can put pressure on districts and create a complaint process. It does not instantly make every Illinois parent’s opt-out a criminal lock on the classroom.

A state can keep an opt-out model unless a court or Congress forces an opt-in model.

So the accurate picture is: Illinois passed a real law requiring schools to offer the screening, with an opt-out. Federal law can constrain how schools do it (notice, consent, complaints, possible future legislation or court rulings). It has not, as of now, erased the Illinois mandate.

"REGULAR CONVERSATIONS" WITH PRIGOZHIN — BUDANOV CONFIRMS

For the first time, Kyrylo Budanov — Ukraine's wartime military intelligence chief, now head of the Presidential Office and Kyiv's lead negotiator — has confirmed to The New York Times that he personally held regular conversations with Wagner founder Yevgeny Prigozhin. The contacts ended shortly before the June 2023 mutiny. Details offered: none.

The confirmation lands three years late — and validates the 2023 US intelligence leak. The Washington Post reported back then that Prigozhin had offered Kyiv the positions of Russian regular troops in exchange for a pullback from Bakhmut, that he phoned GUR officers, and that he met Ukrainian intelligence face-to-face in Africa. Prigozhin mocked it at the time: "We have nothing to hide from foreign intelligence services. Budanov and I are still in Africa." Two months after the mutiny, he was dead.

What was never on record until now: the channel ran to Budanov personally. After the mutiny, he would only dismiss the "rumors."

The second headline from the interview is the forecast. Budanov does not expect the conditions for a ceasefire to materialize before spring 2027 — with Russia spending the winter trying to break Ukraine from the air first. But he insists the talks, which resume this month, will eventually deliver: "You can't fight your whole life."

text:
# The Future of Prediction Market Resolutions: Embracing Automation and Precision

Prediction markets have emerged as powerful tools for aggregating collective intelligence on everything from election outcomes to technological breakthroughs. As platforms like Polymarket and Kalshi continue to grow, the integrity of these markets hinges on one critical element: resolution. How markets are settled determines not only their credibility but also their appeal to serious traders and analysts. In an era of rapid innovation, discussions around faster automation, clearer criteria, and platform-specific best practices are reshaping the landscape.

This article examines the current state of market resolution, drawing on recent industry trends to highlight why precision and efficiency matter more than ever.

## The Case for Automated Resolutions

Traditional resolution processes often rely on human oversight, which introduces delays and potential inconsistencies. Recent advancements in on-chain computation tools, such as those pioneered by protocols like Fermah, are addressing these pain points head-on. By enabling real-time outcomes for recurring markets, automation reduces the lag that has historically plagued prediction platforms.

For instance, automated systems can process verifiable data streams—such as official economic releases or sports results—without manual intervention. This shift not only accelerates settlements but also enhances reliability, minimizing disputes that arise from subjective interpretations. Traders benefit from quicker capital recycling, while platforms gain a competitive edge in attracting high-volume participants. As these tools mature, we can expect broader adoption across Polymarket and Kalshi, particularly for high-frequency event contracts.

## The Imperative of Clear Resolution Criteria

Even the most sophisticated automation cannot compensate for ambiguous rules. Well-defined criteria are the foundation of any valid market, distinguishing true prediction mechanisms from informal sentiment polls. Recent examples underscore this point, including Polymarket contracts tied to AI model releases like OpenAI's Astra. When rules specify exact benchmarks—such as release dates, performance metrics, or official announcements—resolutions become transparent and defensible.

Ambiguity, by contrast, invites challenges and erodes trust. Analysts and market makers have repeatedly emphasized that robust criteria should account for edge cases, including data source hierarchies and fallback procedures. Platforms that invest in this clarity see fewer appeals and higher user retention. For participants, reviewing resolution sources in advance is essential; credible outlets like government statistical agencies or verified corporate disclosures provide the necessary grounding.

## Platform-Specific Outcomes and Historical Lessons

Polymarket and Kalshi offer distinct approaches to resolution that reflect their user bases and regulatory environments. Polymarket, with its crypto-native design, has demonstrated live resolutions for political and tech events, often leveraging decentralized oracles alongside human review. Kalshi, operating under CFTC oversight, emphasizes compliance-driven processes, which can add layers of verification but also bolster institutional confidence.

Historical disputes serve as valuable case studies. Past controversies over event interpretations have prompted calls for improved market design, including standardized templates for recurring categories. Emerging protocols now advertise sub-24-hour automated traces, signaling a move toward hybrid models that combine speed with accountability. These developments suggest that platforms ignoring these lessons risk losing market share to more agile competitors.

## Implications for Traders and Market Integrity

For analysts focused on Polymarket and Kalshi, understanding resolution dynamics is a core competency. Automated features may soon dominate routine markets, freeing human judgment for complex, one-off events. Clear criteria, meanwhile, empower informed positioning rather than reactive speculation.

Looking ahead, the integration of these elements could elevate prediction markets from niche betting arenas to mainstream forecasting instruments. Participants who prioritize platforms with transparent processes stand to gain the most, as reliability becomes a key differentiator.

## Conclusion

Market resolution is no longer a backend detail—it is central to the value proposition of prediction platforms. Through automation and rigorous criteria, the industry is poised to deliver faster, fairer outcomes that benefit all stakeholders. As these trends unfold, staying attuned to credible sources and platform evolutions will remain essential for anyone navigating this space.

Trump will push a Republican candidate over whom he will have leverage, not one over whom Tucker Carlson has leverage. Most likely, once the midterms are over and the MAGA coalition is moot forever, Trump will assert dominance over Vance.

text:
AI Searched 100 Million Possibilities and Found a Cheaper Way to 3D Print a NASA Rocket Alloy | Wonderful Engineering

Researchers at Washington State University have used artificial intelligence to identify a faster and potentially cheaper way to 3D print a high-performance NASA-developed metal alloy. The system found successful printing configurations from a search space containing more than 100 million possibilities while requiring just 40 physical experiments.

The breakthrough could make GRCop-42, a copper, chromium, and niobium alloy designed for extreme aerospace environments, compatible with more widely available commercial 3D printers. The AI-guided approach may also offer a new way to tackle scientific problems where testing every possible option would be prohibitively expensive. The findings were reported by Washington State University researchers.

GRCop-42 was developed by NASA for applications requiring both high thermal conductivity and the ability to withstand extreme temperatures. The alloy is used in aerospace systems, including liquid rocket engine combustion chambers, but its demanding manufacturing requirements have limited its accessibility.

Traditional approaches require researchers to manually test different combinations of printing parameters, including laser power and other machine settings. With more than 100 million potential configurations, a comprehensive trial-and-error approach would be impractical.

The WSU team instead used data from 37 previously unsuccessful printing attempts to train an AI model. The system estimated which untested configurations were most likely to succeed and recommended small groups of experiments that could either produce a viable result or provide valuable information to improve future predictions.

“We were essentially applying the AI so that we efficiently choose candidates from this very large search space,” said Azza Fadhel, a PhD student and the study’s first author.

After three months of testing, the researchers identified six successful configurations while conducting only 40 experiments in total. Most notably, they successfully printed GRCop-42 using a 500-watt laser, a significantly lower power level than previously required for the challenging material.

“Ninety percent of commercial printers cannot print this metal alloy,” said Jana Doppa, who led the research. Finding workable parameters, he said, could help “democratize” access to the material by allowing it to be printed on commercial equipment.

The researchers believe their approach could eventually be applied to other metal alloys and scientific fields, including drug discovery, where researchers face enormous experimental search spaces and high costs.

text:
NSE IPO - A decade-long saga comes to an end with a good story 

Here’s the bare-bones saga of NSE’s long, messy path to its IPO:

1. Co-location – the original sin  
NSE launched co-location in 2009 so brokers could park servers near the trading engine. Globally normal, but NSE’s 2010–2014 run went off-track. A 2015 whistleblower letter (“Ken Fong”) claimed select HFTs like OPG Securities connected to a backup server that got tick data milliseconds early. That split-second edge meant big money. SEBI’s probe confirmed early secondary-server logins. Was it a scam or just sloppy tech? SAT later said NSE didn’t “unjustly enrich” itself. In 2019 SEBI ordered ₹624.89 crore disgorgement plus interest and a 6‑month market-raising ban. NSE appealed. By Jan 2023 SAT slashed the penalty to ₹100 crore. SEBI went to the Supreme Court, where the appeal lingered for years.

2. Dark fibre – the next speed lane  
Some brokers allegedly got exclusive dark-fibre links between NSE and BSE co-lo rooms, shaving off microseconds. SEBI ordered ₹62.6 crore disgorgement. This and colo together became the legal cloud scaring bankers away from any IPO.

3. TAP architecture – the ₹643 crore quiet hit  
NSE’s Trading Access Point (TAP) software from 2008 managed broker connections and fees. SEBI said some HFTs bypassed TAP, dodged fees, and NSE delayed fixes. In Oct 2024, NSE and ex‑MD Vikram Limaye plus tech staff settled for ₹643.05 crore without admitting guilt. File closed, but it cost another year.

4. The Himalayan Yogi bombshell  
Chitra Ramkrishna (CEO 2013–2016) hired Anand Subramanian—an obscure exec from Balmer Lawrie—at sky‑high pay for a part‑time week, later making him Group Operating Officer. No proper board process. SEBI found she was emailing sensitive NSE data to rigyajursama@outlook.com—allegedly a “Himalayan Yogi” guiding her for 20 years. EY suggested it was Subramanian himself. SEBI called her a “puppet” in a “money-making scheme.” She got a ₹3 crore fine and 3‑year ban; NSE and others were also fined and banned briefly. CBI arrested her in 2022; a criminal case drags on.

5. The CBI track that sputtered  
FIR in 2018 promised hawala, foreign trades, and big conspiracy. Seven years later, chargesheets mostly nailed brokers for secondary‑server use. The grand theories fizzled, leaving just enough smoke for SEBI to keep citing “legal overhang.”

6. SEBI’s extra checklist  
Repeated outages, ₹73 crore tech‑glitch settlement, board gaps, conflicts over NSE Clearing stake, RoC show‑cause notices. Even old folklore like locked‑up SEBI officials and the 2012 fat‑finger crash slowed the NOC. Five SEBI chairmen touched the file; every time a “green light” rumor rose, a new SCN hit.

How it finally unstuck  
@ashishchauhan  returned as CEO in 2022, pushed settlements over endless fights:
Oct 2024: ₹643 cr TAP settlement.
Jun 2025: colo + dark fibre settlements filed.
Mar 2026: revised offer ₹1,491.21 cr.
Jul 2026: payment done.
Sep 3, 2026: SC closes SEBI appeals.
Sep 4, 2026: SEBI clears the DRHP.

The IPO is a pure offer for sale — 14.89 crore shares (~6%), no fresh funds. Valuations hover near ₹2,000/share (~₹30,000 cr, ~$55B). Listing set on BSE — ending a decade‑long legal soap opera.

Florida Democratic Senate nominee Angie Nixon, an avowed socialist who has made affordability the centerpiece of her campaign, is reaping the financial benefits of a homestead tax exemption she voted against in the State House of Representatives in 2024, according to a Washington Free Beacon review of property tax records.

Florida offers two property tax exemptions for primary residences, both of which reduce the property's taxable value by $25,000 for a combined total of $50,000 in exemptions. 

In an 86-29 party-line vote in February 2024, the Florida House voted to approve an amendment to the state constitution to adjust one of those homestead exemptions to the rate of inflation every year, with Nixon joining her fellow Democrats in a failed effort to reject the proposal. 

Voters overwhelmingly approved the measure in a 66-34 percent vote during the November 2024 elections.

text:
In 2000, Virginia Roberts was sixteen and working at a Florida resort spa, trying to rebuild her life after surviving childhood abuse. That's when a well-dressed British woman approached her with a job offer that seemed too good to be true.
It was.
Ghislaine Maxwell recruited Virginia to work for Jeffrey Epstein, a wealthy financier whose 'massage services' were actually a cover for systematic sexual abuse. For two years, Virginia was trafficked between Epstein's properties—from Manhattan penthouses to a private Caribbean island—and told to have sex with powerful men she'd never met.
One was Prince Andrew, the Queen's son. A photograph from March 2001 shows them together in London: Virginia at seventeen, Andrew's arm around her waist, Maxwell smiling beside them. That single image would later become crucial evidence in one of the most high-profile abuse cases in modern history.
In 2002, Virginia escaped. She married quickly, moved to Australia, and tried to disappear into normal life. For years, she stayed silent, raising three children in a coastal town far from her past.
Then in 2010, her daughter was born. Looking at her newborn baby girl, Virginia made a decision that would change everything: she would speak.
What followed was a decade-long fight against some of the world's most powerful people. She faced death threats, break-ins, and public attacks on her character. Tabloids called her a liar. Maxwell sued her for defamation. Lawyers tried to discredit her in court.
But Virginia refused to back down.
In 2019, Epstein was finally arrested on federal sex trafficking charges. He died in custody weeks later under circumstances that remain controversial. But Virginia continued fighting. When prosecutors called Epstein's victims to speak, she stood before the court: 'He did not act alone. The reckoning must not end.'
In 2021, Ghislaine Maxwell was convicted and sentenced to twenty years in prison.
That same year, on her thirty-eighth birthday, Virginia sued Prince Andrew in federal court. The Duke of York fought to dismiss the case, but when a judge ruled it could proceed to trial, Andrew settled for an undisclosed sum and stepped down from royal duties. The Queen stripped him of his military titles.
Virginia Roberts Giuffre had achieved something many thought impossible: holding a member of the British royal family accountable for abuse.
Today, she runs organizations that help other trafficking survivors find their voices. She speaks at conferences worldwide. She's written about her experiences to help others understand the long-term impact of abuse and the courage it takes to seek justice against powerful people who believe they're untouchable.
Her message remains clear: survivors have the right to be heard, believed, and supported—no matter who their abusers are or how much power they wield. And every time another survivor steps forward, they're walking through doors Virginia fought to open. 

-Weird & Unusual Things Never Seen Before

text:
The consensus is split between two extreme narratives: either AI is gutting the workforce, or the labor market is falling off a cliff into recession.

Both views ignore the actual plumbing.

Look at our historical tracking of U.S. Job Openings vs. Total Unemployed Persons since 2001:

• Job Openings (July 2026): 7,271,000 
• Unemployed Persons (July 2026): 6,916,000 
• Ratio: 1.05 to 1

How a macro allocator reads this regime:

1.) Regime Normalization: Post-2008 was defined by chronic labor slack, where unemployed workers outnumbered openings by more than two to one. The 2021 to 2022 cycle was an artificial shortage where openings doubled job seekers. Today is neither. The market has normalized back to neutral parity.

2.) Central Bank Reaction Function: When the openings-to-unemployed ratio sits near 1.0, wage-price spiral risk is dead. The Federal Reserve no longer has an incentive to maintain restrictive monetary plumbing to cool labor demand, shifting the liquidity outlook.

3.) Corporate Margin Dispersion: In a balanced labor market, top-line revenue growth slows to trend. The easy beta phase is over. Companies that relied on price hikes rather than real productivity will face margin contraction.

Do not trade apocalyptic headlines. The labor market is not collapsing; it has returned to balance. In this regime, capital flows toward companies with genuine pricing power, durable cash flow, and strong balance sheets.

text:
From My Research Machine:

David Shoemaker — Living Thelema (2013).
William Ramsey — Prophet of Evil (2012).

Likely to say yes

Tobias Churton — teaches at Exeter's esotericism centre and writes trade occult history for Inner Traditions. He produced the 2011 biography plus the Crowley in America / India / England sequence. He gives blurbs, he works in the same publishing register as a Horsley reissue, and he has the least to lose. Start here.

Richard Kaczynski — Perdurabo (revised 2010) remains the factual spine of the field. He works as an independent scholar, appears on panels outside the academy, and answers correspondence. His name on the jacket settles the accuracy question for most reviewers.

Phil Baker — City of the Beast (2022). A literary biographer working London trade publishing. Low friction, and his comment would read to a general audience rather than a specialist one.

Peter-Robert Koenig — the O.T.O. Phenomenon archive. Independent, document-driven, and the one researcher in this neighbourhood who already works the institutional-succession and abuse material Horsley touches. Unpredictable in tone, which may serve you.

Academic weight, real chance of a decline

Henrik Bogdan — Professor at Gothenburg, co-editor with Martin P. Starr of Aleister Crowley and Western Esotericism (Oxford, 2012), and editor of Crowley's correspondence. The most citable name in the field after Pasi. He guards the line between scholarship and the conspiracy register, so frame the ask around a specific chapter.

Martin P. Starr — Teitan Press, The Unknown God. The archival authority on the American O.T.O. He is guarded to the point of severity. Ask him about one documented episode rather than the book's thesis.

Gordan Djurdjevic — India and the Occult, co-editor with Bogdan on Occultism in a Global Perspective. Less exposed than Bogdan, similar credentials.

Wouter Hanegraaff — Amsterdam, the founder of the field's academic chair. Maximum prestige and the highest refusal probability of anyone here.

Adversarial readers worth courting

A serious dissent from a credentialed scholar does more for a reissue than a friendly line from an ally.

Egil Asprem — Stockholm University, currently a Swedish Collegium fellow. He wrote Arguing with Angels and he also publishes on conspiracy theory and the cognitive study of religion. He would read Horsley as both argument and specimen. That comment, printed, would give the reissue standing it cannot buy otherwise.

Manon Hedenborg White — Södertörn, The Eloquent Blood (Oxford, 2020) and the recent Esotericism and Deviance volume. Horsley's reading of the sexual revolution runs crosswise to hers. A dissenting paragraph from her carries real weight.

Per Faxneld — Satanic Feminism. Same logic, adjacent expertise.

Adjacent names that broaden the audience

Ronald Hutton (Bristol) blurbs generously and reads outside the occult niche. Justin Sledge (Esoterica) offers reach rather than credentials, and a video treatment moves more copies than a jacket line.

text:
I want to be careful here because I know exactly how some people are going to read everything I've written so far.

This isn't an anti-ETF rant. It isn't anti-Wall Street, anti-bank, anti-corporation or some purity test about who gets to call themselves a Bitcoiner.

I don't give a shit how you buy your bitcoin.

If an ETF is the easiest way for someone to get exposure inside a retirement account, fine. If somebody isn't comfortable holding their own keys and chooses a custodian, I understand it. If a company wants to put billions of dollars worth of bitcoin on its balance sheet, have at it. If banks eventually make Bitcoin accessible to millions of people who otherwise would never touch it, there is obviously value in that too.

Bitcoin doesn't need everyone to use it the same way.

That's actually part of what makes this thing so interesting.

My concern isn't that these options exist. My concern is that convenience has a funny way of becoming dependency without us noticing when the transition happened.

We've seen this movie before.

People didn't wake up one morning and decide they wanted almost every part of their financial lives sitting behind institutions, passwords, permission systems and databases controlled by somebody else. We got there slowly because each individual step made life easier.

Someone else could store it.

Someone else could secure it.

Someone else could verify it.

Someone else could move it.

Someone else could insure it.

Someone else could make the whole damn thing easier.

Eventually we stopped thinking about how much trust had accumulated because the system worked most of the time.

Bitcoin came along and offered something completely different. It didn't demand that we abandon every institution in our lives. It simply gave us the option not to need one for some incredibly important things.

That's the distinction I'm trying to protect.

Freedom doesn't mean you must self-custody.

Freedom means you can.

Freedom doesn't mean you must run a node.

Freedom means nobody can stop you from verifying for yourself.

Freedom doesn't mean you have to transact peer-to-peer every time you buy a cup of coffee.

Freedom means the ability still exists when you actually need it.

There is nothing wrong with choosing convenience when you understand what you're trading for it.

The danger comes when an entire generation grows up using Bitcoin through intermediaries and eventually forgets that the intermediary was optional in the first place.

That's how I think about all of this.

I'm not worried that Wall Street is going to steal Bitcoin from us.

I'm much more interested in whether we slowly hand back the things Bitcoin gave us because keeping them required a little more work.

There's a huge difference between having freedom and using it.

There might be an even bigger difference between choosing not to use it...

and forgetting you ever had the choice.

text:
Assuming that this is true, and I certainly believe it could be, this is absolutely a violation of this woman's privacy.

Are there websites already that allow you to look up people? Sure, but you pay for those services and even then you have to know who you are looking for.

Now @Meta comes along and does all the hard work. It doesn't ask if you want to be found, it offers. 

It is bad enough it does it at all. Bad enough that it does it for adults. The fact that it will do it for a minor, should be not only a red flag, but illegal. At the very least they should have a toggle in your profile that lets you opt-out of AI searches.

But, be warned, even if they do add that - and you check it - it might get *unchecked* the next time Meta does an update. Same with @Microsoft who is notorious for resetting things that you disable when they push an update.

"Oh you disabled our ability to track you? Let me fix that..."

Technology is a tool. It can be your friend. It can also be used for evil. Plan accordingly.

text:
CASHIER WALKS OFF REGISTER AFTER A CUSTOMER COUNTS OUT A RETURN IN EXACT PENNIES JUST TO BE DIFFICULT

CLEVELAND, OHIO — A grocery store cashier abandoned her register mid-shift Sunday after a customer demanded her $4.73 refund be paid entirely in loose pennies, then spent nearly ten agonizing minutes counting each individual coin onto the belt like she was defusing a bomb. According to the fictional report, cashier Denise had already offered the refund in normal bills and coins twice, both times politely and both times flatly declined.

Witnesses say the customer explained, at length, that she wanted "exact change, in pennies, for principle," a principle nobody in line behind her, now numbering nine deep, was able to identify.

The customer's demands escalated to:

Requesting all 473 individual cents be counted out by hand, one at a time
Refusing a pre-rolled coin option because "that's not really counting"
Recounting the entire pile herself twice more "just to double check the math"
Telling the growing line to "relax, this is a grocery store, not a race track"
Asking Denise to bag the pennies separately "so they don't spill in my purse"

Denise reportedly stood in stunned silence watching the copper pile grow taller by the minute before quietly clocking off her register mid-count and walking away, leaving pennies, customer, and a very confused line behind entirely.

Exact change is technically a customer's right.
Watching someone weaponize it for ten minutes is apparently a cashier's limit.

The Economist
June 20th–26th 2026

Briefing | The unverified state

The Economist June 20th 2026

Who goes there?

One month after a single piece of software stopped working, Britain cannot say who its citizens are. Whoever they are, those who can are seeking asylum abroad

Paris, Delhi, Beijing and Washington, DC

Your correspondent left England in the second week of what the government still calls an outage, in a flimsy boat, from a beach between Dungeness and Hythe, having paid €4,000 in cash to a man who did not give his name and did not need to know hers. The crossing took five hours. She mentions it not for colour but because it is the most efficient available summary of the position: cash money is the only passport on the Channel this summer. The people-smugglers have never required documents and have simply reversed the direction of travel. Their rates going north have collapsed. Going south they have tripled.

It is worth recalling what Britain was arguing about on May 19th. The newspapers, then still printing, were exercised by the number of vape shops on the high street, the licensing regime for pavement tables and whether a cabinet minister had been rude to a select committee. This is not offered as satire. It is the standard condition of a rich, stable, elaborately governed country, and it is what a month ago looked like the natural order of things.

On May 20th an intruder with privileged access reached https://t.co/VWJ2Le8avK One Login, the verification system through which, by then, 250 online public services and some 23m citizen accounts passed. Britain had spent four years consolidating identity onto it and closing every other route as an economy: the civil-service telephone helplines, the counters, the paper forms. On May 21st the government could no longer establish, online, that a citizen was who he claimed to be. Since online was where all the services had been moved, game over.

Sauve qui peut
A month on, the arithmetic is easier to state than to credit. HMRC still receives some VAT, PAYE and national-insurance remittances, but no returns to explain what they consist of: submitting a return requires a working verification system, and there is not one. For the same reason the department issues no repayments at all. Many employers meanwhile hold their tax dues in their own bank accounts, at a rate of something over £25bn a month. Whether they will all survive to hand it over one day is a question nobody at the Treasury wishes to be asked twice.

New DWP benefit claims cannot be established, once again because no one can submit anything. So the dead continue to receive their pensions while the newly unemployed cannot get onto the books. Companies House processes nothing at all.

That last is worth dwelling on, because it is misunderstood abroad. Britain introduced director verification only in 2025, having run for a century and a half a corporate register that required no proof of anything and was, in consequence, a recognised instrument of fraud. Optimists therefore argued that One Login's failure merely returned the register to its previous condition. This has proved wrong in practice. There are no manual forms any more, and no staff in Cardiff to process them if there were, and no functioning postal service to carry them if there were staff. The alternative route—verification through an authorised corporate service provider—is paid, thinly supplied, and widely believed by British privacy campaigners to route back to One Login regardless. Free-at-the-point-of-use crowded out the alternatives before it failed, which is what free-at-the-point-of-use does.

Stocks cannot be marked to market because, as in 2008, there are no prices. The pound is down by roughly three-fifths on a trade-weighted basis. Two gilt auctions have failed. The Bank of England is buying, and saying little. What began as a verification failure has become a fiscal one, and is becoming a monetary one.

Scotland's brief immunity has ended. Holyrood kept its own arrangements and its devolved services worked for a fortnight, to considerable local satisfaction. But tax, benefits, borders, company law and financial regulation are reserved powers, and a Scot is no more able to file a return or start a claim than anyone in Kent. Devolution protects a jurisdiction from London's decisions. It does not protect it from London's absence.

Devolution protects a jurisdiction from London's decisions. It does not protect it from London's absence

The kindness of strangers
Who gains? From Washington, the answer is: nobody deliberately, and America substantially by accident. General counsel who spent June rewriting choice-of-law clauses are choosing New York, and contractual jurisdiction does not migrate back on the strength of an apology. The administration has offered assistance and will expect terms. It has also, more quietly, compartmented intelligence sharing—not as a rebuke but because British vetting cannot presently be assured, and no competent service would do otherwise.

From Beijing, the read is longer. China has the capacity to underwrite a country of Britain's size and no incentive whatever to hurry. Officials speak, without embarrassment, of the difference between assisting a nation that is embarrassed and one that is exhausted. What is on offer, when it comes, will not principally be money. It will be the reconstruction of a digital state, on Chinese infrastructure, inside the G7—a prize that no amount of lending could buy and that Britain has now placed on the table itself.

Moscow's position is more comfortable still. The question who knocked out https://t.co/VWJ2Le8avK One Login remains unanswered and may stay so. It scarcely matters: a Britain that cannot pay its soldiers' families or renew their clearances is a Britain distracted from NATO's eastern flank, where it leads the battlegroup in Estonia—a country of 1.3m people that has run a working national identity system since 2002 and, when a flaw appeared in 2017, switched it off and told its citizens. The comparison is being made in Tallinn with more tact than it deserves.

Pyongyang is the case that analysts find instructive rather than alarming. North Korea does not want to govern Britain; it wants revenue, and it has spent a decade perfecting two techniques. One is ransomware, which took down parts of the UK National Health Service in 2017, not to mention Sony worldwide. The other is the placement of operatives inside Western companies using fabricated identities. A state whose speciality is manufacturing people who do not exist has been presented with an economy that has lost the ability to check. Nobody knows the scale. That is the point.

Which brings us to sunny Romania. Development work on One Login was subcontracted to staff working in Bucharest for the programme's prime contractor, Deloitte. The Government Digital Service did not consult the National Cyber Security Centre before the arrangement was made; its own head recorded, in a review conducted after the fact in 2022, that he was uncomfortable with the clarity of offshore oversight. Ministers later assured Parliament that a handful of people were involved; that even if there were rather more, none of them had access to the production environment; and that even if they did, several thousand times a month, all the program code was checked. Those assurances are now a load-bearing element of a forensic investigation, which is not a position anybody intended them to occupy. Britain spent four years describing One Login as sovereign infrastructure. It cannot presently say with confidence who had access to what while it was being built.

Brussels, meanwhile, can do less than it would like and rather less than Dublin requires. Ireland has the deepest exposure and no responsibility at all: the Irish are the crisis's Icelandic depositors of 2008. The EU has no instrument for a neighbour's administrative collapse, having spent a decade being told by that neighbour that it required nothing, and it is now absorbing British arrivals under a legal framework built on the assumption that asylum-seeker traffic moves the other way.

Institutions of last resort, so called
The IMF is the wrong tool and everybody in Washington knows it. The Fund lends to governments that can execute a programme. Britain's difficulty is not a mere financing gap but the absence of an administration capable of being a counterparty and capable of having conditions imposed on it. In 1976 Britain went to the Fund with a balance-of-payments crisis and a functioning Treasury. It now has a functioning-Treasury problem.

The UN is stranger. Britain is a permanent member of the Security Council, which means it holds a veto over any resolution concerning its own condition. The humanitarian machinery—OCHA, the WFP—is built for states that lack capacity and accept help. Britain lacks capacity and has not yet found a form of words in which to accept anything. Officials in New York describe the file, privately, as the most delicate they have handled, and note that India has views about the seat.

The Commonwealth cannot lend. It can, however, do something more pointed. India, Singapore, Malaysia, Pakistan and Bangladesh hold between them a great deal of the world's practical experience of building identity infrastructure at scale, and from Delhi the offer of technical assistance has been made warmly and in public, which is itself the message. The UIDAI has authenticated identity for over a billion people; NADRA pays welfare to millions in Pakistan and exports the technology; Singapore has run Singpass for two decades; Malaysia's national card dates from 2001.

It should be said that this club is diplomatic rather than technical. The systems Britain would most usefully copy are largely in Europe—the Dutch DigiD, the German card, Italy's SPID, Denmark's MitID, France's federated arrangement, and Estonia's, which Tallinn has offered anyway, membership of anything or no. The direction of capacity-building has reversed on every compass point at once, and everyone involved is being extremely polite about it.

A state whose speciality is manufacturing people who do not exist has been presented with an economy that has lost the ability to check

The experiment nobody would have funded
Among economists, and it is unbecoming how many have said so, this is the most interesting month of their professional lives. The control experiment that no ethics committee would approve has been run: remove a modern state's administrative capacity, leave every physical asset in place, and observe.

Three findings so far. First, the order of collapse follows transaction costs, exactly as Coase would predict. Activity requiring verified strangers to trust one another failed within days—mortgages, insurance, employment of anyone new, cross-border trade. Activity between people who already know each other barely paused. The corner shop extends credit; the wholesaler does not.

Second, substitution was faster than any model allowed. Informal exchange, scrip issued by market traders, and reciprocal labour appeared within a fortnight. Britain has not reverted to barter, which is a journalist's word; it has developed a dozen local monies and a great deal of credit based on reputation.

Third, and least comfortable for the profession, a measurable fraction of recorded British GDP appears to have been the administrative overhead of a state verifying things about itself. Nobody yet knows how large that fraction is. The suspicion that it is not small is doing quiet damage to a good deal of previous work.

The Birmingham anomaly
Which brings one to the case now being examined by every political scientist with a book to update. Across several wards of east Birmingham, daily life is functioning better than in any comparable British city: food is distributed, disputes are settled, elderly people are checked on, and violence is markedly below the national picture.

The socially responsible institutions are, in the main, mosques and their associated charities, operating a system of arbitration and mutual aid that some participants describe with the word sharia and that the few remnants of the British broadcast media have reported with the excitement one would expect. The reality is duller and more interesting. No legal code has been imposed on anyone; jurisdiction extends only to those who consent to it, as with the Beth Din. Non-Muslim residents of those wards report the same improvement and use the same food distribution.

And the mechanism is precisely the subject of this article. These institutions can act because they can identify people. They hold membership rolls, they occupy premises, they handle cash, and above all their members know one another by sight (± the burqa)—which is to say they possess, without a database, the capability the British state has lost. The same dignified orderliness has happened, with less publicity, around Sikh gurdwaras whose langar kitchens are feeding whole districts, in England's thriving evangelical churches, in a handful of Orthodox Jewish communities, and in those rural parishes where the Anglican church (Episcopalians, for Americans) still has a little purchase.

The comparative literature is unambiguous: when a state withdraws, whatever possesses dense mutual recognition inherits the ground. Mogadishu in 2006 got the Islamic Courts Union and, briefly, the safest streets in twenty years. Beirut has lived the arrangement for decades. That the British example is producing decent outcomes is a fact about social capital, not about theology, and it will remain true only for as long as the arrangements stay voluntary—which is the thing nobody can guarantee and which historically does not last.

The dog that did not bark
One observation is owed to a decade of anxious commissioning. Britain built an institute to examine whether artificial intelligence might destabilise the state, convened the world at Bletchley Park to discuss it, and published declarations on frontier risk. Successive governments treated the question as the defining technological threat of the age, and on the available evidence they were sincere.

The state was then brought down by a sign-in page procured in 2021. Nothing was superintelligent. Nothing was even clever. A supplier let a certificate lapse, a red-team finding went eighteen months without being closed, development was offshored without asking the cyber-security agency, and somebody walked in through privileged access that the monitoring could not see. The catastrophe arrived from the direction where nobody had posted a lookout, wearing the clothes of routine IT, mundane and downright boring.

The means of verification
British Marxists have had a disappointing month. The temptation to read this as capitalism's implosion is strong and does not survive contact with the evidence: the factories stand, the capital stock is unimpaired, the market continues in degraded form. What failed was the state, and it failed while performing its most basic function.

Please see Consultants' Charter graphic attached below

There is a Marxian account available, and it is better than the one being offered. For two decades British public administration transferred hundreds of millions of pounds to itself and to consultancies for work it had lost the capacity to specify, assess or absorb. The consultancies were the visible half and took the blame; the officials who commissioned them, rotated out before delivery and were promoted on the announcement rather than the outcome, were the larger half. A rentier class extracting from the state until the state could no longer do the thing it existed to do. Marx would have recognised the pattern. He simply located it elsewhere.

Weber is the better guide. This is a crisis of rational-legal authority: the bureaucracy's claim to legitimacy rested on impersonal, reliable procedure, and the procedure stopped. What has filled the gap in east Birmingham is, precisely as he would have predicted, traditional and charismatic authority—the mosque, the elder, the man everyone knows.

But the century's contribution to political economy may be simpler. Marx asked who owns the means of production. Britain has spent a month establishing that there is a prior question, which nobody thought to ask because the answer had been stable since 1538 and the parish church registers; who owns the means of verification? Britain gave the answer away to a single piece of software, at a medium assurance level, on a certificate due to expire in October, and has not yet been told when it might get it back.

Your correspondent will return when there is a means of proving she is entitled to. ■

text:
Two things.

The Clippers are not the Bulls.
Second, look at the Lakers if they had a first. They’re operating as a cap team, so turning a contract like DJJ’s into a player with full Bird rights is extremely valuable.

Yes, the Lakers could technically offer him something next summer. But now you’re taking the risk of either getting outbid - unlikely - or him being convinced to go somewhere else for the same money.

That’s why the Clippers asking for at least a protected first for DJJ should be the goal. You’re not just trading a contract. You’re trading control over a player you can retain with Bird rights.

text:
Dear Sir Paul, @PaulMcCartney
I have enclosed a link to a video of my three grandchildren acting out your song, Rocky Raccoon. https://t.co/fRrLih898I
My name is Dawn. I am a grandmother in Connecticut, and your music has been part of my life since I was young. I admire that family has remained at the heart of your life.
Since my grandchildren enjoy your songs, I thought it would be fun to have them act out “Rocky Raccoon.” I bought the costumes and helped them with the scenes. Rocky, my daughter’s son, Jack is seven. Lil/Nancy is six, and Dan is four — they are my son’s children, Alexis and Ryan. Watching them, I felt that quiet joy that comes when something you have loved for decades suddenly belongs to the next generation.
It is a small family moment, offered with gratitude. Your song brought three little ones together under one roof, and it would mean a great deal to know it reached you.
Thank you for the music, and for the example of a life that has always made room for family.
With warmest regards,
Dawn Daly (DawnEstella@yahoo.com)

text:
Xi Jinping just completed a state visit to #Egypt, commemorating the 70th anniversary of bilateral diplomatic relations.
#China and Egypt have a "comprehensive strategic partnership" which, over the past three decades has expanded from foundational diplomacy and basic trade into advanced infrastructure, technology, and military cooperation.
China has embedded its economic interests within Egypt, particularly around the Suez Canal, utilizing the country as a strategic logistics and production hub that connects Chinese supply chains to European, African, and Middle Eastern markets. Egypt is a key partner in the Belt and Road Initiative.
Recent bilateral agreements have reinforced this economic integration, including the extension of zero-tariff for Egyptian goods, substantial Chinese FDI (estimated at up to US$2 billion in the first half of 2026), and collaboration in artificial intelligence and digital infrastructure.

A defining feature of this deepening partnership is the increasing alignment of China’s economic footprint with its expanding military reach, a transition vividly illustrated by the "Eagles of Civilization 2026" air force joint exercise that was completed just a few weeks before Xi's visit to Egypt.

This deployment represents a substantial escalation in the scale, complexity, and power projection of Chinese military engagements in Africa.

The movement of an integrated combat package, comprising Shenyang J-16 fighters, YU-20  refueling air tankers, and KJ-500 airborne early-warning and control (AEW&C) aircraft, demonstrated the PLA's Air Force’s capacity to project and sustain combat power over intercontinental distances.

Notably, the exercise featured direct tactical engagements between Chinese J-16s and French-supplied Egyptian Rafales, providing the PLA with valuable insights into Western combat systems.

This progression from the symbolic, low-intensity drills characteristic of the early 2000s, through the anti-piracy missions of the 2010s, to the current era of high-tempo, realistic war-fighting scenarios, reflects a deliberate shift in China’s African military strategy.

For Cairo, this expanding Chinese military and technological presence offers a needed strategic counterweight to Western partnerships, the US and France, but also Russia.
Egypt has maintained a diversified portfolio of defense and diplomatic relations, continuing to receive over USD 1 billion annually in US military assistance while simultaneously cultivating ties with Russia, European powers, and the BRICS grouping.
Russia delivered 46 MiG-29M fighter jets to Cairo between 2017 and 2021 (although Cairo wanted to purchase Su-30s).
But, facing US pressure (CAATSA, which obligates the imposition of U.S. sanctions against any country that makes large arms acquisitions from Russian defense companies), which protect the regional military superiority of Israel, Egypt gave up a subsequent USD 2 billion deal to buy Su-35 fighters in 2018, and replaced some of its order with French Rafales.

By engaging with Chinese military suppliers and participating in advanced joint exercises, Egypt enhances its bargaining power, securing alternative procurement channels and technological access without totally alienating Western "allies".
This dynamic allows many middle powers (such as Turkey, Indonesia, etc.) to navigate great power competition, extracting investment and diplomatic leverage while resisting unilateral pressure.

Egypt sometimes distancing itself from certain US-led military initiatives in the Red Sea (the infamous "Coalition of the Willing"), despite the severe economic repercussions of a 61% decline in Suez Canal revenues due to shipping diversions, illustrates Cairo’s willingness to assert strategic autonomy by leveraging its multiple international partnerships.

The ramifications of this evolving Sino-Egyptian military cooperation extend across the African continent, and give other African states food-for-thought as far as strategic dependency and regional non-alignment are concerned.

While many African states view Chinese military engagement as a means to diversify procurement, and professionalize their armed forces, some African scholars warn that the power asymmetry often allows Beijing to dictate exercise design and operational agendas. The focus of recent drills, such as the BRICS+ "Will for Peace 2026" naval exercises and the "Peace Unity 2024" ground operations, on high-intensity, conventional war-fighting scenarios could be seen as diverging from the typical intra-state security threats predominantly faced by African nations.

While Beijing actively markets platforms such as the J-10C fighter (whose combat credentials were recently highlighted in the conflict involving Pakistani J-10C and Indian Rafales), the J-16, and its J-35 stealth aircraft, the actualization of such deals remains constrained by the threat of secondary sanctions by the US.
The introduction of advanced Chinese weaponry into the Egyptian inventory would provoke security concerns in Washington and Paris, potentially triggering Countering America’s Adversaries Through Sanctions Act (CAATSA, the same measure that foiled Egypt's attempt to acquire Su-35 from Russia), and jeopardizing decades of US-Egyptian military cooperation.
The J-16 (a Su-30 derivative) despite its prominent role in last month's joint exercise, is unlikely to be exported due to Russian licensing restrictions on it, rendering its presence in Egypt purely demonstrative.

Nevertheless, the existing operational presence of Chinese HQ-9B surface-to-air missile systems in Egypt's Sinai Peninsula indicates that Beijing is successfully positioning itself as a viable, high-end alternative to Russian and Western defense suppliers, and as a reliable and non-ideological security partner.

Between low-Earth orbit satellite constellations tracking movement, high-altitude drones, thermal imaging, and digital mapping, a physical hideout no longer offers true invisibility from a centralized system. If a system decides to look, the technology ensures there is nowhere on Earth to physically run away.

•Tangible Skills: Knowing how to fix things, grow food, or administer first aid.

•Community Trusts: Building tight-knit, face-to-face relationships with people you trust implicitly. A satellite can track a meeting, but it cannot track genuine human loyalty and mutual aid.

•If you spend your day consuming algorithmic media that keeps you in a state of constant panic, anger, or division, the system has successfully logged into your consciousness.
•True "off-grid" living in 2026 means reclaiming control of your internal frequency. It is the ability to look directly at a chaotic, rigged world, understand exactly how it works, and still choose internal peace and neutrality.
The satellites can map your house, but they cannot map your spirit, your thoughts, or your refusal to be psychologically controlled. That inner sanctuary is the one place the matrix can never truly conquer unless you willingly hand over the keys.
When you realize that physical hiding is impossible, does that make you feel trapped, or does it shift your focus toward mastering your internal peace as the ultimate form of rebellion?

FACT: When a person purchases a home (condos/co-ops excluded) the land it sits on is included in the purchase price aka sale/mortgage. A person then makes monthly payments to a mortgage company over a period of 30 years and/or until loan is paid off. Once the debt is satisfied, one would think the home is owned free and clear, right? Wrong! 

Even after a senior has finally paid off his/her mortgage, they still don't own the home free and clear. The state has put a ball and chain around their necks in the form of property taxes that go for the rest of their lives. At any given time, if they fall behind on those taxes, the state will swoop in and confiscate (legal seizure/theft of property) the home that one has title to.

Reality: 
Most seniors depend on Social Security in order to survive and what little increase the government gives them is sucked away by increasing cost of food, fuel, utilities, insurance, medical and property taxes. 

Note: 
If one actually checks to see where property taxes go, they will note that the majority of that tax is applied to public schools in their county. When was the last time a senior had a child (if any) attending school? One would think that they paid their dues (fair share) long ago. 

Examples:
A. If a senior's spouse passes away, there are no longer two Social Security checks coming in to pay funeral expenses, run the household and pay bills. If the surviving spouse falls behind in his/her property taxes the state will swoop in and foreclose on the home. 

B. If a senior becomes ill and needs hospitalization
resulting in the need for ongoing medications (huge medical bills) causing the senior to fall behind in their property taxes, the state will swoop in and foreclose on their home. 

Bottom line: 
A senior has worked his/her entire life (30 years or more) to pay off their mortgage, and they still don't own their home free and clear because of state property taxes. The state basically has ghost ownership of a senior's property and is waiting in the wings to take ownership at any given time or occurrence. Does anyone think this is fair? I think it's a legal form of corruption and theft.

PS: Don't buy into that BS where some states offer a senior tax freeze. They are still obliged to pay ever increasing property taxes each year and what they receive in return (freeze) from the state is crumbs.  The most unconscionable thing a state can do is to continue to place the burden of property taxes on a senior citizen's back.

text:
Am Sonntag wählen knapp 1,7 Millionen Wahlberechtigte in Sachsen-Anhalt den neuen Landtag. Die Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) um Spitzenkandidat Ulrich Siegmund liegt mit weit über 40 Prozent der Stimmen in Umfragen deutlich vorn. Ob es für eine absolute Mehrheit reicht, ist allerdings noch nicht sicher. Die AfD-Bundessprecher Tino Chrupalla und Alice Weidel erklären deshalb zum Wahl-Endspurt:

„In Sachsen-Anhalt geht es um die Zukunft Deutschlands. Die AfD hat ein klares Ziel für den Wahlsieg formuliert: Sie möchte geltendes Recht – beispielsweise mit Blick auf illegale Migration – durchsetzen und dafür sorgen, dass Deutschland lebenswert bleibt. Die anderen Parteien haben die Fehler der vergangenen Jahre beispielsweise auch mit Blick auf Energiewende und Bildungspolitik nicht korrigiert und zeigen wenig Interesse an einem echten Kurswechsel.

Entsprechend ist eine absolute Mehrheit für Ulrich Siegmund und die AfD fast die einzige Chance, das Ruder doch noch herumzureißen. Wir glauben fest daran, dass diese absolute Mehrheit möglich ist. Um sicherzustellen, dass dafür alles rechtlich einwandfrei abläuft, bitten wir alle Demokraten in Sachsen-Anhalt und in den angrenzenden Bundesländern, sich am Sonntag als Wahlbeobachter in einem Wahllokal und während der Auszählung der Stimmen einzubringen.

Wer über entsprechende Kontakte verfügt, kann ältere oder körperlich beeinträchtigte Menschen gern ins Wahllokal bringen, um sicherzustellen, dass sie dort frei und geheim wählen können. 

Wir hoffen darauf, dass es im Endspurt des Wahlkampfs, am Wahltag selbst und in der Zeit danach in Sachsen-Anhalt, Berlin und Deutschland insgesamt friedlich bleibt. Wir danken schon heute der Polizei für ihren Einsatz für unser Land und den unzähligen Wahlhelfern und Beobachtern für ihre so wichtige Arbeit für unsere Demokratie.“

He made $6.2 billion and never had a losing year for 30 years in a row, with an average return of 30%: the legendary Stanley Druckenmiller revealed the secret 99% of traders don't tell you

In a landmark speech to USC Marshall students, George Soros's former right-hand man harshly smashed the crowd mentality and explained why retail speculators are doomed to lose their deposits.

The key lessons from the Wall Street legend:

Don't worry about winning percentages-it's the math that matters: The crowd is chasing pretty statistics on their trades. But the market doesn't care how many times you're right. Only one thing matters: how much money you make when you're right, and how much you lose when you're wrong.

See a perfect opportunity? Put the pedal to the metal: When Druckenmiller shorted the British pound for $1 billion, Soros laughed and replied, "You call that a position? Go for $5 billion." If the market offers a rock-solid setup, squandering your capital in pennies is a crime against your deposit.

Kill your ego and slaughter your losers mercilessly: What separates great traders from losers is their ability to immediately close losing trades. If the market goes against your logic, get out. Hope is the most expensive vice in the stock market.

The deadly sin of the retail investor: 99% of small players take a paltry $100 profit, but sit out a $10,000 drawdown for months, hoping for a reversal until they get a margin call.

text:
Paths forward for states with NGRI defenses. 

Per Grok:

The four states that have abolished the traditional not guilty by reason of insanity defense are Montana , Idaho , Utah , and Kansas . Instead of letting someone walk free if they prove they didn’t know right from wrong due to mental illness, these states only let mental health evidence show the person lacked the specific intent or knowledge required for the crime — basically a narrow mens rea defense. 

Montana went first in 1979, driven by distrust of psychiatrists. The bill’s sponsor called them unscientific and said they made arbitrary and God-like determinations that should be kept out of courtrooms. Idaho and Utah followed right after John Hinckley’s 1982 acquittal for shooting Reagan — public outrage pushed them to scrap the defense in ‘82 and ‘83. Kansas did it in 1995, partly to cut down on confusing expert battles at trial. The Supreme Court backed this approach in 2020’s Kahler v. Kansas ruling, saying states don’t have to offer a full moral blameworthiness test — they can decide how to handle mental illness themselves. 

Three of them — Idaho, Montana, and Utah — also have guilty but mentally ill verdicts, which means the person still gets convicted and serves prison time but might get some treatment. Kansas is stricter and doesn’t offer that option. It’s a much tougher road for defendants than what Massachusetts gives.
