Veterans, before your next VA appointment, check your phone and inbox. You may receive a secure link from VA, via BHL-Screener, to complete a health questionnaire.  

The BHL-Screener, formally e-screening, streamlines the collection and processing of Clinical Reminder questionnaires by automating Veteran outreach, response capture, CPRS Progress Note generation, and when applicable, completion of the Clinical Reminder. It reduces staff workload, minimizes variability in how questions are asked, and enables Veterans to complete important screenings before their appointments, thereby giving their primary care physician a more complete picture of the Veteran’s medical issues.

BHL Touch, a VA-approved web-based tool supporting measurement-based mental health care, now offers a new mode for Veterans to complete assessments anytime using their own device, in addition to traditional iPad entry in the office. This allows Veterans to receive and answer questions in advance of appointments, increasing the time they have with their primary care physician and reducing the time Veterans spend filling out paperwork when they arrive for their appointment. 
This new feature allows providers to text or email a secure link to a Veteran for convenient completion from anywhere. When the requested assessments are completed, the provider is immediately notified via email, and they can then review the results, track the patient’s progress over time, and seamlessly upload them to the electronic health record.

The benefits of this technology include:
•expanded implementation of MBC

increased overall patient and provider satisfaction

text:
Electric-vehicle major Tesla Inc. has started offering Cybercab rides in limited areas of Austin, Texas. The two-seater vehicle comes without a steering wheel or pedals.

The exclusive Cybercab launch event was conducted in Austin on Thursday for the golden, butterfly-door cars. In the event, which was attended by investors, potential customers and social media personalities, the executives detailed on dynamic pricing plans, which would rise with demand, along with its manufacturing and technology.

Meanwhile, U.S. auto safety agency, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, reportedly responded that it is in contact with Tesla and is evaluating the situation. As per federal safety rules, vehicles require human controls, and and sales of vehicles without a steering wheel and pedals are limited. Meanwhile, established manufacturers are allowed to deploy an unlimited number of such vehicles for testing.

Tesla founder and CEO Elon Musk has called the vehicle the first car that is specifically built for unsupervised full self-driving.

Cybercab is considered a key to transforming Tesla ?into a dominant force in driverless vehicles, and that eventually, it will be Tesla's largest-volume vehicle, supplying a global network of robotaxis.

The development comes as Tesla's core EV business faces pressure from global competition, mainly Chinese EV makers.

According to Musk, expanding the robotaxi service and wider adoption of its full self-driving software is key to Tesla's growth strategy.

Tesla has a limited robotaxi ride-hailing service with a network of autonomous Model Ys. Over time, the company plans to make the no-steering-wheel Cybercab the main driverless vehicle model operating within a larger robotaxi network.

The company launched a pilot robotaxi service in Austin in June 2025, and since then has expanded it into certain other cities. Tesla currently offers driverless rides in several U.S. cities, including Austin, Dallas, Houston, Miami, Orlando and Tampa.

Tesla reportedly has 420 autonomous vehicles registered in Texas as of Wednesday evening, including 45 Cybercab vehicles.

Alphabet's Waymo, Tesla's rival in the autonomous driverless taxis, has 988 vehicles registered in the state. https://t.co/X6LiaX2dT7

text:
Chief Leatherlips Monument, an 11-foot-tall limestone sculpture of a Native American leader created by artist Ralph Helmick in 1990. Built out of stacked dry-laid limestone blocks, the sphinx-like face emerges from a grassy hillside; located at Scioto Park in Dublin, Ohio, on the banks of the Scioto River. Dublin holds a Leatherlips ceremony some years.

Leatherlips was a Wyandot chief executed by his own people in 1810, and his story is more complicated than the monument suggests. His Wyandot name was Shateyaronyah. The English name came from his reputation for keeping his word, the idea being that his lips were as good as leather.

He signed the Treaty of Greenville in 1795, which ceded most of Ohio after the defeat at Fallen Timbers. He continued to favor accommodation with American settlers through the following years, living along the Scioto River near what is now Dublin.

That position put him in direct conflict with Tecumseh and his brother Tenskwatawa, the Prophet, who were building a pan-tribal confederacy to resist further land cessions. The Prophet's movement also included a campaign against those accused of witchcraft, which in practice targeted Native leaders who cooperated with the Americans.

In June 1810 a party of Wyandot came to Leatherlips, accused him of witchcraft, tried him and sentenced him to death. Settlers who were present tried to intervene and offered payment. It was refused. Leatherlips ate a meal, painted himself, sang his death song, knelt and prayed, and was killed with a tomahawk.

Whether the charge was genuinely about witchcraft or was political cover for eliminating a signer of Greenville is the question historians raise, and there is no clean answer.

text:
Rosamund Pike says she was trapped on a remote island in Vietnam during 9/11 and didn't learn about it until 3 days after

"The Beach, had just come out, and everybody was obsessed with it, and a film had been made with Leonardo DiCaprio, and everybody who was traveling in Southeast Asia at that point was in search of the beach"

"And it didn't really occur to any young person at that time that it was highly unlikely you would be able to find an undiscovered beach as in the novel."

"So we, armed with maps, because there was no Google Maps at the time, were scouring maps of the country, the coast, looking for places you might be able to access that weren't on the normal routes."

"So anyway, we got to some area outside of Hanoi, and we got on what seemed to be a sort of supply boat, everyone communicating in sign language a lot, and we got on this supply boat going to an island, which was the island we were aiming for."

"And when we got to this island, people welcomed us. They clearly were not used to tourists. We traveled a bit further inland, and a family were very, very welcoming and offered us to stay. We went out walking, trying to find the beach."

"Anyway, we came back, we had a lovely meal with his family, and we paid them for our bed and board. And then other members of the village clearly got wind of the fact that there were these tourists here who had dollars, and we suddenly found that it was quite difficult to leave."

"And the rides that were so easy to get from the place where the boat came in were suddenly not forthcoming when we wanted to go back."

"And we thought, 'Oh my goodness, we're actually kind of trapped here in a way.' And so, very early one morning, we made a pact with each other to walk back in the direction we thought the port was."

"And we made it, and we just sat there to wait. But we'd had no idea when a boat would come. Anyway, a boat came, we got on the boat, we realized we'd been very stupid, very, very stupid."

"We got back to Hanoi, and we went to a restaurant to just sort of unwind, have a beer, have some rice. And there on the TV in the restaurant was a movie of this plane coming into New York City and crashing into the Twin Towers."

"And of course, we then saw that it wasn't a movie. It was the news, but also that this was sort of three-day-old news."

"So we were probably in one of the only places in the world where we didn't know that that monumental human disaster had occurred, which was a very, very weird feeling."

text:
Regular Dysfunction On the First of the Month 

Bike Lanes, Open Air Drugs, Stolen Puppies, Homicide, Mental Health Crisis and Abandoned Streets

@drkugler https://t.co/MPWurl9uLk® 
Street Report Sept 3, 2026

Seven hours on Chicago streets produced more than a collection of unrelated police calls.

Starting near the University of Illinois Health Campus and continuing through downtown, Stony Island, 79th Street and King Drive, the September 3 reporting ride documented sharply different versions of Chicago operating on the same night.

Luxury development was moving forward. Hospital towers were being planned. Thousands headed toward Soldier Field for the Ye concert.

Only blocks away, open air drug activity, stolen cars, a homicide, people in crisis, shuttered businesses and abandoned buildings were part of everyday street life.

UIC Health Campus: Where Are the Bikes?

Rush hour near the University of Illinois Health Campus provided the first street-level test of Chicago's expanding bicycle infrastructure.

Only three cyclists were observed during the reporting window despite being inside a major university and medical district at one of the busiest transportation periods of the day.

Chicago has committed roadway and public space to bicycle infrastructure as part of its transportation strategy.

Street-level use observed during the ride told a different story.

Where were the bicycles?

More importantly, does actual daily use justify the amount of public roadway committed to the system?

K2 Development: Tents and Open Air Drug Activity

Conditions near the K2 development at Halsted appeared considerably worse than during previous visits.

What had previously looked like roughly five or six tents had grown into what appeared to be approximately 20 tents or structures.

Visible drug use and dealing surrounded the encampment.

Calling the location simply a homeless camp misses what was happening on the street. Homelessness, addiction and an open air drug economy were occupying the same public space.

Government's failure was not the existence of tents.

Allowing criminal activity and addiction to become normalized around them was the larger problem visible during the ride.

Mayor's Detail Passes Lower South Water Drug Activity

Lower South Water provided another example.

Groups gathered around convenience stores, smoke shops and nearby businesses while open air drug activity continued downtown.

Mayor Brandon Johnson's security detail passed through the area during the reporting ride.

Nothing visibly changed.

Nobody needs to claim the mayor personally witnessed a particular transaction to understand the significance of the scene.

Drug activity was operating within the same downtown environment traveled by the mayor, workers, residents and tourists.

It was not hidden miles from City Hall.

Auto Thefts and Carjacking Traffic Stack Up

Police radio kept returning to stolen vehicles.

One car disappeared from 33 W. Delaware with a Pomeranian still inside.

Tracking information later placed a gray 2018 Audi Q5 carrying the dog westbound on I-290.

More stolen-vehicle traffic followed: a tan Nissan Sentra, an older woman's van, a Hyundai Genesis, a PT Cruiser and a gray Hyundai SUV.

By the middle of the ride, approximately five or six stolen vehicles had crossed the radio traffic.

Having a dog trapped inside one of those vehicles transformed an ordinary auto-theft broadcast into something more personal.

Someone's pet was moving through Chicago's expressway system inside a stolen car while police tried to follow electronic location updates.

Shooting on Stony Island

Then came the shooting call.

Police radio broadcast a person shot near 73rd and Stony Island, originally placing the incident at a Boost Mobile location.

One caller reported her brother had been shot.

Dispatchers soon classified the shooting as bona fide and broadcast information describing a female offender reportedly wearing no shirt who fled through an alley behind the businesses.

Stony Island became the next destination.

Officers searched around the laundromat and surrounding alleys while a helicopter worked overhead.

Homicide at 73rd and Stony Island

What began as a person-shot call became a homicide investigation outside Total Wireless in the strip mall on the west side of Stony Island near 73rd Street.

37-year-old man was in front of the commercial business when an unknown female approached, produced a handgun and fired.

Gunfire struck him in the chest. He was transported to the University of Chicago Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead.

Police tape stretched across the strip mall as detectives processed the homicide scene. 

Shooting disrupted the surrounding businesses, including the laundromat, restaurants and other storefronts sharing the shopping center.

Delivery drivers and customers arriving for businesses suddenly found themselves facing a homicide scene.

One person was killed, but the disruption spread across an entire strip mall.

Workers lost customers.

Delivery drivers lost orders.

Businesses were effectively cut off while police processed the scene.

One homicide became an economic event for every business surrounding it.

Nobody approaching the strip mall necessarily knew what they were walking into.

Gig workers following delivery apps were still being routed toward businesses inside or alongside an active homicide scene.

Customers arriving for food or other services encountered police tape, detectives and a murder investigation with little warning.

Violence does not stop with the victim or the police report. Everyone working, shopping or simply passing through the surrounding commercial area gets pulled into its aftermath.

Police Process the Scene

Nearly a dozen officers, detectives and technicians could be seen working around the homicide scene.

Evidence markers appeared near the business while investigators processed the area.

Watching that manpower concentrated at a static scene raised an immediate question during the live report: who was actively looking for the shooter?

Businesses surrounding the scene had cameras.

City surveillance infrastructure covered the area.

Police already had an offender description and reported direction of flight.

Crime-scene processing matters, but residents watching from the sidewalk also want to see urgency directed toward finding whoever pulled the trigger.

Walk In Gunshot Victim

Another shooting entered the radio traffic while detectives remained on Stony Island.

University of Chicago Medical Center reported a 23-year-old walk-in victim suffering from a gunshot wound to the right foot.

Police did not know where that shooting occurred.

No confirmed connection between the walk-in victim and the Stony Island homicide was established during the ride.

Without evidence connecting them, they remain separate incidents.

Leone Beach Park Life Preserver Call

Farther north, police received an unusual call from Leon Beach Park.

Man reportedly broke glass, took a life preserver and began playing with it on the beach.

Behavior described over the radio appeared consistent with someone experiencing a mental-health crisis.

Calls like it place police and emergency personnel in situations that sit somewhere between criminal conduct, addiction and untreated mental illness.

Later that night, a much more serious example unfolded directly in front of the reporting ride.

79th and Stony: Woman in Apparent Crisis

Near White Castle at 79th and Stony Island, a woman was outside partially or completely naked, screaming, yelling and behaving erratically.

Drug-induced psychosis or a serious mental-health crisis appeared possible.

911 call went out at 8:04 p.m.

Dispatch was specifically told that no weapon was visible and that the woman appeared to need medical assistance.

Rather than leave, the reporting ride remained nearby to document the response and make sure someone stayed aware of what was happening to her.

Fire and EMS reached the location first.

Still moving around the property, the woman eventually ran inside White Castle.

Ambulance 71 and Engine 34 became involved.

What followed illustrated the fragmentation of Chicago's crisis-response system.

One person was moving between public space and a private business while separate emergency agencies arrived at different times and attempted to respond to the same evolving situation.

Police reached the location around 8:39 p.m.

Roughly 35 minutes had passed since the original 8:04 p.m. call.

Eventually, responders restrained and transported the woman.

Documenting her crisis was never about ridiculing someone at one of the lowest moments of her life.

Response time and coordination were the story.

Chicago has spent years discussing alternative crisis response. 

Street-level reality that night still involved fire, EMS and police arriving separately while an obvious crisis continued unfolding in a heavily traveled commercial area.

79th Street: The Economic Divide

Driving west along 79th Street changed the story again.

Closed stores appeared one after another.

Dark commercial strips.

Abandoned buildings.

Shuttered Walgreens.

Vacant storefronts.

Long stretches offered almost no meaningful nighttime commercial activity.

Near 79th and Jeffrey, one of Chicago's major South Side corridors looked less like part of America's third-largest city and more like a commercial district being allowed to disappear.

Years of political promises have centered on neighborhood investment and equity.

Street conditions offered their own measurement.

New Towers Rise Elsewhere

Meanwhile, billions of dollars in development continue moving elsewhere in Chicago.

Northwestern Medicine is planning a 24-story hospital tower in Streeterville, including inpatient floors, underground parking and major support infrastructure.

Construction is also moving forward at the former Chicago Spire site at 400 Lake Shore Drive.

Investment clearly has not abandoned Chicago.

Its distribution is the question.

While cranes and major projects reshape some of the city's most valuable neighborhoods, stretches of 79th Street remain dark and boarded.

$882 Million Budget Shortfall

Hovering over those contrasts is Chicago's projected $882 million budget shortfall.

Residents are again entering a budget cycle in which government will debate revenue, spending and potentially new ways of closing the gap.

Numbers on a city spreadsheet mean something very different from the driver's seat on 79th Street.

There, municipal economics look like empty buildings, disappearing retailers, deteriorating property and commercial blocks with almost nowhere left to spend money.

Interstate Crime on the Radio

Radio traffic became a second soundtrack to the ride.

Stolen cars moved onto expressways.

Police tracked the vehicle carrying the stolen puppy.

Marine units received a distress call near Granville and Sheridan.

Burglary calls followed.

Someone reportedly used tools to break into a Divvy bicycle.

Elsewhere, dispatchers broadcast a battery involving a woman reportedly being held in a headlock.

Calls kept stacking while officers were simultaneously assigned to routine patrols, emergencies and major events.

Ye Concert: The Other Chicago

Soldier Field offered perhaps the night's clearest contrast.

Ye, formerly Kanye West, was performing as thousands of concertgoers traveled downtown and along the lakefront.

Police units were assigned to the event.

Visitors dressed for a major entertainment night moved through a downtown where homelessness and drug activity remained visible only blocks away.

Chicago can host a massive concert, move thousands of visitors and generate enormous economic activity in a matter of hours.

Travel several miles south and entire commercial corridors struggle to remain alive after dark.

Both Chicagos existed simultaneously.

Downtown Walgreens Theft

Later, police radio carried a theft call from a Walgreens on State Street.

People were reportedly placing stolen merchandise into a stroller.

One retail theft is hardly an economic trend.

Repeated theft, however, becomes part of the calculation retailers make about security, operating hours, inventory and whether maintaining a location remains worthwhile.

Freight Train Theft

Near 2608 Gladys, another report involved people stealing from freight trains.

Property crime during the ride was no longer limited to automobiles or retail stores.

Freight infrastructure had entered the night's running ledger as well.

Men With Weapons Near Cars

Kingsbury produced another call.

Males with weapons were reportedly attempting to break into vehicles.

Hours of auto-theft and carjacking traffic had already preceded it.

Geography changed repeatedly.

Property crime did not.

Pretrial Release and the Court System

Crime policy does not end when someone is arrested.

During the ride, I discussed my own ongoing dispute with the pretrial release system.

Pretrial release officer represented in court that I had failed to make required contact. 

My notes and written documentation show otherwise.

The experience raises another part of Chicago’s public safety system rarely visible from a crime scene.

Police make arrests.

Prosecutors, courts, supervision agencies and pretrial services determine much of what follows.

Accountability has to apply to every part of that system, including the people responsible for supervising defendants and providing information to the court.

CHA Fence and Former Migrant Housing

Near the 6100 block of South King Drive, headlights illuminated a different kind of abandonment.

Boarded doors and windows sat behind fencing. Weeds had pushed through the property. Buildings once used for migrant housing stood largely empty.

Earlier reporting from the location documented claims that Black residents had been pushed out before the property was used to house migrants.

Now the migrants were gone too.

Fresh fencing around nearby CHA land raised a new question: what comes next?

Vacant public land generally does not get fenced without a reason.

Whether redevelopment, disposition or another CHA plan is coming remains unknown.

What could be documented from the street was simpler.

People had lived there.
People were moved.
Migrants later lived there.

Now buildings were boarded and the property was abandoned.

Ride Ends

Seven hours earlier, the reporting began beside bicycle lanes near a major medical campus.

Before the night ended, open air drug activity downtown had entered the reporting.

Stolen vehicles repeatedly crossed police radio.

Gunfire brought the ride to a homicide scene at 73rd and Stony Island.

Crisis response became the focus at 79th and Stony as a woman waited for help.

Farther west, 79th Street revealed a hollowed-out commercial corridor.

King Drive provided the final contrast: boarded former migrant housing sitting abandoned behind fencing.

Luxury towers were rising.
Hospital expansion was coming.
Thousands were attending a concert.

Elsewhere, police tape surrounded businesses, naked women in distress and weeds grew outside abandoned apartments.

September 3, 2026 was not one story.

It was one ride through several different Chicagos.

text:
Today is the feast of Moses, a grandson of Levi raised in Pharaoh's Palace. Moses had access to all the treasures and power of Egypt and yet he "regarded disgrace for the sake of Christ as of greater value than the treasures of Egypt, because he was looking ahead to his reward." 

He spent 40 years as a humble shepherd until Jesus appeared to him in a burning bush, declaring "I AM, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob". Moses and his brother Aaron initiated the Ten Plagues and many Egyptians joined the Israelites in the Exodus, as Moses sought to save all who would believe.

The Lord parted the Red Sea, delivering His people and destroying Pharaoh's army. At Mt. Horeb, God the Father descended to give Moses the Ten Commandments and the Law, revealing His Form but not His Face to Moses in a way He did to none other.

So Christlike did Moses become that he offered to be blotted out of God's book for the sake of his people. He humbly knew his role was to foreshadow a coming Prophet like himself. As he neared death, God took him to Mt. Nebo to see the Promised Land before secretly burying him, a fitting end for a prophet whose entire life was in foreseen imitation of our Saviour.

ℭ𝔬𝔩𝔩𝔢𝔠𝔱
Almighty God, whose servant Moses Thy faithful prophet led Thy people Israel from bondage in Egypt through the wilderness to the borders of the Promised Land, and who gave them Thy law to be a schoolmaster to bring them unto Christ: Grant that we, walking in the path of faith and obedience, may be delivered from the slavery of sin, guided by Thy law written in our hearts and brought at last into the land of everlasting life; through the same Jesus Christ our Lord, who is the Prophet greater than Moses, the true Deliverer of Thy people, and who with Thee and the Holy Spirit liveth and reigneth, one God, world without end. ᴀᴍᴇɴ.
